children.text: śrīmadvidyācakravartiviracitā sañjīvanyākhyā vyākhyā viśvaṃ prakāśayati yā jātiguṇādyātmakaiḥ nijaiḥ prasaraiḥ /
children.translated_text: The commentary called <s>Sañjīvanī</s>, composed by the illustrious <s>Vidyācakravartin</s>, illuminates the universe through its own extensions in the form of <s>jāti</s> (universal), <s>guṇa</s> (quality), and the like.
May the speech (<s>Vāṇī</s>) that is enriched by the qualities of refinement, of straightforward composition, protect me.
Upon this <s>Alaṅkārasarvasva</s>, originated by the teacher <s>Rucaka</s> (i.e. <s>Ruyyaka</s>),
a commentary called <s>Sañjīvanī</s> is composed by the illustrious <s>Vidyācakravartin</s>.
The remainder of examples here, not provided by the author of the work in the section on <s>Dhvani</s> (suggestion),
I shall fill with my own verses, composed in accordance with his principles.
O poets of discernment, who are devoted to the doctrine of <s>Dhvani</s>, having examined my commentary with subtle vision,
even though you are already conscious, extend the empire of literature (<s>sāhitya</s>).

children.text: kiṃ vistareṇa bahunā ṭīkāṃ sañjīvanīmimāṃ kaścit /
children.translated_text: What need of lengthy elaboration? If any dull person finds fault with this <s>Sañjīvanī</s> commentary,
he finds fault with his own learning.

body.text: tatra tāvadadhikṛteṣṭadevatānamaskāra puraskāreṇa prakaraṇapratipādyamarthaṃ pratijānīte namaskṛtya paramiti /
body.translated_text: There, first, with the preliminary obeisance to the chosen deity (<s>iṣṭadevatā</s>), he declares the subject matter to be expounded in the treatise, beginning with '<s>namaskṛtya param</s>' (having bowed to the Supreme).

body.text:
sarvaiva khalviyaṃ vāk parā paśyantī madhyamā vaikharīti caturbhiḥ padaiḥ parimīyate /
yacchutiḥ - "catvāri vākparimitā padāni"ityādikā /
tatra parā nāma nirupadhikaṃ rūpam /
paśyantyādīni trīṇi punaraupādhikāni sthūlatvāt vigrahasthānīyāni /

children.translated_text: As the scriptural tradition states—
<s>Parā</s> speech is the inner light of one's own nature, imperishable,
in which, when its true nature is perceived, the threefold domain ceases.

body.translated_text: All speech indeed is measured by four stages: <s>Parā</s> (transcendent), <s>Paśyantī</s> (visionary), <s>Madhyamā</s> (intermediate), and <s>Vaikharī</s> (articulate). As the Vedic text says: 'Speech is measured in four stages' and so forth. Among these, <s>Parā</s> is the unconditioned form. The three beginning with <s>Paśyantī</s> are conditioned, and being gross, they serve as the analyzed counterparts.

children.translated_text: With letters undifferentiated, with sequence withdrawn from all,
<s>Paśyantī</s>, resting in the vital breath (<s>prāṇa</s>), is like the essence within a peacock's egg.
<s>Madhyamā</s>, taken up by the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), having assumed the form of letters,
is in the form of inner speech and does not reach the ear.
Manifested through the activity of the palate and lips, revealing knowledge to others,
the external speech accessible to all humans is considered <s>Vaikharī</s>.

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text:
tatra paśyantyādya paravāktrayāpekṣayā jyeṣṭhatvādādya parā /
dvitīyā viśvābhimukhībhāvātpaśyantī /
tṛtīyā nābhyantarī na ca bāhyeti kṛtvā madhyamā /
turīyā tuparāvabodhārthaṃ pravṛtteti vaikharī /
yadvā "khaṃ sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ ca; tadviśiṣya rāti dadātīti vikharo dehendriyasaṅghātaḥ tatra bhavā vaikharīti" jñeyam /
tadevābhisandhāyoktam-vācaṃ trividhavigrahāmiti /
caturvidhāmapi /
kīdṛśīṃ devīm? parādibhiścaturbhiḥ padaiḥ krīḍantīṃ nāmapūrvakatvāt sarvasyaiva rūpasya jagadetadvijigīṣamāṇāṃ samastavyavahārātmikāṃ svarūpāvabodhakṣamatayā dyutimayīmanyastutaustotavyatāyāṃ ca prabhavantīmavimarśāndhatamasa dhvaṃsanāt kāntimayīmapratihataprasaratvāt gatyātmikāñcetyarthaḥ /
tāmimāṃ namaskṛtya /
namaskāro hi nāma pṛthagahaṅkāraparityāgena namaskartavyamahimodghāṭanaṃ sāmarasyamiti yāvat /
tathāhi-yeyaṃ parā sā śaktatvam /
yā paśyantī sodyuktatā /
yā tu madhyamā sā pravṛttatā /
yā punarvaikharī sā nirvāhakateti /
śaktimato vaktureva svarūpaṃ parādiśaktayaḥ /
itthamimāṃ vācaṃ namaskṛtya nijānāṃ svenaiva praṇītānām alaṅkārasūtrāṇāṃ tātparyamucyate /
hṛdayamudghāṭyate /
kena prakāreṇa? vṛttyā vṛtti svarūpeṇa sandarbheṇa /
atha dhvanidarśanānusāreṇa prakāraṇaṃ praṇinīṣuḥ bhāmahodbhaṭādīnāṃ darśanasthitiṃ pūrvapakṣatveno panyasyati-iha hi tāvadbhāmahodbhaṭetyādinā /
atreyaṃ darśanasthiti dik /

children.translated_text: <s>Kāvya</s> (poetry) is indeed that whose essence consists of distinguished word and meaning.
Therein, meaning is of two kinds: <s>vācya</s> (denoted) and <s>pratīyamāna</s> (suggested).

children.text: yathā- bhama dhaṃmia vīsattho so suṇāo ajja mārio deṇa /
children.translated_text: For example: 'O virtuous one, that <s>Śunāka</s> is killed today by the enemy,

children.text: golāṇai kaccha kuḍaṅga vāsiṇā daria sīheṇa //
children.translated_text: the one dwelling on the bank of the <s>Godāvarī</s> at <s>Kacchakuḍaṅga</s>, the lion of the forest.'

body.translated_text: Among these, <s>Paśyantī</s> and the others—relative to the three forms of <s>Parā</s> speech, the first is <s>Parā</s> because of its seniority. The second is <s>Paśyantī</s> because of its facing toward the universe. The third is <s>Madhyamā</s> because it is neither internal nor external. The fourth is <s>Vaikharī</s> because it is engaged for the purpose of communicating with others. Alternatively, one should understand: '<s>kha</s> means pleasure and pain; that which gives (<s>rāti</s>) these distinctly is <s>vikhara</s>, the aggregate of body and senses; that which exists in it is <s>Vaikharī</s>.' With this very intention it was stated: 'Speech having a threefold body'—even though it is fourfold. What kind of goddess? One who plays through the four stages beginning with <s>Parā</s>; because all forms are preceded by name, she desires to conquer the world; she embodies all conventional usage; being capable of revealing her own nature, she is radiant; being the source of the praiseworthiness of one praised by others, she is brilliant; dispelling the darkness of blindness of non-reflection, she is luminous; being of unobstructed extension, she is dynamic in nature—such is the meaning. Having bowed to this speech. For obeisance means the opening of the greatness of the object of reverence through the abandonment of the separate ego, resulting in unity (<s>sāmarasya</s>). Thus: what is <s>Parā</s>, that is potentiality (<s>śaktatva</s>); what is <s>Paśyantī</s>, that is readiness (<s>udyuktatā</s>); what is <s>Madhyamā</s>, that is engagement (<s>pravṛttatā</s>); and what is <s>Vaikharī</s>, that is accomplishment (<s>nirvāhakatā</s>). The stages beginning with <s>Parā</s> are the very nature of the capable speaker. Having thus bowed to this speech, the purport of his own <s>alaṅkāra-sūtras</s> (aphorisms on poetic ornamentation), composed by himself, is stated. The heart is opened. By what means? By <s>vṛtti</s>—a composition in the form of a commentary. Now, wishing to propound the treatise following the doctrine of <s>Dhvani</s>, he presents the positions of <s>Bhāmaha</s>, <s>Udbhaṭa</s>, and others as the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prima facie view), beginning with '<s>iha hi tāvad bhāmodbhaṭa</s>' etc. Here is the outline of these doctrinal positions.

body.text:
atra svairiṇyuktau śvabhayanivṛttyā dhārmikabhramaṇāvidhirvācyatvena sthitaḥ, sākṣātsaṅketitatvenā vyavadhāna pratītikatvāt; godāvarītīre siṃhopalabdhyā bhramaṇaniṣedhastu pratīyamānaḥ, vākyārthasamanvayasamanantaramasaṅketitatvena pratīteḥ /
itthaṃ vācyavilakṣiṇaḥ pratīyamāno yor'thaḥ sa yathāyogaṃ rasavastvalaṅkārasvarūpeṇa triskandhaḥ san sacamatkāratvāt kavisaṃrambha gocaratvāt sahṛdayapratīti viśrāntiviṣayatvāñca kāvyātmā /
tasya mādhuryādayo guṇāḥ śauryādivatsamavāyavṛttyā upakurvate /
upamādayaḥ punaḥ kaṭakāditsaṃyogatavṛttyeti dhvanyācāryāḥ /
trividho 'pi pratīyamāno vācyopaskārakatvādalaṅkārakakṣyaivetyanye /
atha granthamavayavaśo vyākurmaḥ /
iha kāvyamārge /
alaṅkārapakṣa nikṣiptaṃ manyante, tattvaṃ punaranyatheti yāvat /
yanmanyante tatsaviśeṣaṃ darśiyitumāha-tathāhītyādinā /
paryāyoktamaprastutapraśaṃsā samāsokti rākṣepaḥ vyājastutirupameyopamā ananvayaḥ ityādiṣu vastumātrameva pratīyate na tu rasālaṅkārau /
vyañjanāvyāpārasyeha lakṣaghaṇāmūlatvāt /
lakṣaṇāmūlatve rasālaṅkārayorvyaṅgyatvāsambhavāt /

children.translated_text: Therein, the expression of a suggested meaning through an alternative mode is <s>paryāyokta</s> (circumlocution).
As he will state: 'The expression of even what is understood, through a different turn, is <s>paryāyokta</s>.'
For example: 'Those flower clusters of the <s>Pārijāta</s> tree, caressed through contact with <s>Śacī</s>'s hair, were touched in <s>Nandana</s> garden
contemptuously by his soldiers.'

body.translated_text: Here, in the speech of a wanton woman, the injunction to wander under the pretext of the cessation of fear of dogs is the <s>vācya</s> (denoted meaning), since the convention is directly and unobstructedly understood. But the prohibition of wandering due to the sighting of a lion on the bank of the <s>Godāvarī</s> is the <s>pratīyamāna</s> (suggested meaning), since it is understood as unconventional, immediately following the syntactic construal of the sentence meaning. Thus, the suggested meaning, which is distinct from the denoted meaning, being of three kinds by its nature as <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion), <s>vastu</s> (subject matter), and <s>alaṅkāra</s> (figure of speech), is the soul of poetry, because it possesses <s>camatkāra</s> (aesthetic wonder), because it falls within the scope of poetic passion, and because it is the resting place of the connoisseur's (<s>sahṛdaya</s>'s) realization. Its qualities such as <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness) and others support it through inherent relation (<s>samavāya</s>), like valor and the like. Figures such as <s>upamā</s> (simile) and others, however, support it through the relation of conjunction, like a bracelet—so say the teachers of <s>Dhvani</s>. Others say that all three kinds of suggested meaning, being subsidiary to the denoted meaning, fall only within the category of <s>alaṅkāra</s>. Now we shall analyze the text part by part. Here, in the path of poetry, they consider [the suggested meaning] as placed within the category of <s>alaṅkāra</s>, but the truth is otherwise—such is the intent. To show specifically what they hold, he says beginning with '<s>tathāhi</s>' etc. In <s>paryāyokta</s> (circumlocution), <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant), <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression), <s>ākṣepa</s> (objection), <s>vyājastuti</s> (ironic praise), <s>upameyopamā</s> (mutual simile), <s>ananvaya</s> (non-correlation), and so forth, only subject matter (<s>vastu</s>) is suggested, not <s>rasa</s> or <s>alaṅkāra</s>—because the operation of suggestion (<s>vyañjanā</s>) here is rooted in <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification). If it is rooted in <s>lakṣaṇā</s>, there is no possibility of <s>rasa</s> and <s>alaṅkāra</s> being suggested.

body.text: atra hayagrīvasya svargavijayaḥ sainikasāvaghajñapārijātamañjarī sparśalakṣaṇena kāryeṇa pratyāyyate /

children.translated_text: When the relevant subject is understood from the irrelevant through the connection of universal-particular and the like, that is <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant).

children.text: yadvakṣyati - "aprastutātsāmānyaviśeṣabhāve kāryakāraṇabhāve sārūpye ca prastutapratītāvaprastutapraśaṃsā" iti /
children.translated_text: As he will state: 'When the relevant is understood from the irrelevant through the relation of universal and particular, cause and effect, or resemblance, that is <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s>.'

children.text: yathā- taṇṇātthiṃ kiṃpi pahaṇo pakappiyaṃ jaṃ ṇa ṇiai gharaṇīe /
children.translated_text: For example: 'There is nothing of the husband that is not prepared, which fate's housewife does not [consume]—
of him whose nature is unceasing travel, the provisions of that time-traveler.'

body.translated_text: Here, <s>Hayagrīva</s>'s conquest of heaven is conveyed through the effect characterized by his soldiers' contemptuous touching of the <s>Pārijāta</s> blossoms.

children.translated_text: 'There is nothing of the husband that is prepared, which fate's housewife does not [take]—
of him whose nature is unceasing travel, the provisions of that time-traveler.'

body.text:
iti cchrāyā] /
atra anavaratagamanaśīlasya patyurnijagṛhiṇyā pātheyatvena yanna kalpitaṃ tadyathā nāsti, tathā kālapathikasya pāthematvena yadakalpitaṃ tannāstītyatra kālaḥsava grasatīti sāmānyarūpādaprastutāt prastuto viśeṣātmā prahastavadhaḥ pratyāyyate /

children.translated_text: When an irrelevant subject is understood due to the similarity of qualifiers, that is <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression).
As he will state: 'When the irrelevant is understood through the similarity of qualifiers, that is <s>samāsokti</s>.'

children.text: yathā- upoḍharāgeṇa vilolatārakaṃ tathā gṛhītaṃ śaśinā niśāmukham /
children.translated_text: For example: 'The face of the night was seized by the moon with heightened passion and trembling stars,

children.text: yathā samastaṃ timirāṃśukaṃ tayā puro 'pi rāgādgalitaṃ na lakṣyitam //
children.translated_text: just as the entire veil of darkness had slipped away from her in passion, yet was not noticed.'

body.translated_text: Thus is the Sanskrit rendering. Here, just as there is nothing that has not been prepared as provisions for the husband whose nature is unceasing travel by his own housewife, so too there is nothing that has not been prepared as provisions for the time-traveler—from the irrelevant, which is in the universal form 'time devours all,' the relevant particular meaning, namely the death of the husband, is conveyed.

body.text: atropoḍharāgatvādinā viśeṣaṇasāmyenāprastuto nāyakavṛttāntaḥ pratīyate /

children.text: uktasya vakṣyamāṇasya vā prākāraṇikasya viśeṣapratītyartham ābhāsato niṣedhanamākṣepaḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>Ākṣepa</s> (objection) is the apparent negation of what has been stated or is about to be stated, which is contextually relevant, for the purpose of conveying a particular emphasis.

children.text: yadvakṣyati uktavakṣyamāṇayoḥ prākaraṇikayorviśeṣapratītyarthaṃ niṣedhābhāsa ākṣepaḥ iti /
children.translated_text: As he will state: 'The apparent negation of what has been stated or is about to be stated, when contextually relevant, for the purpose of conveying a particular emphasis, is <s>ākṣepa</s>.'

children.text: yathā - bālagra!ṇāhaṃ dūri tīe piosit ti ṇāmhavāvāro /
children.translated_text: For example: 'Young man! I am not her messenger, [nor am I saying] "she loves you"—that is not our concern.

children.text: sā marai tujbhpha ayaso eaṃ dhaṃmakkharaṃ bhaṇimo //
children.translated_text: She is dying—this is a virtuous statement we make for the sake of your honor.'

body.translated_text: Here, through the similarity of qualifiers such as 'heightened passion' and the like, the irrelevant narrative of the hero and heroine is suggested.

children.translated_text: 'Young man! I am not her messenger, [nor am I saying] "she loves you"—that is not our concern.
She is dying—this is a virtuous statement we make for the sake of your honor.'

body.text: iti cchrāyā '] atra 'nāhaṃ dītiti' dītitvaniṣedho viśiṣṭāsmi dūtītyavagamayati /

children.translated_text: When through praise and blame, blame and praise respectively are conveyed, that is <s>vyājastuti</s> (ironic praise).
As he will state: 'When through praise and blame, blame and praise respectively are conveyed, that is <s>vyājastuti</s>.'

children.text: yathā - he helājitabodhisattva vacasāṃ kiṃ vistaraistoyadhe! nāsti tvatsadṛśaḥ paraḥ parahitādhāne gṛhītavrataḥ /
children.translated_text: For example: 'O <s>Bodhisattva</s> conquered by mere playfulness! What need for elaborate speeches, O rain cloud! There is no one equal to you, one who has taken a vow for the welfare of others.
Having gained fame through your aversion to helping thirsty travelers on the road, you compassionately assist <s>Maru</s> (the desert) in carrying the burden!'

body.translated_text: Thus is the Sanskrit rendering. Here, the denial of being a messenger—'I am not a messenger'—conveys the understanding that 'I am indeed a distinguished messenger.'

body.text:
atra marorupakāraṃ karoṣīti stutirnindāmavagamayati /
upamānopameyayoḥ paryāyeṇa tathātvaṃ cedupameyopamā /
yadvakṣyati- "dvayoḥ paryāyeṇa tasminnupameyopamā" iti /
yathā-'khamiva jalaṃ jalamiva khaṃ haṃsaśvandra iva haṃsa iva candraḥ' /
atropamānopameyabhāvavinimayaḥ tṛtīya sabrahmacāriṇāṃ nivartayati /
ekasyaivopamānopameya bhāvakatve 'nanvayaḥ /
yadvakṣyati-"ekasyaivopamānopameyatve 'nanvaya" iti /
yathā -'yuddhe 'rjunor'juna iva prathitaprabhāvaḥ'-iti /
atra dvitīyasabrahmacārinivṛttiḥ /
ādi śabdāllāṭānuprāsādi parigrahaḥ /
eṣu paryāyoktāduṣu yadetadvastumātraṃ pratīyate svargavijayādikaṃ rasālaṅkāraparihāreṇa tadidaṃ sarvairapi pramāṇairātmatvenā vabhāsamānameva sadgaja nimīlikayā vācyāpaskārakatvena tairudbhaṭādibhiḥ pratipāditam /
nyagbhāvitavācyasya vācyakakṣyātilaṅghinaḥ kathamastu vācyopaskārakatvamiti bhāvaḥ /
kena prakāreṇa pratipāditam? "svasiddhaye parākṣepaḥ parārthaṃ svasamarpaṇam" iti dvividhayā bhaṅgyā /
bhaṅgi prakāraḥ /
atrāyamāśayaḥ /
lakṣaṇamūlo 'yaṃ paryāyoktādiṣu pratīyamānor'thaḥ /
lakṣaṇā ca dvirūpā-ajahatsvārthaikā "kuntāḥ praviśanti" ityādau /
parā tu jahatsvārthā "gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ" ityādau /
tatrājahastvārthāyāṃ kuntānāṃ svataḥ praveśāsaṃbhave kauntikān ākṣipya praveśasaṃbhavaḥ /
ataḥsva siddhaye parānākṣipatīti tatra lakṣaṇā /
svakīya praveśādeḥsiddhaye parasya kauntikasyākṣepa iti /
jahatsvārthāyāṃ tu gaṅgādermukhyārthasyātyantamanupapattireva /
ataḥ parārthaṃ svasamarpaṇamiti lakṣaṇam /
parārthaṃ taṭāderghoṣādyadhikaraṇārthaṃ svasamarpaṇaṃ svasvarūpaparityāga iti /
itthaṃ ca satispṛṣṭāstā nandana' iti paryāyoktodāharaṇe sainikānāṃ sāvajñapārijātamañjarīsparśaḥ svargavijayamanākṣipya na saṃbhavatīti kuntādinayena svasiddhaye parākṣepaḥ /
evam "upoḍharāgeṇa" iti samāsoktyudāharaṇe 'pi jñeyam /
nāyakatvākṣepe sati niśādeḥ timirāṃśukādiyogasaṃbhavāt ajahatsvārthatvam /
atha "taṃ ṇātthī" ti aprastutapraśaṃsodāharaṇe mukhyārthasyāprastutatvāt; "bāḷagraṇāham"ityākṣepodāharaṇe dūtītvaniṣedhasyābhāsarūpatvāt "he helājite" ti vyājastutyudāharaṇe khajalayordvayorapi caikasyānekattvalābhābhāvāt mukhyārthasya atyantamanupapattireva /
ataḥ parārthaṃ svasamarpaṇāmiti lakṣaṇam /
tamimaṃ viṣayavibhāgam abhisandhāyoktam-yathāyogaṃ dvividhayeti /
yogo yogyatā tāmanatikramyetyarthaḥ /
itthaṃ vastudhvanau vimatirbhāmahādiṣu darśitā /

children.translated_text: Now he presents <s>Rudraṭa</s>'s disagreement regarding <s>rasa-dhvani</s> and <s>alaṅkāra-dhvani</s> (suggestion of aesthetic emotion and figures), beginning with '<s>rudraṭenāpi</s>' etc.
<s>Bhāvālaṅkāra</s> (the figure of emotional states) is also called <s>preyas</s> (the endearing)—thus it has been stated as twofold.

children.text: tathā hi- yasya vikāraḥ prabhavannapratibandhena hetunā yena /
children.translated_text: As follows: 'That modification which, arising from an unobstructed cause,

children.text: gamayati tadabhiprāyaṃ tatprati bandhaṃ ca bhāvo 'sau //
children.translated_text: conveys the intention toward that [cause] and the obstruction [to it]—that is <s>bhāva</s> (emotional state).'

body.translated_text: Here, the praise 'you help <s>Maru</s>' conveys blame. When the positions of <s>upamāna</s> (standard of comparison) and <s>upameya</s> (object of comparison) are reciprocally exchanged, that is <s>upameyopamā</s> (mutual simile). As he will state: 'When the two are reciprocally [compared], that is <s>upameyopamā</s>.' For example: 'The sky is like water, the water is like the sky; the swan is like the moon, the moon is like the swan.' Here, the interchange of the positions of <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s> excludes a third associate. When one thing alone serves as both <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>, that is <s>ananvaya</s> (non-correlation). As he will state: 'When one thing alone serves as both <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>, that is <s>ananvaya</s>.' For example: 'In battle, <s>Arjuna</s> is like <s>Arjuna</s> alone in his renowned power.' Here, the second associate is excluded. The word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.) includes <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> and others. In these, from <s>paryāyokta</s> onwards, the subject matter alone that is suggested—such as the conquest of heaven—to the exclusion of <s>rasa</s> and <s>alaṅkāra</s>, this, even while appearing as the essential content by all means of knowledge, has been presented by those such as <s>Udbhaṭa</s> as subsidiary to the denoted meaning, through the concealment technique of <s>gajanimilikā</s> (elephant's wink). The implied objection is: how can that which transcends the category of the denoted, having subordinated the denoted meaning, be subsidiary to the denoted? By what method was it presented? Through a twofold turn: '<s>svasiddhaye parākṣepaḥ</s>' (imputation of the other for one's own establishment) and '<s>parārthaṃ svasamarpaṇam</s>' (self-surrender for the sake of the other). '<s>Bhaṅgi</s>' means 'mode.' The idea here is this: the suggested meaning in <s>paryāyokta</s> and the rest is rooted in <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification). And <s>lakṣaṇā</s> is of two kinds: one is <s>ajahatsvārthā</s> (non-abandoning its own meaning), as in '<s>kuntāḥ praviśanti</s>' (the spears enter); the other is <s>jahatsvārthā</s> (abandoning its own meaning), as in '<s>gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ</s>' (a village on the Ganges). In the <s>ajahatsvārthā</s>, when the spears themselves cannot enter, by imputing spear-bearers, entry becomes possible. Therefore, the <s>lakṣaṇā</s> there is: 'it imputes the other for its own establishment'—that is, for the establishment of its own entry and such, the other, namely the spear-bearer, is imputed. In the <s>jahatsvārthā</s>, however, the primary meaning of <s>Gaṅgā</s> (the river) is completely inapplicable. Therefore, the <s>lakṣaṇā</s> is: 'self-surrender for the sake of the other'—for the sake of the other, namely the bank as the substratum for the village, self-surrender means abandonment of one's own form. Thus, in the <s>paryāyokta</s> example '<s>spṛṣṭāstā nandane</s>' (they were touched in Nandana), the soldiers' contemptuous touching of the <s>Pārijāta</s> blossoms is impossible without imputing the conquest of heaven, following the model of spears—hence 'imputation of the other for one's own establishment.' The same should be understood in the <s>samāsokti</s> example '<s>upoḍharāgeṇa</s>' (with heightened passion). When the hero's presence is imputed, the night's association with the darkness-veil and such becomes possible—hence it is <s>ajahatsvārthā</s>. Now, in the <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> example '<s>taṃ ṇātthī</s>', the primary meaning is irrelevant; in the <s>ākṣepa</s> example '<s>bāḷagraṇāham</s>', the denial of being a messenger is only apparent; in the <s>vyājastuti</s> example '<s>he helājite</s>', neither of the two—sky and water—nor one alone can attain multiplicity; the primary meaning is completely inapplicable. Therefore, the <s>lakṣaṇā</s> is: 'self-surrender for the sake of the other.' Keeping this division of subject matter in mind, he said: '<s>yathāyogam</s>' (as appropriate) through a twofold turn. '<s>Yoga</s>' means appropriateness—without transgressing it, such is the meaning. Thus the disagreement regarding <s>vastudhvani</s> (suggestion of subject matter) has been shown with respect to <s>Bhāmaha</s> and others.

children.text: tathā ca sūtritaṃ tena - "rītiḥ ātmā kāvyasya"iti /
children.translated_text: And thus it has been stated by him in a <s>sūtra</s> (aphorism): '<s>Rīti</s> (style) is the soul of poetry.'

children.text: prakhyāpitaṃ ca - aviditaguṇāpi satkavibhaṇitiḥ karṇoṣu vamati madhudhārām /
children.translated_text: And it has been proclaimed: 'Even when the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) are not known, the utterance of a good poet pours a stream of honey into the ears.'
'Even without perceiving its fragrance, a garland of <s>mālatī</s> (jasmine) captivates the sight.'
Thus.

body.translated_text:
<s>Rudraṭa</s> has described the <s>bhāvālaṅkāra</s> (figure of emotional states) in only two forms: as the persistence of an emotional state and the cessation of an emotional state.
The idea is that this should be treated as a form of <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy).
Because varieties of <s>bhāvāsaṅkara</s> (confusion of emotions) characterized by <s>sandhiśabalatā</s> (complexity of junctures) and the like are also possible.
For he will state: '<s>Bhāvodaya</s> (arising of emotion), <s>sandhiśabalatā</s>, etc. are separate figures.'
Regarding <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) and others, he reveals what has been superficially shown — '<s>rūpaka</s>, <s>dīpaka</s>,' etc.
<s>Rūpaka</s> (metaphor), <s>Dīpaka</s> (illumination), <s>Apahnuti</s> (denial), <s>Tulyayogitā</s> (equal connection) —
the word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.) indicates <s>Nidarśanā</s> (illustration) and the like.
Among these, the <s>upamā</s> (simile) figure, being suggested, has not been stated as primary because it serves as a cause of beauty of the expressed meaning and is therefore subordinate.
The idea is that this too is insubstantial.
Because the <s>upamā</s> figure, being a cause of beauty of the expressed meaning and thus subordinated, primarily resides in those very figures when brought to prominence.
Now he reveals that <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic flavor) and <s>bhāva</s> (emotional state) have not been properly treated — '<s>Rasavat</s>, <s>Preyas</s>, <s>Ūrjasvī</s>,' etc.
<s>Rasa</s>, when subordinated, is the figure called <s>Rasavat</s>; <s>bhāva</s> is <s>Preyas</s>; <s>rasābhāsa</s> (semblance of rasa) is <s>Ūrjasvī</s>; <s>bhāvābhāsa</s> (semblance of bhāva) is <s>Samāhita</s>.
Thus <s>rasa</s>, <s>bhāva</s>, etc. have been stated as causes of beauty of the expressed meaning.
The idea is that this too is weak.
Because the status of <s>rasa</s> etc. as figures is not permanent, since in their primary state they are the adorned (<s>alaṅkārya</s>), not ornaments.
'As <s>utprekṣā</s>' — the suggested is itself stated; though suggested, it is stated as the adorned — this is the meaning.
The idea is that this too is not profound.
Because in the suggested state, it is an established principle that every figure becomes the adorned.
The threefold subject matter — object (<s>vastu</s>), figure (<s>alaṅkāra</s>), and <s>rasa</s> — has been declared as the adorned.
As the life of poetry, it is precisely the adorned; it has not been properly understood — this is the purport.
Having thus presented the view of those who are averse to investigating the life-giving element of poetry and who relish only surface figures, being superficial observers, he now properly presents the views of those who attend to the life-giving element of poetry — beginning with 'By <s>Vāmana</s>, however...'
By saying 'based on similarity,' those who state that similarity is the linguistic function — the secondary usage (<s>gauṇī vṛtti</s>) based on connection — are censured.
The teachers of <s>Dhvani</s> (suggestion) do not accept the inclusion of secondary usage within <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (indication).
By declaring that 'indication based on similarity is the <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) figure,' a certain variety of <s>dhvani</s> based on <s>lakṣaṇā</s>, called '<s>atyantatirasktavācya</s>' (that in which the expressed meaning is completely concealed), has been stated as a figure though it is the very soul of poetry; it has not been recognized as the adorned — this is the purport.
That element which is not a figure is also stated as the adorned — he says 'merely endowed with <s>guṇas</s> (qualities)...'
By the word 'merely,' independence from <s>rasa</s> and <s>alaṅkāra</s> is indicated.
That <s>rīti</s> (style), which in the form of <s>Vaidarbhī</s> etc. is a property of composition, distinguished by <s>guṇas</s> such as <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness) etc. that are independent of <s>rasa</s> and <s>alaṅkāra</s> — that alone has been called the soul of poetry.

children.translated_text: <s>Guṇas</s> (qualities) invariably cause excellence; <s>alaṅkāras</s> (figures), however, do so optionally.
<s>Guṇas</s> exist in inherent relation (<s>samavāya</s>); <s>alaṅkāras</s>, however, in conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>).
As has been said: 'Those properties of <s>rasa</s>, the principal element, like valor and the like of the self,
which cause excellence and are permanently established — those are <s>guṇas</s> (qualities).

body.translated_text:
The idea is that this too is unjustified.
For: the body of poetry is word and meaning (<s>śabda</s> and <s>artha</s>); <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration), <s>upamā</s> (simile), etc. are like bracelets and crowns.
But the suggested meaning (<s>vyaṅgyārtha</s>) is the soul — this being established, even beyond the sound-figures, that which is the external ornament of sound, namely <s>anuprāsa</s>, is on the same level as these <s>rītis</s> (styles).
Because both are properties of phonemes.
With this in view, in the discussion of <s>vṛttyanuprāsa</s> (compositional alliteration) and phonetic ornament, the <s>Vaidarbhī</s> and other <s>rītis</s> have been analyzed by the author of <s>Kāvyaprakāśa</s> and others.
The author of this work too will analyze them there.
In these, which are evocative (<s>vyañjaka</s>), the proximity to the suggested <s>rasa</s> creates a confusion of soul-hood among the superficial-minded.
This applies equally to <s>anuprāsa</s> etc., so this partiality for <s>rīti</s> alone is weak.
In reality, the suggested meaning alone is the soul of poetry.
Now, he says that <s>Udbhaṭa</s> and others have also not properly distinguished between <s>guṇa</s> (quality) and <s>alaṅkāra</s> (figure) — 'By <s>Udbhaṭa</s> and others, however...'
Similarity means belonging to the same class — this is the meaning.
The reason given is: 'because the distinction is based on subject matter alone.'
By the word 'alone,' the absence of a difference in essential nature is indicated.
Their view is that the essential nature, characterized as causing poetic beauty, is of one kind only.
He shows the difference in subject matter — 'composition' etc.
'<s>Guṇas</s> are properties of composition; <s>alaṅkāras</s> are properties of word and meaning.'
The idea is that this too is not profound.
Because <s>guṇa</s> and <s>alaṅkāra</s> are, in their essential nature, extremely different.
For: <s>guṇas</s> are properties of <s>rasa</s>, which is the principal element; <s>alaṅkāras</s>, however, are properties of word and meaning, which are the subordinate elements.

children.translated_text: Those which sometimes enhance the principal element through the medium of the subordinate parts,
like necklaces and the like, are <s>alaṅkāras</s> (ornaments) — <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration), <s>upamā</s> (simile), and so on.'

children.translated_text: When, through not abandoning its own meaning (<s>Ajahatsvārthatā</s>), there is an additional reference for establishing itself, it is [called] <s>Arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya</s> (where the literal meaning is transferred to another meaning).

children.text: yathā - prārambhe śrutisundaraṃ pariṇātau pathyaṃ janaiḥsugrahaṃ /
children.translated_text: For example: 'At the outset, beautiful to hear; at maturity, wholesome; easily grasped by people;
washed at every syllable with the clear and sweet essences of various <s>Śāstras</s> (sciences);

children.text: āhlādāya na kasya nāma viduṣāṃ vaktrāmbujādudgataṃ cittāntarvikasadviveka mukulāmodānubiddhaṃ vacaḥ //
children.translated_text: for whose delight is it not — speech that has arisen from the lotus-mouth of the learned, pervaded by the fragrance of the bud of discernment blossoming within the heart!'

body.translated_text: This being so, in relation to <s>Alaṃkāras</s> (figures of speech), the superior embellishment of poetry lies precisely in the <s>Guṇas</s> (poetic qualities) — just as the status of being poetry is accepted even when the <s>Alaṃkāras</s> are not manifest, but not when the <s>Guṇas</s> are not manifest. As it has been said: 'But [poetry] without ornamentation [is accepted] in some cases.' This being the supremacy of <s>Guṇas</s> and <s>Alaṃkāras</s> of this kind, [the author shows that] even the view of the ancients regarding this is not sound, saying: 'Thus, [the view that] <s>Alaṃkāras</s> alone [constitute the soul of poetry].' Now, with the intention [of showing] that the views of the author of the <s>Vakroktijīvita</s> (Kuntaka) and <s>Bhaṭṭanāyaka</s> are close to the <s>Dhvani</s> (suggestion) doctrine, he says: 'The author of <s>Vakroktijīvita</s>, however,' and so on. '<s>Vaidagdhyabhaṅgībhaṇitisvabhāvā</s>' means: having as its nature a mode of expression endowed with varieties of elegance — this is the meaning. [The statement] 'he declared it the life [of poetry]' indicates the absence of a stubborn insistence on <s>Alaṃkāras</s> alone. With the intention [of showing] that another essential, subtle aspect was also recognized by him, he says: 'and the primacy of the function (<s>Vyāpāra</s>).' The function (<s>Vyāpāra</s>) is that which has the nature of conveying <s>Rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment). He accepted its primacy — not that of the non-primary <s>Alaṃkāra</s> alone. But <s>Alaṃkāras</s> fall within the domain of the expressible (<s>Vācya</s>) according to his view — he says: 'by the modes of <s>Abhidhā</s> (denotation)' and so on. And the threefold suggested meaning (<s>Pratīyamānārtha</s>), consisting of <s>Vastu</s> (matter), <s>Alaṃkāra</s> (figure), and <s>Rasa</s> (sentiment) — even where [all three] exist, the primacy belongs to the function characterized by their conveyance — this is his view, as stated: 'Even though [they exist],' and so on. The figurative usage (<s>Upacāra</s>), the resorting to <s>Lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) — through that obliqueness, the entire range of <s>Dhvani</s> including <s>Avivakṣitavācya</s> (where the literal meaning is not intended) is indicated. This being so, [he shows] that this view differs from the <s>Dhvani</s> doctrine only slightly, saying: 'Merely the variety of expression.' Now [regarding] <s>Bhaṭṭanāyaka</s>'s view: 'By <s>Bhaṭṭanāyaka</s>, however,' and so on. 'Of that which is accepted through bold assertion (<s>Prauḍhokti</s>)' — <s>Bhoga</s> (aesthetic enjoyment) is a term coined by him; through that bold assertion, 'of that which is accepted' — this is the meaning. By declaring such a function of suggestion (<s>Vyañjana</s>) to be the soul of poetry, he has subordinated the intrinsic nature of word and meaning — the primacy of that function alone was stated. And that function is not mundane (<s>Laukika</s>), he says: 'Even there, [regarding] the <s>Abhidhā</s> (denotation) and <s>Bhāvakatva</s> (generalization),' and so on. 'There,' i.e., among those functions, the middle one: <s>Abhidhā</s> (denotation) is the power whose object is the meaning directly connected by convention. <s>Bhāvakatva</s> (generalization) is the power that takes the form of making universal what is apprehended through its unique characteristics. Having passed through the gateway of these two functions, the function whose nature is the savoring of <s>Rasa</s> (<s>Rasacarvaṇā</s>) in the universalized <s>Vibhāvas</s> (determinants) and other elements — called by the alternative name <s>Bhoga</s> (aesthetic enjoyment) — is accepted as primary, being the resting place [of aesthetic experience]. In this doctrine, the primacy of the coined term <s>Bhoga</s> and its self-invented function is what differs from the <s>Dhvani</s> doctrine. Now the established conclusion: 'The <s>Dhvanikāra</s> (author of <s>Dhvanyāloka</s>), however,' and so on. The <s>Dhvanikāra</s> has established that the soul of poetry is the suggested sentence-meaning (<s>Vyaṅgya Vākyārtha</s>) itself. The reason here: 'Because the function of suggestion (<s>Vyañjana Vyāpāra</s>) must necessarily be accepted.' Of what kind? One that transcends the three functions called <s>Abhidhā</s> (denotation), <s>Lakṣaṇā</s> (indication), and <s>Tātparya</s> (purport). <s>Tātparya</s> is the synthesizing power that arises immediately after the comprehension of word-meanings. 'That which transcends these three' — thus a fourth level is posited. <s>Dhvanana</s>, <s>Dyotana</s> (illumination), <s>Pratyāyana</s> (conveying), <s>Vyañjana</s> (suggestion) — since [this function] must necessarily be accepted along with these well-known synonyms, and since without accepting it there would be no other way to account for the apprehension of the suggested meaning — therefore the suggested meaning itself is the soul [of poetry]. But why is the function of suggestion (<s>Vyañjanā Vyāpāra</s>) not the primary [soul]? — to this he says: 'Because the function does not have the status of sentence-meaning.' Since it is imperceptible and thus not amenable to etymological analysis, it lacks sentence-meaning status. All powers of word-meaning are merely inferred from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of effect and so on. Therefore the function is not primary. And the reason that would establish primacy applies to the suggested meaning (<s>Vyaṅgya</s>) itself, not to the function of suggestion — he says: 'Of the sentence-meaning itself.' Being embellished by <s>Guṇas</s> and <s>Alaṃkāras</s>, and being the resting place [of aesthetic experience] — these are the reasons for primacy. Therefore the suggested meaning alone is the soul of poetry — thus he has established. Now he adduces further arguments: 'Of the function, through the medium of its object,' and so on. The function of suggestion and the like achieves its own identity only through the medium of the suggested meaning. Therefore the status of sentence-meaning is not possible [for the function]. Just as its form is apprehended through the medium of the object, so too its primacy and its worthiness of investigation [depend] on that medium — he says: 'Through the primacy of that, primacy [accrues]'; 'Because there is no investigability in its own form.' But the object alone deserves the full status of sentence-meaning — he says: 'Of the object alone.' Direct apprehension of one's own form, primacy from itself, investigability in its own form — the entire weight [rests on the object]. The capacity to bear that entire weight belongs to the object characterized as suggested meaning. Therefore the status of soul belongs to the object alone — he says: 'Therefore the object alone.' Because it can bear the entire weight, it deserves the complete range of excellences — therefore he says: 'Whose <s>Guṇas</s> and <s>Alaṃkāras</s>,' and so on. But <s>Rasa</s> and other [sentiments] were regarded by the ancients as <s>Alaṃkāras</s> (figures) like <s>Rasavat</s> and others. How can they be that which is ornamented? — to this he says: '<s>Rasa</s> and others, however.' The reason: 'Because <s>Alaṃkāras</s> serve as embellishments, while <s>Rasa</s> and others are primarily that which is embellished.' When <s>Rasa</s> and others are subordinate, they have the status of <s>Alaṃkāra</s>; but when they are primary, they are precisely that which is to be ornamented. Since the arrangement is thus, he concludes: the suggested meaning alone is the soul of poetry — 'Therefore the suggested [meaning] alone,' and so on. 'Having become sentence-meaning' indicates the state of primacy, since in the state of non-primacy it is not the soul. This is the doctrine of the author of <s>Dhvani</s> [theory]. To show that his own view follows this, he says: 'This very position,' and so on. By the word 'alone' (<s>Eva</s>), the impossibility of other positions is made manifest. <s>Āvarjaka</s> means: that which forcefully turns one toward itself. The reason: 'Because of the function of suggestion,' and so on. Those who desire the suggested meaning to be the soul of poetry, and those who do not desire it — by all of them, the function of suggestion cannot be denied. If it is not denied, what then? — to this he says: 'And in resorting to that,' and so on. The untenability of the other positions has been established by the arguments of the followers of this doctrine. Now he presents the objection raised by the author of <s>Vyaktiviveka</s>: 'But the author of <s>Vyaktiviveka</s>,' and so on. <s>Liṅgatayā</s> means: by way of being an inferential mark. 'Because of the absence of essential identity (<s>Tādātmya</s>) and origination from that (<s>Tadutpatti</s>).' In the relation of inferential mark and what it marks — between property and property-bearer — <s>Tādātmya</s> is the invariable connection. Between cause and effect, <s>Tadutpatti</s> (origination from that) exists when [the effect occurs] in the absence of [anything else]. If either of these two invariable connections were absent, then due to deviation, the mark-marked relation would not hold. Since this is so, the author of <s>Vyaktiviveka</s>'s statement [against <s>Dhvani</s>] is made without proper examination — it is like the cawing of a crow. Thus, the entire body of arguments for establishing the <s>Dhvani</s> doctrine is extremely profound. It is applicable to the investigation of <s>Dhvani</s> and <s>Guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> (subordinated suggested meaning) poetry; but it is not very applicable to the investigation of <s>Citra</s> (ornate) poetry — with this intention he concludes: 'This [matter], which is for the sharp-witted,' and so on. 'Here' [means] in <s>Citra</s> poetry. 'Is not elaborated' — it is only mentioned as far as it is useful. Now, he mentions <s>Dhvani</s> only to the extent useful in the context of <s>Citra</s> [poetry]: 'There is, to begin with,' and so on. If it exists, what then? — to this he says: 'Of the suggested [meaning] there,' and so on. When [the suggested meaning] is primary, the poetry is called <s>Dhvani</s> — the highest type of poetry. When it is non-primary, it is called <s>Guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> (subordinated suggestion) — the middling type. He states the scope of <s>Citra</s>: 'Of these, the highest, <s>Dhvani</s>,' and so on. And it manifests through being rooted in <s>Lakṣaṇā</s> (indication) or <s>Abhidhā</s> (denotation) — he says: 'Through being rooted in <s>Lakṣaṇā</s> or <s>Abhidhā</s>.' When rooted in <s>Lakṣaṇā</s>, it is called <s>Avivakṣitavācya</s> (where the literal meaning is not intended), because in <s>Lakṣaṇā</s> — which involves obstruction of the primary meaning — the literal aspect is not intended. When rooted in <s>Abhidhā</s>, it is called <s>Vivakṣitānyaparavācya</s> (where the literal meaning is intended but subordinate to another), because in <s>Abhidhā</s> there is no obstruction of the literal meaning, hence it is intended; but since it is intended as ancillary to the suggested meaning, it is subordinate to another — thus <s>Vivakṣitānyaparatva</s> (being intended but directed toward another). Thus <s>Dhvani</s> rooted in <s>Lakṣaṇā</s> and <s>Dhvani</s> rooted in <s>Abhidhā</s> — in general, <s>Dhvani</s> is of two kinds. Of these, he states the sub-varieties of the one rooted in <s>Lakṣaṇā</s>: 'The first, <s>Arthāntara</s>,' and so on. The first, rooted in <s>Lakṣaṇā</s>, is of two kinds: <s>Arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya</s> (where the literal meaning is transferred to another meaning) and <s>Atyantatiraskṛtavācya</s> (where the literal meaning is completely concealed).

body.text: atraivaṃvidhavaca upadeśālakṣaṇe arthāntare saṅkrāmati /

children.translated_text: Because such excellence is not possible for mere speech [alone].

children.text: atha yadā jahatsvārthatayā parārthaṃ svasamarpaṇaṃ tadātyantatiraskṛtavācyākhyaḥ /
children.translated_text: Now, when through abandoning its own meaning (<s>Jahatsvārthatā</s>), there is a surrender of oneself for another's purpose, it is called <s>Atyantatiraskṛtavācya</s> (where the literal meaning is completely concealed).

children.text: yathā - eke mūkavadāsate jaḍadhiyo jihneti tatsannidhā vanye durviciktsitaṃ vidadhate tebhyo 'pi bībhatsate /
children.translated_text: For example: 'Some sit mute like the dumb; the dull-witted cringe in its presence; others attempt an incurable [remedy] — one is disgusted even with them;

children.text: asthāne bahudhā stuvanti katicittairulkayā dahyate vidyā viklavate kayā na vidhayā prāpyāntikaṃ duṣprabhoḥ //
children.translated_text: a few praise [it] in wrong places in many ways — the heart is burned by their torch-like [praise]. Knowledge (<s>Vidyā</s>) trembles — by what means can one approach the ill-tempered master!'

body.translated_text: Here, such speech transfers to another meaning — that of instruction characterized by <s>Lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification).

body.text:
atra vidyāyāṃ hlībībhatsādiḥ gaṅgādau ghoṣādhikaraṇatādīva sarvathā svasaṃyogino svārthaṃ parityajya na saṃbhavatītyatyanta tiraskṛtavācyatā /
itthama vivakṣitavācyasyārthāntarasaṃkramita vācyo 'tyantatiraskṛtavācyaśceti dvau bhedau /
athābhidhāmūla prabhedadik /
dvitīyo 'pīti /
dvitīyo 'bhidhāmūlo vivakṣitānyaparavācyākhyaḥ /

athānayoḥ sakṣaṇābhidhāmūladhvanyorvastvalaṅkāra rasarūpatā viṣayaviśeṣaṃ vyavasthāpayitumāha-lakṣaṇāmūla ityādinā /
