rasāstu vibhāvānubhāvavyabhicāribhivyājyamānā ratyādayaḥ sahṛdayapratītiviśeṣāḥ /
atha vivakṣitānyaparavācyo yo 'yaṃ asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgyaḥ sa niyamenārthaśaktimūla ubhayaśaktimūlaśca bhavati /

children.translated_text: It necessarily takes the form of <s>Vastu</s> (matter) or <s>Alaṃkāra</s> (figure).

children.text: tatra yadā rasabhāvarasābhāsa bhāvābhāsabhāvodayabhāvaśānti bhāvasandhibhāvaśabalatā vyajyante, tadā kramo na saṃlakṣyata iti asaṃlakṣyakramatvam /
children.translated_text: When <s>Rasa</s> (sentiment), <s>Bhāva</s> (transitory emotion), <s>Rasābhāsa</s> (semblance of sentiment), <s>Bhāvābhāsa</s> (semblance of emotion), <s>Bhāvodaya</s> (emergence of emotion), <s>Bhāvaśānti</s> (subsidence of emotion), <s>Bhāvasandhi</s> (juncture of emotions), or <s>Bhāvaśabalatā</s> (mixing of emotions) are suggested, the sequence is not perceptible — hence it is called <s>Asaṃlakṣyakrama</s> (imperceptible sequence).

children.text: tatra raseṣu śṛṅgāraḥsaṃbhogātmā yathā- puṣpodbhedamavāpya keliśayanāddarasthayā cumbane kāntena sphuritādhareṇa nibhṛtaṃ bhrūsaṃjñayā yācite /
children.translated_text: Among the <s>Rasas</s>, <s>Śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment) in its <s>Saṃbhoga</s> (union) form — for example: 'Having attained the blossoming of flowers, at the bed of sport, when her lover with quivering lips softly begged for a kiss with a gesture of his brows, while she rested against his chest —

children.text: ācchādya smitapūrṇā gaṇḍaphalakaṃ celāñcalenānanaṃ mandāndolitakuṇḍalastabakayā tanvyā vidhūtaṃ śiraḥ //
children.translated_text: covering her cheek bright with a full smile with the edge of her garment over her face, the slender maiden, with gently swaying clusters of earrings, shook her head [in refusal].'

body.translated_text: Here, [the attribution of] shrinking, disgust, and other [emotions] to <s>Vidyā</s> (knowledge) — just as in '<s>Gaṅgā</s>' etc., [the word] does not function at all in connection with its literal meaning, like the locus of a hamlet [transferred] to the river — completely abandoning the literal meaning connected with itself, it cannot [function otherwise] — therefore it is <s>Atyantatiraskṛtavācya</s> (complete concealment of the literal meaning). Thus, <s>Avivakṣitavācya</s> (where the literal meaning is not intended) has two varieties: <s>Arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya</s> and <s>Atyantatiraskṛtavācya</s>. Now the direction of the sub-divisions of [<s>Dhvani</s>] rooted in <s>Abhidhā</s>: 'The second also,' and so on. The second, rooted in <s>Abhidhā</s>, is called <s>Vivakṣitānyaparavācya</s>. In some [cases], the sequence of the suggested meaning is not perceptible; in others, it is perceptible. Therefore <s>Vivakṣitānyaparavācya</s> is also of two kinds: <s>Asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya</s> (where the sequence of suggestion is imperceptible) and <s>Saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya</s> (where the sequence of suggestion is perceptible). Now, to establish the subject-matter distinction — that both <s>Lakṣaṇā</s>-based and <s>Abhidhā</s>-based <s>Dhvani</s> can take the form of <s>Vastu</s> (matter), <s>Alaṃkāra</s> (figure), or <s>Rasa</s> (sentiment) — he says: 'The one rooted in <s>Lakṣaṇā</s>,' and so on. That which is rooted in <s>Lakṣaṇā</s> is necessarily based on the power of the word (<s>Śabdaśakti</s>) and has the form of <s>Vastu</s> (matter). Whatever is the totality of word-meanings, consisting of universals (<s>Jāti</s>), qualities (<s>Guṇa</s>), actions (<s>Kriyā</s>), and so on — all of that is called <s>Vastu</s>. That same [content], when it possesses felicitous arrangement devised by the poet, is an <s>Alaṃkāra</s> (figure). <s>Rasas</s> (aesthetic sentiments) are the [permanent emotions such as] <s>Rati</s> (love) etc., suggested through <s>Vibhāvas</s> (determinants), <s>Anubhāvas</s> (consequents), and <s>Vyabhicārins</s> (transitory emotions) — they are special cognitions in the heart of the <s>Sahṛdaya</s> (connoisseur). Now, <s>Vivakṣitānyaparavācya</s> which is <s>Asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya</s> (imperceptible sequence of suggestion) is necessarily based on the power of meaning (<s>Arthaśakti</s>) or the power of both [word and meaning].

children.text: atra nāyikānāyakavṛttāntalakṣaṇo yo vācyor'thaḥ yā ca sahṛdayapratīteḥ vedyāntaravigalanena varṇyavastutanmayībhāvalakṣaṇā rasasaṃvit, na khalu tayoḥ kramaḥsaṃlakṣyate /
children.translated_text: Here, the literal meaning (<s>Vācyārtha</s>) characterized by the behavior of the heroine (<s>Nāyikā</s>) and the hero (<s>Nāyaka</s>), and the aesthetic cognition of <s>Rasa</s> (<s>Rasasaṃvit</s>) characterized by identification with the subject being depicted — through the dissolution of [the boundary of] the spectator's distinct self into the depicted subject — the sequence between these two is indeed not perceptible.
Even though existing [as a sequence], it is perceived as if non-existent, in the manner of [a needle] piercing through a hundred lotus petals [simultaneously].

children.text: vipralambhaśṛṅgāro yathā - nāntaḥ praveśamaruṇādvimukhī na cāsī dācaṣṭaroṣa paruṣāṇi na cākṣarāṇi /
children.translated_text: <s>Vipralambha Śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment in separation) — for example: 'She did not refuse entry to her beloved, nor was she turned away; she did not utter harsh words of anger;

children.text: sā kevalaṃ saralapakṣmabhirakṣipātaiḥ kāntaṃ vilokitavatī jananirviśeṣam //
children.translated_text: she merely looked at her lover with glances from her straight lashes, just as [she would look at] any person.'
In such cases, the absence of sequence should be understood as before.

children.text: hāsyo yathā - paimaraṇāmaṇḍaṇājjalavesā pāsaṃga esu taruṇesu /
children.translated_text: <s>Hāsya</s> (comic sentiment) — for example [in Prakrit]: 'With the makeup of the wrestling arena adorning [her], dressed in water-garments, among those young men with their side-garments —

children.text: ṇiddhasaraṃ parugrantī savibbhamaṃ haṇā i thaṇāvaṭṭham //
children.translated_text: tying up her loosened hair, she playfully strikes [at] the pitcher on [her] breast.'

children.text: atra patimaraṇāmaṇḍanojjvalaveṣāyāḥ taruṇeṣu pārśvamupagateṣu satsu sadyaḥ snigdhasvaraṃprarudatyāḥ savibhramaṃ yadetatstanavṛttahananaṃ tat pracchannānurāgasyānaucityena pravṛtterhāsyamabhivyanakti /
children.translated_text: Here, when a woman — unadorned due to her husband's death, yet radiant in appearance — is approached by young men at her side, and immediately weeps in a tender voice while making coquettish gestures of striking her breast, this indicates humor (<s>hāsya</s>) arising from the impropriety of concealed passion.

children.text: karuṇasya yathā - sāhityalakṣaṇakale samupaiṣi navya vaidhavyamadya virate guruviṣṇudeve /
children.translated_text: An example of the compassionate (<s>karuṇa</s>) [<s>rasa</s>]: 'O one skilled in the art of literary theory, you attain widowhood today when the revered <s>Viṣṇudeva</s> passes away.'
'For the festival of love whispered near the ear, henceforth the offering of a palm-leaf fan alone is fit for you.'

children.text: raudranya yathā - dṛpyatsūkara kālakaṇṭha śakalavyākīrṇa dhārāntarā krodhottālalulāyakaṇṭhanalakacchedārdhavaktrānanāḥ /
children.translated_text: An example of the furious (<s>raudra</s>) [<s>rasa</s>]: 'O <s>Śrī Ballāla</s>, with the streams scattered with fragments of the bristling boar's dark neck, with faces and mouths half-severed where the throat-locks are torn loose by swelling rage,'

children.text: śrīballāla vidhāya keli mṛgayāmāvartamānasya te śārdūlendravasābhiṣekasamaye jīyāsurugrāḥśarāḥ //
children.translated_text: 'At the time of anointing with the fat of the lord of tigers, as you, having arranged a sportive hunt, are turning about — may your fierce arrows be victorious!'

children.text: vīrasya yathā - ādhāturbhuvanaṃ tadetadakhilaṃ cakṣuṣmadākīṭakā-d divyaṃ cakṣurananyalabhya mubhayatrāste paraṃ duḥsaham /
children.translated_text: An example of the heroic (<s>vīra</s>) [<s>rasa</s>]: 'That eye — from the creator of the four worlds to the smallest insect — the divine eye, unobtainable by any other, abides in both [places], supremely unbearable:'

children.text: phāle bhūtapatermanobhavamukha kṣudra kṣayojjāgaraṃ bāṇe ca pratirājadarpadalanaṃ ballāla pṛthvīpateḥ //
children.translated_text: 'On the forehead of the Lord of Beings (<s>Bhūtapati</s>) [it is] the awakening of the destruction of the trifling <s>Manobhava</s> (Kāma, god of love), and on the arrow of King <s>Ballāla</s> [it is] the crushing of the pride of rival kings.'

children.text: bhayānakasya yathā - girikuñjeṣu gūḍhānāṃ tavāri varayoṣitām /
children.translated_text: An example of the fearful (<s>bhayānaka</s>) [<s>rasa</s>]: 'Of the excellent women of your enemies, hidden in mountain caves,'
'Who never see the sun — their foreheads alone were visible by the marks of sacred ash.'

children.text: bībhatsasya yathā - svātmānandaṃ kimapi paramaṃ sādhu saṃbhuñjate ye teṣāmasyāṃ viṣayavitatau jāyate heyabuddhiḥ /
children.translated_text: An example of the disgusting (<s>bībhatsa</s>) [<s>rasa</s>]: 'Those who rightly enjoy a certain supreme bliss of the self — for them, in this expanse of sense objects, a sense of rejection arises.'

children.text: anyeṣāṃ tu prasaratitarāṃ pratyutāsvādanecchā chardiklinne kaphakaluṣite makṣikāṇāmivānne //
children.translated_text: 'But for others, the desire for tasting increases even more — like flies on food that is soiled with vomit and polluted with phlegm.'

children.text: adbhutasya yathā - ākarṇitottamaguṇānuguṇeti kṛtvā yāmullilekha sucireṇa mano madīyam /
children.translated_text: An example of the wondrous (<s>adbhuta</s>) [<s>rasa</s>]: 'Having heard that she possesses excellent qualities, my mind traced her [form] over a long time, making her proportionate [to those qualities].'

children.text: tāmākṛtiṃ visadṛśīmatimātramasyā dāsye 'pi nāsmi viniveśayituṃ vidagdhaḥ //
children.translated_text: 'Yet I am not skilled enough to assign that form — so utterly unlike the reality of her appearance — even to her maidservant.'

children.text: atra sucira madṛṣṭacaranāyikārūpasyānuguṇa śravaṇānurāgiṇo nāyakasya nāyikāprathamadarśane ākarṇitottama guṇānuguṇatayā manasā samullikhitacarī yā nāyikāmūrtiḥ, sā samprati sāśrātkṛtanāyikāmūrteratimātraṃ visadṛśī satī dāsītvenāpi niveśayituṃ na śakyata ityuktirābhirūpyanibandhanasya parāṃ kāṣṭhāmāviṣkaroti /
children.translated_text: Here, the hero, enamored by hearing about the qualities of the heroine whom he has not seen for a long time, traced a form of the heroine in his mind proportionate to the excellent qualities he had heard. Now, when the heroine's actual form is seen, it is so utterly unlike [the imagined one] that it cannot even be assigned to a maidservant — this statement reveals the utmost extreme of surpassing beauty.

children.text: śāntasya yathā - mā bhaiṣīḥ kula mā vyathasva vinaya kleśo 'stu mā te śruta pradhvaṃsāya yatasva mā khalu mate māhātmya mā mā tyaja /
children.translated_text: An example of the tranquil (<s>śānta</s>) [<s>rasa</s>]: 'Fear not, O family! Be not distressed, O good conduct! Let there be no suffering, O learning! Strive not for destruction, O reputation! O magnanimity, do not abandon me!'

children.text: yuṣmadrauravasāradāraṇāparānmatvā tṛṇāya prabhūn bhikṣāparyaṭanārjitena kalaye piṇḍena piṇḍasthitim //
children.translated_text: 'Considering the lords, whose essence is the tearing apart of the terrible [bonds] of your [worldly] attachments, as mere straw — I sustain my bodily existence with a morsel obtained by wandering for alms.'
Thus, <s>rasa-dhvani</s> (suggestion of aesthetic sentiment) has been illustrated by way of a brief indication.

children.text: atha bhāvadhvaniḥ-bhāvo hi nāma nāyikāvyatirikte devatāgurunṛpaputrādau vyajyamānā ratirvākyārthatvena vyajyamānā nirvedādayo vyabhicāriṇāśca /
children.translated_text: Now, <s>bhāva-dhvani</s> (suggestion of emotional states): <s>Bhāva</s> (emotional state) refers to <s>rati</s> (love) suggested in characters other than the heroine — such as deities, teachers, kings, sons, etc. — [or] suggested as the meaning of a sentence, as well as <s>nirveda</s> (world-weariness) and other <s>vyabhicārin</s> (transitory) emotions.

children.text: yathā- adya svapnamupāgatena yamunātīre mayāvasthitaṃ dṛṣṭastatra ca veṇuvādanipuṇo bālo gavāṃ pālakaḥ /
children.translated_text: For example: 'Today, having come [to me] in a dream, I stood on the bank of the <s>Yamunā</s>, and there I saw a young boy, skilled in playing the flute, a cowherd.'

children.text: taṃ dṛṣṭvā karaṇairananyaviṣayairantarvilīno 'bhavaṃ yāvattāvadahaṃ cirādupacitaiḥ pāpaiḥ prabodhaṃ gataḥ //
children.translated_text: 'Seeing him, with my senses having no other object, I became absorbed within — but then, after a long time, I awoke due to accumulated sins.'

children.text: yathā ca - saṃsārārtyā vidhuravidhuro brahma yatnādvicinvan nānārūpaṃ jagadidamahaṃ dṛṣṭavāneva pūrvam /
children.translated_text: And for example: 'Weary and distressed by the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), diligently seeking <s>Brahman</s>, I had previously seen this world in its manifold forms.'

children.text: haste nyaste sati tava guro sāṃprataṃ mastake 'smim brahmaivaitatsakalamabhavanno jagannāpi cāham //
children.translated_text: 'But now, O teacher, when your hand is placed upon my head, all this has become <s>Brahman</s> alone — neither is there a world, nor am I [separate from it].'

children.text: yathā ca - kāṣṭhāprātpiriyaṃ parā khalu parīpākasya bhāgyonnateḥ śrī ballāla nṛpāla!yadvayamiṃmau pādau tavopāsmahe /
children.translated_text: And for example: 'This is the ultimate limit of the ripening of the elevation of fortune, O King <s>Śrī Ballāla</s>, that we two worship these feet of yours.'

children.text: yastiṣṭhetpratihāra sīmni bhavato ruddhapraveśaściraṃ kiṃ nāsāvapi colapāṇḍyapṛthvīpālaiḥsamaṃ gaṇyate //
children.translated_text: 'He who would stand for a long time at the boundary of your gatekeepers, denied entry — would not even he be counted equal to the <s>Coḷa</s>, <s>Pāṇḍya</s>, and other kings of the earth?'
Thus, <s>bhāva</s> (emotional state) directed toward sons and others, and in the form of transitory emotions (<s>vyabhicārin</s>), should be inferred by the reader.

An example of <s>rasābhāsa</s> (semblance of <s>rasa</s>): 'Smelling again and again the fragrance of the blossom whose scent is enhanced by the radiance of its opening face, with eyes reddened and half-closed,'
'The bee kisses the mango sprout previously touched by the beak of his beloved.'

body.text: ityādi //
body.translated_text: And so forth.

body.text: atra tiryagviṣayatvādrarasasyābhāsatā /

children.translated_text: Due to the absence of the quality of being a <s>dhīrodātta</s> (exalted-noble hero) and other [requirements].
As stated: '<s>Śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic sentiment) requires a character of noble nature and brilliant appearance.'

children.text: bhāvābhāso yathā - kvaṇādūdvirephāvalinīlaṅkaṇāṃ prasāryaṃ śākhābhujamāmra vallarī /
children.translated_text: An example of <s>bhāvābhāsa</s> (semblance of emotional state): 'Extending the branch-arm adorned with a line of dark bees that hum,'
'The mango vine, having embraced [the tree], inquires of the southern breeze about its well-being through the cooing of the <s>kalakaṇṭha</s> (cuckoo).'

body.translated_text: Here, because the subject is an animal, the <s>rasa</s> becomes a mere semblance (<s>ābhāsa</s>).

children.translated_text: Here, because the friendship is superimposed [on non-sentient beings], the <s>bhāva</s> becomes a mere semblance.

children.text: bhāvodayo yathā - kelitalpagatamaṅghriyāvakaṃ, sūcayatyuṣasi cakṣuṣā priye /
children.translated_text: An example of <s>bhāvodaya</s> (arising of an emotional state): 'At dawn, the beloved points out with her eye the lac-dye on the foot [that marks] the pleasure-bed,'

children.text: bhū[bhrū] tribhāgamupakalpya bhaṅguraṃ, gūḍha hāsa madhuraṃ cukopa sā //
children.translated_text: 'And making a curve of three-quarters of her brow, she became sweetly angry with a hidden smile.'
Here there is the arising of modesty (<s>lajjā</s>) and delight (<s>harṣa</s>).

children.text: bhāvasandhiryathā - netre jihyakharāruṇe kṣaṇāmatha vyāmīlyamānekṣaṇāṃ hastaṃ vyagragamāganaṃ kṣaṇāmatho dante śayānaṃ kṣaṇam /
children.translated_text: An example of <s>bhāvasandhi</s> (juncture of emotional states): 'His eyes bloody-red with the tongue; for a moment the gaze is half-closed; his trunk-hand moves restlessly back and forth for a moment; then for a moment he rests his tusk;'

children.text: sañcāraṃ viṣamākulaṃ kṣaṇamatha prakrāntalīlaṃ kṣaṇaṃ dhatte totriṣu ṣaṭpadeṣu ca samaṃ dattāvadhāno gajaḥ //
children.translated_text: 'His gait unsteadily agitated for a moment; then for a moment proceeding in playful sport — the elephant, attentive, gives equal attention to the goad-bearers and the bees.'

body.text:
atra gajasya madākulasya yadetatkṣaṇamātraṃ netrayoḥ jihyākharā ruṇāyoḥ dharaṇāṃ samanantarameva yaccaitadūvyāmīlanaṃ, tathā haste ca yatkṣaṇāmatraṃ vyagro gamāgamaḥ yacca samanantarameva dante śayanaṃ, sañcāre ca kṣāṇāmātraṃ yeyaṃ viṣamākulatā, samantarameva yaścāyaṃ līlāprakramaḥ, tadetat vividhaṃ vilakṣaṇaṃ viceṣṭitadvayaṃ udbhavābhibhavadharmitayā kṣaṇaṃ kṣaṇāmāvirbhavat totriviṣayaṃ roṣaṃ ṣaṭpadaśabdalakṣitaṣaṭpadagītaviṣayaṃ harṣa ca parasparasyādattā vasaratayāsamutkṣubhitam abhivyanakti /
dvandva vṛttiṣu ca triṣvapi vākyeṣu pratisvaṃ kṣaṇaṃ kṣaṇamityupādānādyathā yathā samutkṣubhitābdhikallolakatpa [la]tayo totriṇāmuparyupari vinipāta janmāno roṣāveśamahāvegāḥ tathā tathā tadabhibhavakṣamāṇāṃ ṣaṭpadagītākarṇānasukhābhiniveśavikāsānāṃ madhye prādurbhāva iti pratyāyyante /
dhatta iti vartamānanirdeśena prārabdhāparisamātpabhāvādekatarasyāṃ koṭāvaniṣṭheti dyotyate /

children.text: tathā jihvākharāruṇatvavyagragamāgamatvaviṣamākulatvalakṣaṇādharmayogādvyālayamānatvadanteśayanatvaprakāntalīlatvalakṣaṇādharmayogāccānukṣaṇāmākulībhāvamāpādyamānairnaitrahastasañcārairliṅgairyadetadvodhyate, totriṣuṣaṭpadeṣu ca tulitamavadhānadānaṃ tadapyeka tarasyāṃ koṭā vaniṣṭāmeva vyanakti /
children.translated_text: Moreover, from the conjunction of attributes characterized by bloody-red-eye-ness, restless-back-and-forth-movement, and unsteady-agitation, and from the conjunction of attributes characterized by eye-closing, tusk-resting, and commencement-of-playful-movement — the progressive agitation conveyed by the indicative signs of the eye, trunk, and gait that change moment by moment, and the equal allocation of attention to the goads and the bees — this too reveals non-resolution in either extreme.
Therefore, this is the juncture (<s>sandhi</s>) of the emotional states of anger (<s>roṣa</s>) and joy (<s>harṣa</s>).

children.text: bhāvaśabalatā yathā - madhyesakhījanamupahvaravṛttajātaṃ vācā prakāśayati mayyupadeśavṛttyā /
children.translated_text: An example of <s>bhāvaśabalatā</s> (variegation of emotional states): 'She reveals in the midst of her girlfriends what happened during the secret rendezvous, by way of speech in the form of instruction directed at me.'

children.text: sāsūyasapraṇāyasatrapa saprasādaiḥ sā māṃ vilokitavatī caṭulaiḥ kaṭākṣaiḥ //
children.translated_text: 'She glanced at me with sidelong looks that were flirtatious — [mingled] with jealousy, with affection, with modesty, and with graciousness.'

body.translated_text:
Here, in the case of the elephant maddened with rut: the momentary holding of the bloody-red eyes with the tongue followed immediately by their closing; the momentary restless back-and-forth movement of the trunk-hand followed immediately by resting on the tusk; and the momentary agitated unsteadiness of gait followed immediately by the commencement of playful movement — these various and distinctive pairs of behavior, characterized by arising and suppression, manifesting moment by moment, reveal the agitation caused by anger directed at the goad as its object and joy directed at the bee's song. The mutual inability to remain indicates the turbulence.
In all three clauses with compound expressions, the repeated use of 'for a moment, for a moment' conveys that just as the great waves of rage — arising from the successive blows of the goad-bearers — crash one upon another, so too do the blossomings of pleasure from hearing the bee's song arise amid them and overcome [the rage].
The use of the present tense in 'gives' indicates that, since it has begun but not concluded, it does not rest in either extreme.

children.translated_text: Here, the superimposition of jealousy and other [emotions] onto the sidelong glances should not be considered as directly stated meaning.
Therefore, in the heart, the variegation of emotional states (<s>bhāvaśabalatā</s>) is suggested.

children.text: bhāvaśāntiryathā tau saṃmukhapracalitau savidhe guruṇāṃ mārgapradānarabhasaskhalitāvadhānau /
children.translated_text: An example of <s>bhāvaśānti</s> (cessation of emotional states): 'Those two, having set forth toward each other in the presence of elders, with their attention stumbling in the eagerness to give way on the path,'
'Both, having swerved aside in different directions, departed again and again with bashfulness.'

body.text:
atra mativibodha yorupaśamaḥ /
eṣu rasādidhvaniṣu prapañco 'nyato jñeyaḥ /

children.translated_text: Since the author of this treatise was excessively concise, being occupied with elaborating <s>citra-kāvya</s> (ornate poetry), we have shown only a brief indication through examples.

children.text: atha saṃlakṣyakrame śabdaśaktimūlo 'laṅkārarūpo vasturūpaśca niyamena bhavati /
children.translated_text: Now, in the perceptible sequence (<s>saṃlakṣyakrama</s>), [suggestion] based on the power of words necessarily takes the form of <s>alaṃkāra</s> (figure of speech) or <s>vastu</s> (content/theme).

children.text: tatrālaṅkārarūpo yathā - prāpyādharadvayadhurāṃ paricumbatīva līlottaraṃ vilikhatīva nakhatvametya /
children.translated_text: An example of the <s>alaṃkāra</s>-form: 'Having reached the burden of her two lips, it seems to kiss playfully; having attained the state of nails, it seems to scratch;'

children.text: tasyāḥ kaṭākṣavalanaṃ gurusannidhau māmāśrliṣyatīva samavāpya ca bāhubhāvam //
children.translated_text: 'Her sidelong glance-turn, in the presence of the elders, seems to embrace me, having attained the nature of arms.'

body.translated_text: Here there is the subsidence of attraction (<s>mati</s>) and awakening [of love]. The elaboration of these <s>rasa</s>-and-other <s>dhvanis</s> should be understood from other [works].

children.text: atrotprekṣālaṅkāreṇa cumbanādikāraṇā bhāve 'pi saṃbhogasukhā vātpilakṣaṇākāryotpattirūpā vibhāvanā vyajyate /
children.translated_text: Here, through the figure of <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy), <s>vibhāvanā</s> (an extraordinary causal relation) is suggested — namely, the production of an effect characteristic of the enjoyment of love, even in the state of being a mere cause such as kissing, etc.

children.text: vastudhvaniryathā - dṛṣṭiḥ kātaratāmupaiti sahasā tasminpuro 'vasthite, narmālāpini tatra na prativaco jihvāgramārohati /
children.translated_text: An example of <s>vastu-dhvani</s> (suggestion of content): 'My gaze suddenly becomes anxious when he stands before me; when he engages in witty conversation, no reply ascends to the tip of my tongue;'

children.text: saṃsparśaṃ ca na tasya vetyupacitastambhaṃ mamaitadvapuḥ saṃvṛttaḥsakhi saṅgamo 'pi virahaprāyo vidhātāsmi kim //
children.translated_text: 'And my body, overwhelmed by numbness, does not perceive his touch. O friend, even union has become like separation — what has the Creator done to me?'

body.text:
atra vastuni avastutvabhramāt maugdhyalakṣaṇaṃ vastu pratyāyyate /
athārthaśaktimūlovyañjakor'thaḥ svataḥ saṃbhavī kaviprauḍhoktiniṣpāditaḥ kavirnibaddhavaktṛprauḍhoktiniṣpāditaśceti trirūpaḥ /
sa cālaṅkārarūpo vasturūpaśceti pratyekaṃ dvaividhye ṣoḍhā /
ṣaḍvidhasya ca vyaṅgyor'tho vasturūpo 'laṅkārarūpaśceti dvādaśaṃbhedo 'yam /
tathā hi - svataḥsaṃbhavinā vastunā vastu svataḥsaṃbhavinā vastunā alaṅkāraḥ /
svataḥsaṃbhavinālaṅkāroṇa vastu, tena alaṅkāra iti caturdhā /
tathā kaviprauḍhoktiniṣpāditena vastunā vastu, tenālaṅkāraḥ kaviprauḍhoktiniṣpāditena alaṅkāreṇa vastu tena alaṅkāraḥ ityapi caturdhā /
itthaṅkavinibaddhavaktṝprauḍhoktiniṣpādite 'pi viṣayecāturvidhyamanusandheyam /

children.text: atra prapañcaḥ saṃpradāyaprakāśinyāṃ kāvyaprakāśaṭokāyāṃ asmābhiḥ vitatyopa darśita iti tato 'vadhāryaḥ /
children.translated_text: The elaboration of this has been shown in detail by us in the <s>Saṃpradāyaprakāśinī</s> [commentary] on the <s>Kāvyaprakāśa</s>, and should be learned from there.

children.text: iha tu granthagauravabhayāt prastāvānupayogācca na pratanyate /
children.translated_text: Here, however, due to fear of excessive length and irrelevance to the present topic, it is not elaborated.

children.text: diṅmātrantūdāhliyate- tatra svataḥsaṃbhavinā vastunā vastu yathā - adyāpi loke na kavirna so 'sti prācāṃ tulāṃ yaḥ prabalo 'dhiroḍhum /
children.translated_text: Only a brief indication is illustrated. An example of content suggesting content through a naturally occurring object: 'Even today in the world, there is no poet who is powerful enough to ascend the scales of the ancients.'

children.text: purātano nāyamitīya deva tathāpi nindā yadi kiṃ karotu //
children.translated_text: '"This one is not ancient" — O Lord, even so, if there is blame, what can he do?'

body.translated_text:
Here, through the confusion of taking a real thing for an unreal one, the content characterized by naïveté (<s>maugdhya</s>) is conveyed.
Now, suggestion based on the power of meaning: the suggested meaning is of three kinds — naturally occurring, produced by the poet's bold expression, and produced by the bold expression of a character created by the poet.
With each being twofold as <s>alaṃkāra</s>-form and <s>vastu</s>-form, there are six varieties.
And the suggested meaning of each of the six types of suggestion being either <s>vastu</s>-form or <s>alaṃkāra</s>-form, there are twelve divisions.
Thus: by a naturally occurring content — content [is suggested]; by a naturally occurring content — a figure of speech [is suggested]; by a naturally occurring figure of speech — content; by that — a figure of speech: thus fourfold.
Likewise: by a content produced by the poet's bold expression — content; by that — a figure; by a figure produced by the poet's bold expression — content; by that — a figure: thus also fourfold.
Similarly, in the domain of bold expression by a character created by the poet, the fourfold division should be traced.

body.text: atra svataḥsaṃbhavinā vastunā aham evaṃvidha iti vaktuḥ svamāhātmyaprakhyāpanalakṣaghaṇaṃ vastu pratyāyyate //
body.translated_text: Here, through the naturally occurring content, the content of the speaker's self-proclamation of his own greatness — 'I am of such a nature' — is conveyed.

children.text: kavinibaddhenālaṅkāreṇa vastu yathā - dṛṣṭirniṣṭhura baddhasārakhadirāṅgāra sphuliṅgopamā jihve sajjanatarjanolbaṇābalatkālāṅgulīcañcale /
children.translated_text: An example of a figure of speech created by the poet suggesting content: 'The gaze is like the sparks of a bonfire built of firmly-bound Khadira heartwood; the tongue, O friend, is a wagging finger of Death, violently threatening good people;'

children.text: dantāścāntakakelikānanaviṣāṃ (?)kūrānukāraḥsakhe jaṅghe dve yadi tebhujaṅgabhuvanaṃ valmīkaśeṣaṃ bhavet //
children.translated_text: 'The teeth are an imitation of the fangs of the serpents of Death's pleasure-garden; if these were your two legs, O friend, the serpent-world would be reduced to an anthill.'

children.text: atra kaviprauḍhoktiniṣpāditena aprastutapraśaṃsālaṅkāreṇa vidhivihitamanāryāṇāṃ kvicidaṃśe daurbalyaṃ viśvamabhirakṣatīti vastu /
children.translated_text: Here, through the figure of <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant) produced by the poet's bold expression, the content is conveyed that Providence protects the world by giving weakness to the wicked in certain respects.
An example of a figure of speech suggesting a figure of speech through the bold expression of a character created by the poet (in Prākrit): '<s>aṇivāritovagūhaṇa saṃchanda ālāvasoa vavasajaṇā</s>'
'<s>bandhavamaraṇāmahūsava diahe diahe samo arasu</s>'
Translation (chāyā): 'With unrestrained embracing, with spontaneous weeping, with people overwhelmed by grief,'
'May a great festival of the death of relatives descend day after day!'

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text:
kavinibaddhāyāḥ svairiṇyāḥ prauḍhoktiniṣpāditena rūpakālaṅkāreṇa upagūhanādinivāraṇāśālibhyo 'sya bāndhavamaraṇamahotsavasya atiśayapratyāyanātmā vyatirekālaṅkāraḥ pratyāyyate /
itthamanyadapyūhyam /
atha guṇībhūtavyaṅgyasvarūpadik /
guṇībhūtavyaṅgyaṃ vācyāṅgetyādi /
vācyāṅgatvamagūḍhatvamaparāṅgatvamasphuṭatvam, sandigdhaprādhānyaṃ tulyaprādhānyaṃ kākkākṣitpa masundaratvam iti vācyāṅgatvādayo bhedāḥ /

children.translated_text: As has been shown in [the discussion of] <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression) and other [figures].
This should be completed [with the words] 'by the author of the <s>Dhvani</s> [treatise] and others.'

children.text: tatra vācyāṅgatvaṃ yathā - śūnye tvadripurājadhāmni sudṛśāṃ citrārpitā nāṃ karaṃ saṃllāpaspṛhayā patannapi muhuḥ kīraḥsamārohati /
children.translated_text: An example of subordination to the expressed meaning (<s>vācyāṅgatva</s>): 'In the empty palace of your enemy-king, O <s>Śrī Ballāla</s> lord of kings, the parrot, even while falling, repeatedly climbs the hand of the women depicted in paintings, eager for conversation.'

children.text: śrīballālanṛpāla! śiñjitarasānmañjīrarekhāmukhaṃ cañcvagreṇa ca hanta haṃsapṛthukaḥsañcālayankrandati //
children.translated_text: 'And, alas, the young swan, moving with its beak-tip the <s>mañjīra</s> (anklet) chain which seems to have the flavor of jingling sounds, cries out!'

body.translated_text:
Through the <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) figure produced by the bold expression of the libertine woman created by the poet — whereby the great festival of her relatives' death is shown to exceed [even] those who restrain embracing and other [displays] — a <s>vyatireka</s> (contrast) figure is conveyed, whose essence is the demonstration of the surpassing [nature of the festival].
Thus other [examples] should also be inferred.
Now, an indication of the nature of <s>guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> (suggestion subordinated [to the expressed meaning]).
<s>Guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> [is defined as] 'subordinate to the expressed meaning,' etc.
The varieties [are]: subordination to the expressed meaning (<s>vācyāṅgatva</s>), non-concealment (<s>agūḍhatva</s>), non-prominence (<s>aparāṅgatva</s>), indistinctness (<s>asphuṭatva</s>), doubtful predominance, equal predominance, and 'crow-eye-ness' (<s>kākākṣitva</s>, i.e., apparent beauty), etc.

body.text:
atra śūnyīkṛtaripurājaveśmā nāyakaprabhāvātiśayaḥ pratīyamāno 'pi śukahaṃsavṛttāntopapādakatvena sthita iti vācyāṅgatvam /
itthamagūḍhatvādayo 'pi bhedā jñeyāḥ /
itthaṃ dhvaniguṇībhūtavyaṅgyayoḥ kāvyayoḥsvarūpamupodgadhātatvena yathāyogamupanyasya prakaraṇā pratipipādayiṣitaṃ citrākhyaṃ kāvyamadhikīrṣurāha-citraṃ tviti /
dhvaniguṇībhūtavyaṅgyāpekṣayā bhedabāhulyaṃ tarabarthaḥ /
athādisūtramavatārayitumāha-tathāhīti-atha sūtram /
body.translated_text:
Here, the surpassing power of the hero, who has emptied the enemy-king's palace, is perceived; yet since it serves [merely] as a basis for presenting the episode of the parrot and the swan, it has subordination to the expressed meaning (<s>vācyāṅgatva</s>).
Thus the varieties of non-concealment (<s>agūḍhatva</s>) and others should also be understood.
Thus, having presented the nature of both <s>dhvani</s> and <s>guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> poetry by way of preliminary exposition and as appropriate, he [the author] is about to undertake the [discussion of] poetry called <s>citra</s> (ornate), and says: 'As for <s>citra</s>...'
The comparative suffix [-tara] signifies the greater abundance of varieties compared to <s>dhvani</s> and <s>guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s>.
Now, to introduce the opening aphorism, he says: 'Thus...' — and then the aphorism.

body.text: ihārthapaunaruktyaṃ śabdapaunaruktyaṃ śabdārthapaunaruktyaṃ ceti trayaḥ paunaruktyaprakārāḥ || 1 ||
body.translated_text: Here, repetition of meaning (<s>arthapaunaruktya</s>), repetition of sound (<s>śabdapaunaruktya</s>), and repetition of both sound and meaning (<s>śabdārthapaunaruktya</s>) — these are the three types of repetition (<s>paunaruktya</s>). // RuAss 1 //

body.text:
nanu citramityupakramya paunaruktyaprakārakathane kā saṅgatiḥ ityata āha ādau paunakuktyetyādi /
paunaruktyaprakārāṇām eṣāṃ yadetadādau vacanantinnirūpayiṣyamāṇānāṃ śabdārthobhayāśrayatayā kakṣyāvibhāgaṃ ghaṭayituṃ kakṣyāvibhāgasyaiva ca sphuṭīkārāya pratyekaṃ paunaruktyagrahaṇam /
ato 'nuprāsayamakādayaḥ śabdālaṅkārāḥ /
upamārūpakādayor'thālaṅkārāḥ /
lāṭānuprāsādayastūbhayālaṅkārāḥ iti kakṣyāvibhāgo 'nusandheyaḥ /
nanu śabdapratītipūrvakatvādarthapratīteḥ prathamaṃ arthapaunaruktyanirdeśo na yujyata ityata āha-arthāpekṣayetyādi /
antaraṅgatvaṃ prāthamikatvaṃ, arthagatanirdeśaḥ arthaviṣayaka paunaruktya nirdeśa ityarthaḥ /
cirantanaprasiddhyā bhāmahodbhaṭādipūrvācāryaprasiddhyanusāreṇa /
te hi punaruktavadābhāsākhyamarthālaṅkārameva pūrvaṃ lakṣitavantaḥ /
nirdiṣṭasya ca paunaruktyatrayasya sampabratipannatāmabhisandhāyāha-śābde prasthāna ityādi /
itiśabdaṃ yogyer'the vyavasthāpayati -itiśabdaḥ prakāra iti /
nanu traya evetisamāptyarthatā kiṃ neṣyata ityata āha-triśabdādevetyādi /
atrāyamāśayaḥ /
vibhāgenaiva tritvamavagatam /
triśabdāttu parisamātpiḥsiddhā, 'siddhe satyārambho niyamāya' iti nyāyāt /
ata itiśabdaḥ prakāre vivakṣyate /

children.text: na ca mantavyaṃ sati prakāraśabde paunaruktyaṃ prasajediti /
children.translated_text: And one should not think that the word 'type' (<s>prakāra</s>) would produce redundancy [with the enumeration].

children.text: prakāraśabdo hi paunaruktyaprakāramābaha-sa ca paunaruktyaprakāraḥ kena prakāreṇa triprakāra iti jijñāsāyām itiśabdaḥ tatprakāra vacana iti sarvamavadātam /
children.translated_text: For the word 'type' conveys [here] the type of repetition — and when that type of repetition is questioned as 'In what way is it threefold?' — the word <s>iti</s> expresses that type. Thus everything is clear.
The threefold nature ascertained through analysis is concluded by the word <s>tri</s> (three).
The word <s>iti</s> is therefore understood as expressing the threefold nature.

body.translated_text: Now, [one might ask:] having begun with '<s>citra</s>' (the marvelous), what is the connection with the discussion of types of repetition? To this he says, beginning with 'First, repetition...' The statement at the outset of these types of repetition that are to be analyzed — [serves] to organize the classification (<s>kakṣyāvibhāga</s>) according to whether they are based on sound, meaning, or both, and to clarify the classification itself through individual treatment of each type of repetition. Thus, <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration), <s>yamaka</s> (rhyming), etc. are figures of sound (<s>śabdālaṃkāras</s>); <s>upamā</s> (simile), <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor), etc. are figures of meaning (<s>arthālaṃkāras</s>); and <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> (repetition with changed meaning) etc. are figures of both (<s>ubhayālaṃkāras</s>) — this classification should be understood. Now, since the apprehension of meaning presupposes the apprehension of words, the listing of meaning-repetition first seems improper — to this he says, beginning with 'With respect to meaning...' 'Being more intrinsic' (<s>antaraṅgatva</s>) means 'having priority'; 'statement regarding meaning' means 'statement of repetition pertaining to meaning' — this is the sense. 'According to ancient tradition' means 'following the established [views] of earlier masters such as <s>Bhāmaha</s> and <s>Udbhaṭa</s>.' For they indeed defined the figure called <s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s> ('seeming repetition'), which is a figure of meaning, first. Having established the acceptance of the threefold repetition thus stated, he says beginning with 'In the context of sound...' He assigns the word '<s>iti</s>' to its proper sense: 'The word <s>iti</s> [means] type (<s>prakāra</s>).' Now, why is the meaning 'these three only' as indicating completion not intended? To this he says, beginning with 'From the word <s>tri</s> alone...' Here the import is: the threefold nature is already known from the enumeration itself. But from the word <s>tri</s>, completeness is established; [and] by the principle 'When [something] is already established, a [further] statement serves as a restriction' — therefore the word <s>iti</s> is intended in the sense of 'type.'

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus. //

body.text: athaiṣu paunaruktyeṣu heyāṃśaṃ vibhaktuṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: Now, to distinguish the objectionable portion among these types of repetition, the <s>sūtra</s> [states]:

body.text: tatrārthapaunaruktyaṃ prarūḍhandoṣaḥ || 2 ||
body.translated_text: Among these, repetition of meaning (<s>arthapaunaruktya</s>) when full-blown (<s>prarūḍha</s>) is a fault (<s>doṣa</s>). // RuAss 2 //

body.text:
praruḍhagrahaṇasya vyāvartyamudghāṭayati-praruḍhāpraruḍhatveneti /
upādeye viśrāntyarthamiti /
upādeye pratiyegyantare prasṛtāyāḥ pratipattṝ pratīteḥ avyākṣepāya ityarthaḥ /
heyāṃśairhi vivicya tyaktake svarasā bhavatyupādeyamīmāṃsā /
trayanirdhāraṇa iti /
bhāvānayane dravyānayanamiha anusartavyaṃ nirdhārite paunaruktyatraya ityarthaḥ /
nanu praruḍhaṃ doṣa ityucyate /
ko 'yaṃ praroha ityata āha-yathāvabhāsanamityādi /
yacchravaṇasamanantaraṃ yathāvadavabhātaṃ tattathaiva cetpratītiḥviśrāntyantaṃ nirbādham avatiṣṭheta sa praroha ityarthaḥ /
yathoddeśaṃ paunaruktyamadhikṛtya sūtram-
body.translated_text: He reveals what is excluded by the qualifier 'full-blown' — beginning with 'as full-blown and not full-blown.' 'For the purpose of resting in the acceptable' — the meaning is: for the non-obstruction of the cognition (<s>pratīti</s>) that extends to another object to be accepted, arriving at repose. For when the objectionable portions are distinguished and set aside, the investigation of the acceptable [portion] proceeds naturally. 'In the determination of the three' — the meaning is: the procedure of bringing in substances should be followed here, in the sense of 'when the three types of repetition have been determined.' Now, it is said 'Full-blown is a fault.' What is this 'blooming' (<s>praroha</s>)? To this he says, beginning with 'As it manifests...' That which, immediately upon hearing, appears as it is — if the cognition [of it] remains undisturbed until repose (the final understanding) — that is the 'blooming.' This is the meaning. Regarding repetition as introduced, the <s>sūtra</s> [states]:

body.text: āmukhāva bhāsanaṃ punaruktavadābhāsam || 3 ||
body.translated_text: The appearance [of repetition] up to the opening (<s>āmukha</s>) is <s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s> (seeming repetition). // RuAss 3 //

body.text:
āmukham ārambhaḥ /
paryavasānānyathātva ityanena heyāt vaidharmyaṃ darśitam /
nanu lakṣyapade punaruktavadābhāsa iti svarūpaprādhānyena nirdeśo nyāyyaḥ, na tu punaruktavadābhāsamiti kāvyaparatantratayā ityata āha-lakṣyanirdeśa ityādinā /
nāpuṃsakaḥ saṃskāraḥ punaruktavadābhāso yatreti bahubrīhisamāsāśrayaṇenālaṅkāryapāratantryadhvananārthaḥ iti laukikālaṅkāravanna kāvyālaṅkārāṇāṃ alaṅkāryapṛthagbhāvenāpyavasthānasaṃbhavaḥ /
api tu niyamena kāvyapāratantryameveti /
atigambhīreṃ'śe vṛthāprāthanabhīrutāmāviśrikīrṣurāha-prabhedāstviti /
avāntarabhedāḥ prabhedāḥ /
maṅkhīye maṅkhākhyakavikartṛke /
ahīneti /
inaḥsvāmī ahīnām ino bhujaṅgānāmadhīśaśceti /
valayaṃ kaṅkaṇāñceti āmukhe paunaruktyā vabhāsanaṃ, paryavasāneṣu ahīnasya mahato bhujaṅgādhīśasya vapurvalayaṃ kaṅkaṇamasyetyanyathātvam /
itthaṃ śilāderapatyaṃ śailādiḥ śailādeḥ nandina iva caritamasyeti, śailādiṃ nandayati caritamasyeti ca /
tayā kṣataḥ kandarpo darpaśceti, kṣataḥ kandarpadarpo yeneti ca /
tathā vṛṣaḥ puṃrūpo gauśceti, vṛṣaḥśreṣṭha iti ca /
tathā śikhī pāvakaśca locane yasyeti ca śikhipāvakalocana iti ca /
tathā sarvamaṅgalāsahitaḥ pārvatīśa iti ca sarvairmaṅgalaismahitaśteti paunaruktyaṃ cāmukhābhāsanaṃ, paryavasānānyathātvaṃ ca anusandheyam /
atha vyastatayā samāsāntarāyaśrayatayā ca darśiyitumudāharaṇāntaraṃ-dāruṇa iti /
paunaruktyāpekṣayā dāruṇā iti pañcamyantam /
paryavasāne tu prathamāntam /
itthaṃ bhasma ca bhūtiśceti bhasmavano 'bhivṛddiriti ca /
tathā raktaṃ ca śoṇāṃ ceti ca rudhiravacchreṇamiti cāvagantavyamṣa /
itthaṃ subantāpekṣayā dvidhodāhṛtam /
atha tiṅantāpokṣayā-bhujaṅgeti /
kuṇḍalī sarpo bhujaṅgaśca kuṇḍalī ceti bhujaṅgakuṇḍalavāniti ca /
śaśī śubhrāśuḥ, śītaguśceti /
śaṃ śivaḥ śubhraiḥ aṃśubhiḥ śītaṃ cakṣurindriyamiti ca /
haraḥśiva iti ceto hara iti ca yojanīyam /

children.translated_text: In '<s>śaśiśubhrāṃśuśīta-guru</s>' etc., the [apparent] repetition has been shown.

children.text: pāyādavyācceti tu tiṅantāpekṣayā ita ityapāyaviśeṣaṇatvena paryavasāne pañcamyantatayā pāyādavyādityanyathātvam /
children.translated_text: But in '<s>pāyād avyāt</s>' (may he protect, may he guard), with respect to the verbal form, the word '<s>ita</s>' [functions] as a qualifier of 'departure'; at the conclusion, being in the ablative, '<s>pāyād avyāt</s>' [shows] the otherness [of meaning].
'Where there is <s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s>' — thus indeed the formation [is understood].
It is employed for the manifestation of the oneness of the object to be adorned (<s>alaṅkārya</s>).

body.translated_text: 'Opening' (<s>āmukha</s>) means 'beginning.' 'The otherness at the conclusion' — by this, the difference from the fault [of actual repetition] is shown. Now, in the term to be defined (<s>lakṣyapada</s>), the designation <s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s> by its own form as primary would be proper, not the [neuter form] <s>punaruktavadābhāsam</s> as dependent on poetry — to this he says beginning with 'The designation of the defined term...' The neuter formation [is used] because of the <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound construction 'that in which there is <s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s>' — the purpose being to indicate the dependence on the object to be adorned (<s>alaṅkārya</s>). Just as with worldly ornaments, poetic ornaments (<s>kāvyālaṃkāras</s>) cannot exist independently of the object to be adorned; rather, they are necessarily dependent on the poem. Wishing to display caution against vain elaboration on a profoundly deep topic, he says: 'The sub-divisions, however...' Sub-types (<s>avāntarabhedāḥ</s>) are the sub-divisions. 'In the [work] of <s>Maṅkha</s>' — in [the work] composed by the poet <s>Maṅkha</s>. '<s>Ahīna</s>' — the lord of <s>inas</s> (snakes), the sovereign of serpents. 'Bracelet' (<s>valaya</s>) means 'armlet.' In the opening, there is the appearance of repetition [between 'ahīna' and 'serpent-lord']; at the conclusion, 'the body-bracelet of the great lord of serpents' — [showing] the otherness [of meaning]. Similarly, 'the offspring of <s>Śilā</s> etc.' [means] <s>Śailādi</s>; '<s>Śailādi</s>'s conduct like that of <s>Nandin</s>' or 'he who delights <s>Śailādi</s> by his conduct.' 'By her, <s>Kandarpa</s> is wounded, and [his] pride' or 'he whose pride of <s>Kandarpa</s> (love-god) is wounded.' Likewise, '<s>Vṛṣa</s>' [means] a bull, a male-formed cow, or '<s>Vṛṣa</s>' [means] the best. Similarly, '<s>Śikhin</s>' [means] fire, and 'the eyes of whom [are like peacocks]' or '<s>Śikhipāvaka-locana</s>' (having eyes [bright as] peacock and fire). Similarly, 'accompanied by <s>Sarvamaṅgalā</s>, the lord of <s>Pārvatī</s>' or 'honored by all auspicious things' — the [apparent] repetition and the appearance of [repetition in] the opening, and the otherness at the conclusion, should be understood. Now, to show [examples] separately and through alternative compound constructions, another example — '<s>dāruṇa</s>' (terrible). With respect to the repetition, '<s>dāruṇā</s>' is in the ablative case; but at the conclusion, it is in the nominative. Similarly, 'ashes' (<s>bhasma</s>) and 'prosperity' (<s>bhūti</s>) [both mean ash/prosperity], and 'the prosperity of one who has ashes.' Likewise, 'red' (<s>rakta</s>) and 'crimson' (<s>śoṇā</s>), and 'blood-colored row' — this should be understood. Thus, with respect to nominal forms (<s>subanta</s>), examples have been given in two ways. Now, with respect to verbal forms (<s>tiṅanta</s>) — '<s>bhujaṅga</s>' (serpent): '<s>kuṇḍalī</s>' means 'snake,' 'serpent and coiled one' or 'one who has serpent-earrings.' '<s>Śaśin</s>' [means the moon], 'having bright rays,' 'cool-rayed.' '<s>Śam</s>' [means] auspicious, '<s>Śiva</s>'; 'with bright rays' [means] 'the eye-sense [is made] cool' — the construction should be understood thus.

body.text:
atha śabdapaunaruktyaprastāvāya sūtram-
śabdapaunaruktyaṃ vyañjanamātrapaunaruktyaṃ svaravyañjanasamudāyapaunaruktyaṃ ca /
atrādyaṃ padamuddeśyaṃ caramaṃ tu dvayaṃ vidheyam /
śabdapaunaruktayaṃ vyañjanamātraniṣṭatayā, svaravyañjanasamudāyaniṣṭhatayā ca dviprakāramityarthaḥ /
nanu kevalasvarapaunaruktyasya kiṃ vṛttamityata āha-alaṅkāraprastāva ityādi /
alaṅkāro hi vicchrittiḥ, tatprastāve kevalasvarapaunaruktyama cārutvāt na gaṇanāmarhatīti bhāvaḥ /
tatra vyañjanamātramadhikṛtya sūtram-
body.translated_text: Now, the <s>sūtra</s> introducing repetition of sound (<s>śabdapaunaruktya</s>): Repetition of sound is [either] repetition of consonants alone or repetition of the combination of vowels and consonants. Here, the first term is the subject (<s>uddeśya</s>), and the last two are the predicate (<s>vidheya</s>). The meaning is: repetition of sound is of two types — as established in consonants alone, and as established in the combination of vowels and consonants. Now, what about repetition of vowels alone? To this he says, beginning with 'In the context of ornament...' An ornament is a beautification (<s>vicchṛtti</s>); in that context, repetition of vowels alone, not being charming, does not merit being counted — this is the purport. Regarding consonants alone, the <s>sūtra</s> [states]:

body.text: saṅkhyāniyame pūrvaṃ chekānuprāsaḥ || 4 ||
body.translated_text: When there is a restriction on the number [of repeated consonants], first [comes] <s>chekānuprāsa</s> (artful alliteration). // RuAss 4 //

body.text:
ko 'yaṃ saṅkhyāniyama ityata āha-dvayorvyañjanetyādi /
yugmaśo 'vasthitānāṃ vyañjanasamudāyānāṃ parasparamanekadhāsādṛśyam iha saṅkhyāniyamaḥ /
kinnāmeti /
darduro bhekaḥ /
kāyaṃ nipīḍya vapurāyāsya /
sitacchradāḥ haṃsāḥ /
atra darduraduradhyavasāya ityādau saṅkhyāniyamaḥ /
nanu sāyaṃ kāyamityatra ko 'laṅkāra ityata āha-atra sāyaṃ śabdetyādi /
yakāramātrasādṛśyāpekṣayā hi sāya sāyeticchrekānuprāsaḥ /
sāyaṃ kāyamiti tusānusvāra yakāramātrāpekṣayā vṛttyanuprāsaḥ /
itthaṃ ca sati sāyaṃ śabde dvayorekābhidhānalakṣaṇāḥsaṅkaraḥ abhidhatta ityabhidhānaṃ vācaka śabdaḥ ekavācakānupraveśalakṣaṇā ityarthaḥ /
lakṣyapadaṃ nirvivakṣurāha-chrekā vidagdhāḥ iti /
chekopalālitatvācchekānuprāsa ityarthaḥ /
athānuprāsāntarāya sūtram-
body.translated_text: What is this 'restriction on number'? To this he says, beginning with 'Of two consonants...' The multiform mutual similarity of groups of consonants arranged in pairs — this is the restriction on number here. '<s>Kinnāma</s>' — <s>dardura</s> means 'frog.' '<s>Kāyam nipīḍya</s>' — exerting the body. '<s>Sitacchadāḥ</s>' — swans. Here, in '<s>darduraduradhyavasāya</s>' etc., there is the restriction on number [of paired consonants]. Now, what is the ornament in '<s>sāyaṃ kāyam</s>'? To this he says, beginning with 'Here, in the word <s>sāyam</s>...' With respect to the similarity of the <s>ya</s>-consonant alone, '<s>sāya sāya</s>' constitutes <s>chekānuprāsa</s>. But '<s>sāyaṃ kāyam</s>' — with respect to the <s>anusvāra</s> and <s>ya</s>-consonant together — constitutes <s>vṛttyanuprāsa</s> (style-alliteration). And this being the case, in the word <s>sāyam</s>, the confusion (<s>saṅkara</s>) characterized by two [types] being expressed in a single expression [occurs] — '<s>abhidhāna</s>' means 'expressive word,' and the characteristic is the entry of a single expression [for both types] — this is the meaning. Explaining the term to be defined, he says: '<s>chekā</s>' means 'the skillful' (<s>vidagdha</s>). Because it is caressed/nurtured by the skillful, it is <s>chekānuprāsa</s> — this is the meaning. Now, the <s>sūtra</s> for the other type of alliteration:

body.text: anyathā tu vṛttyanuprāsaḥ || 5 ||
body.translated_text: Otherwise, it is <s>vṛttyanuprāsa</s> (style-alliteration). // RuAss 5 //

body.text:
anayathātvaṃ tridhā saṃbhavatītyāha-kevalavyañjanetyādi /
kevalavyañjanasādṛśyaṃ samudāyatvābhāvādanyathātvam /
ekadhā samudāyasādṛśyaṃ tvanekadhātvavirahāt /
tryādīnāṃ punaḥsamudāyānāṃ dvayātiriktatvādanyathātvam anusandheyam /
lakṣyapadaṃ nirvakti-vṛttistviti /
śṛṅgārādirasaviṣayo yo 'yaṃ pratiniyamabhājāṃ varṇānāṃ vyañjanavyāpāraḥ sa vṛttirucyate /
so 'yaṃ varṇavyāpāro 'smin varṇāracanātmake kavivyāpāre 'stītyupacāreṇa varṇaracanāvṛttirityāha-tadvatī punarityādi /
tasyāstraividhyaṃ darśayati - sā ca paruṣetyādi /
śrutipratikūlatā varṇānāṃ paruṣatvam /
yā paruṣavarṇārabdhā sā gauḍīyī rītiḥ /
yā tu komalavarṇārabdhā sāvaidarbhī /
madhyamavarṇārabdhā tu pāñcālī /
etā rītayo vāmanādibhiḥ kāvyātmatvena siddhintatāḥ /
upapattiparyālocanāyāṃ tu kāvyātmakathā tāvadāstām /
yāvatā śabdālaṅkāreṣvapi yo bahiraṅgo vṛttyanuprāsātmā varṇālaṅkāraḥ taddharmatvāt tacchreṣabhūtā etā ityalamaprāsaṅgikavaidaddhya pravacanena /
sahyā iti /
viṣadravamuca iti /
kiraṇāpekṣayā duḥsahatvam /
vāyvapekṣayā tu garalakalpajalakaṇāyogaḥ /
saralā anarālapātinyaḥ /
sitāsitaruceḥ uttaralatārakatvāt anavasthitavarṇasanniveśāḥ sācīkṛtāḥ apāṅgānnirgantum ivehamānāḥsālasā rasānuśayaṃ nivartamānāḥ /
yaduktaṃ bhāvaprakāśe-"ālasyaṃ tadabhīṣṭārthāt vrīḍāderyannivartanam" iti /
sākūtā bhavatu paśyāma itīva vyāharantyaḥ sarasāḥ /
raso rāge viṣe vīrye tiktādau pārade drave /
roṣāruṇimnā viṣayaṃ viṃliṃpantyaḥ mānānuvidvāḥ dṛṣṭaśrutādyaparādhajanmā roṣomānastena saṃmūrcchitāḥ jvalatkalpā ityarthaḥ /
atra kevalavyañjanapaunaruktyalakṣaṇāmanyathātvam /
vṛttistu roṣavarṇanātparuṣā /
āṭopeneti /
yadyapi kavervāṇī prabalena śabdāḍambareṇa khelantī prārambhe prathate, tathāpi satāṃ mānorañjanaṃ na kurute amandaiḥ sundaraiśca guṇālaṅkāraiḥ mukharīkṛtaḥ saniṣpandaṃ vilasadrasāyana rasā sārānusārī śṛṅgārādiko raso yāvanna syādityatra kevalavarṇā sāmyañcaturṣvapi pādeṣvalaṅkāraḥ /

children.text: bhphaṅkāritetyādāvekadhā samudāyasādṛśyaṃ rasāyana rasetyatra tu raseti samudāyatrayasya parasparasādṛśyamityanusandheyam /
children.translated_text: In '<s>bhphaṅkārita</s>' etc., there is a similarity of a group in one way; but in '<s>rasāyana rase</s>' etc., the mutual similarity of three [instances of] the group '<s>rasa</s>' should be understood.

children.text: tathā ca "āṭope" tyādau gauḍīyā "amandasundare" tyādau vaidarbhī, "guṇālaṅkāre"tyādau pāñcālīyā ca tattadarthānusāreṇa draṣṭavyā /
children.translated_text: And thus in '<s>āṭope</s>' etc., the <s>Gauḍīyā</s> [style]; in '<s>amandasundare</s>' etc., the <s>Vaidarbhī</s>; and in '<s>guṇālaṃkāre</s>' etc., the <s>Pāñcālī</s> — should be observed according to the respective content.
That arrangement of sounds which is excellent and follows the <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment) etc. —

children.text: so 'nuprāsaḥsa ca cheka vṛttyu pādhiva śādrūdvidhā //
children.translated_text: that is <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration); and it is of two kinds: <s>cheka</s> (artful) and <s>vṛtti</s> (style-based).

body.translated_text: He says that this 'otherwise' is possible in three ways, beginning with 'A single consonant...' Similarity of a single consonant alone constitutes 'otherwise' because of the absence of a group. Similarity of a group in one way [constitutes 'otherwise'] because of the absence of manifold [repetition]. And the groups of three etc. [constitute 'otherwise'] because they exceed two — this should be understood. He explains the term to be defined: '<s>Vṛtti</s>' (style) is... The operation of consonants that are specially assigned to the emotional states (<s>rasas</s>) such as <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (love) etc. — that is called <s>vṛtti</s>. This operation of sounds exists in this compositional activity of the poet, which consists of the arrangement of sounds — thus by figurative usage, 'the <s>vṛtti</s> of sound-arrangement' — he says beginning with 'That which possesses it...' He shows the threefold nature of this, beginning with 'It is either <s>paruṣa</s>...' Harshness to the ear constitutes the roughness (<s>paruṣatva</s>) of sounds. That which is composed of rough sounds is the <s>Gauḍīyā</s> style. That which is composed of soft sounds is the <s>Vaidarbhī</s>. That which is composed of medium sounds is the <s>Pāñcālī</s>. These styles have been established as the soul of poetry by <s>Vāmana</s> and others. But upon reflective examination, let the question of whether they are the soul of poetry be set aside; insofar as even among the figures of sound, the figure of sound-arrangement in the form of <s>vṛttyanuprāsa</s>, being external — since these [styles] are properties of that, they are its superiors. Enough of this digression into irrelevant erudition! '<s>Sahyā</s>' [means] the Sahya mountains. '<s>Viṣadravamucaḥ</s>' — with respect to [the sun's] rays, [the clouds are] unbearable; with respect to the wind, [they are] discharging drops of water like poison. '<s>Saralāḥ</s>' — falling in straight lines, not crooked. '<s>Sitāsitaruceḥ</s>' — because of having later-visible stars, having an unstable arrangement of colors; '<s>sācīkṛtāḥ</s>' — as if striving to emerge from the corner-glances; '<s>sālasāḥ</s>' — turning back with the aftermath of emotion. As stated in the <s>Bhāvaprakāśa</s>: 'Lassitude (<s>ālasya</s>) is the turning back from the desired object due to bashfulness etc.' '<s>Sākūtāḥ</s>' — as if saying 'Look!'; '<s>sarasāḥ</s>' — full of flavor. '<s>Rasa</s>' [is used] in [the senses of] love, poison, vigor, bitter taste, mercury, and fluid. 'Painting their object with the redness of anger' — <s>māna</s> (indignant love) is anger born from offenses seen or heard; overcome by it, they appear as if blazing — this is the meaning. Here, the 'otherwise' characterized by the repetition of single consonants [is illustrated]. The style, however, is rough (<s>paruṣā</s>) because of the description of anger. '<s>Āṭopena</s>' (with ostentation) — although the speech of the poet, sporting with powerful verbal grandeur, spreads forth at the beginning, it does not delight the minds of the good — unless the <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment), such as <s>śṛṅgāra</s> etc., following the essence, quivering vitally, made vocal by fine and beautiful qualities and ornaments, should arise. Here, the similarity of single sounds in all four quarters [of the verse] constitutes the ornament.

children.translated_text: Where a pair of [consonant] groups attains manifold similarity,
that, because of its being caressed by the skillful (<s>cheka</s>), is called <s>chekānuprāsa</s> by the learned.
The operation (<s>vyāpṛti</s>) of consonants pertaining to <s>rasa</s> is [called] <s>vṛtti</s> (style).
The arrangement of sounds possessing that [quality] is called <s>vṛtti</s> (style).
It has been analyzed as threefold by the ancients, with the divisions of <s>Vaidarbhī</s> etc.
Because it is characterized by that [style], it is called <s>vṛttyanuprāsa</s> (style-alliteration).

body.text: itthaṃ varṇālaṅkāro dvidhā darśitaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus, the figure of sound (<s>varṇālaṃkāra</s>) has been shown to be twofold.

body.text:
atha śabdālaṅkāraprastāvaḥ /
tatra yamakalakṣaṇāya sūtram /
body.translated_text: Now [begins] the introduction to figures of sound (<s>śabdālaṃkāra</s>). Here, the <s>sūtra</s> defining <s>yamaka</s> (rhyming):

children.translated_text: Repetition of the combination of vowels and consonants is <s>yamaka</s> (rhyming). // RuAss 6 //

body.text:
svaravyañjanātmakasya śabdasamudāyasya yattenaiva rūpeṇa punarvacanaṃ tadyamanādyamakam /
tasya pādāvṛttyardhāvṛttādayo bhedāścirantanaireva bahudhā prapañcitāḥ /
te kāvyagaḍubhūtā iti nehapratanyante /
kintu sarveṣāmevaiṣāṃ bhedānāmetadvaicitryatrayam āvahatīti abhiprāyeṇāha-atra kacidbhinnārthetyādi /
yamyamānayoḥ samudāyayordvayorapi kacidbhinnārthatā, kvacidanarthakatakā, kvacidekasasyārtha vattvamaparasya anarthakatvamiti kroḍīkṛtasakalaviśeṣametadbhedatrayam /

children.translated_text: '<s>Yo ya</s>' (whoever) —

children.text: rucire ramye vanajāyate padmadalavat dīrghe tasyāḥ netre yo yaḥ paśyayati, tasya tasyānyanetreṣu abhiratireva na jāyate /
children.translated_text: In her charming, lotus-petal-like long eyes — whoever (<s>yo yaḥ</s>) gazes [upon them], for him no delight arises in other eyes.

children.text: idaṃ dvayoḥsārthakatve anarthakatve dvairūpye yathā- tvaṃ rāvaṇa! jagatpuṇyairlaṅkālaṅkārabhūrabhūḥ /
children.translated_text: This [illustrates the case] where both [repeated groups] are meaningful and where both are meaningless, as a twofold [example]: 'You, O <s>Rāvaṇa</s>! By the merits of the world, you were the ornament of <s>Laṅkā</s> — you were, [and now] you were not!'
By whom the essence of <s>Vālmīki's</s> work, born of <s>Sārasvatī</s> (the goddess of speech), grew of its own accord.

body.translated_text: The re-statement of a sound-combination consisting of vowels and consonants in that same form — that is <s>yamaka</s> (the 'twin'). Its varieties — recurrence in a quarter-verse, half-verse, etc. — have been elaborated in many ways by the ancients. Since these are the very lifeblood of poetry (<s>kāvyagaḍu</s>), they are not elaborated here. Rather, [the author] states with the intent that all these varieties embody this threefold distinction, beginning with 'Here, sometimes with different meanings...' Of the two 'twinned' [sound-]groups, sometimes both have different meanings, sometimes [both are] meaningless, and sometimes one has meaning while the other is meaningless — this threefold division encompasses all the specific types.

body.text:
atra "rabhūrabhūri" ti anarthakatā /
"laṅkālaṅkāre"tyādaudvairūpyam /
itthamarthapaunaruktye punaruktavadābhāsaṃ śabdapaunaruktye tu anuprāsayamakālaṅkārau ca vivecitau /
ayobhayapaunaruktye heyāṃśaṃ vibhaktuṃ sūtram /
body.translated_text:
Here '<s>rabhū rabhūri</s>' is meaningless.
In '<s>laṅkā laṅkāre</s>' etc. there is confusion of form.
Thus, in the case of repetition of meaning, <s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s> (semblance of repetition) has been analyzed; and in the case of repetition of words, the figures of <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration) and <s>yamaka</s> (rhyming) have been analyzed.
To distinguish the objectionable element in the case of both types of repetition, the <s>sūtra</s> (aphorism) states:

body.text: śabdārthapaunaruktyaṃ praruḍhaṃ doṣaḥ || 7 ||
body.translated_text: Repetition of word and meaning that is well-established (<s>praruḍha</s>) is a fault. || <s>RuAss</s> 7 ||

body.text: praruḍhagrahaṇasya prayojanamāha-praruḍhagrahaṇamityādi //
body.translated_text: He explains the purpose of the qualification 'well-established' — 'the qualification <s>praruḍha</s>...' etc.

body.text:
apraruḍhapaunaruktyaṃ vakṣyamāṇo bhedaḥ /
tasya praruḍhādvailakṣaṇyamadoṣātmakakatvam /
tadevādoṣātmakatvamabhiyuktasaṃvādena draḍhayati-yadāhurityādi /
śabdasyārthasya ca punarvacanamanuvādādatirikte viṣaye doṣaḥ ityarthaḥ /
athopādeyāṃśamadhikṛtya sūtram /
body.translated_text:
Repetition that is not well-established is a variety to be discussed later.
Its distinction from well-established repetition lies in its not being a fault.
He confirms this non-faulty nature through agreement with competent authorities — 'as has been said' etc.
The meaning is: repetition of word and meaning, when it occurs in a domain beyond mere reiteration (<s>anuvāda</s>), is a fault.
Now, regarding the acceptable element, the <s>sūtra</s> states:

body.text: tātparyabhedavattu lāṭānuprāsaḥ || 8 ||
body.translated_text: But when there is a difference in purport (<s>tātparya</s>), it is <s>Lāṭānuprāsa</s>. || <s>RuAss</s> 8 ||

body.text:
yatra paunaruktye śabdārthau tāveva, tātparyamātraṃ tvanyat /
so 'yaṃ lāṭopalālanāt lāṭānuprāsaḥ /

children.translated_text: Therefore, because it is not universal, some call it <s>Grāmyānuprāsa</s> (rustic alliteration).
'The locks (<s>tālā</s>) are awake' — [an example].

children.text: tadā jāyante guṇāḥ yadā te sahṛdayairgṛhyante /
children.translated_text: Qualities (<s>guṇas</s>) are born only when they are apprehended by sensitive readers (<s>sahṛdayas</s>).
'Graced by the rays of the sun, the lotuses become lotuses indeed.'

body.translated_text:
Where in the repetition the word and meaning are the very same, but only the purport is different —
that is <s>Lāṭānuprāsa</s>, so called because of its association with the <s>Lāṭa</s> people (as a term of endearment/fondling).

body.text:
atra dvitīyayorguṇa kamalaśabdayoḥ ślāghādyā śrayatvaṃ tātparyabhedaḥ /
nanu yatra prakṛtimatraṃ tadarthaśca punarucyate, na pratyayatadarthau, atra ko 'laṅkāra ityata āha-atrābja patretyādi /
vibhaktyāderiti /
ādyohi nayanaśabdo bahuvrīhivartitvāt anyapadārthaliṅga vacanavibhaktikaḥ /
dvitīyastu svaliṅgavacanavibhaktikaḥ /
ato neha vibhaktyādeḥ punaruktiḥ /
nāpi lāṭānuprāsatvahāniḥ /
kuta ityata āha-bahutaraśabdārthapaunaruktyāditi /
itthaṃ ca sati padanubandhanatayā prātipadika mātranibandhanatayā ca lāṭānuprāso dvidhā mantavyaḥ /
ananvayādviśeṣamasya darśayati-kāśāḥ kāśā ivetyādi /
ananvaye hyekasyaivopamānopameyatvam /
tatra yadyapi arthapaunaruktyaṃ lakṣaṇam, athāpi śabdapaunaruktyaṃ doṣabhayādaṅgīkriyata eva /
"yathoddeśastathaiva pratinirdeśa" iti nyāyollaṅghane paryāyaprakramabhedadoṣaprasaṅgāt /
lāṭānuprāse tu śabdapaunaruktyamapi lakṣaṇamiti viśeṣaḥ /
tadetadāha-anyonyāpekṣetyādi /

children.translated_text: The repetition of word and meaning that are mutually dependent is <s>Lāṭānuprāsa</s>.
In <s>Ananvaya</s>, however, it is repetition of meaning alone — this is the meaning.
A summary verse on the subject of meaning — '<s>ananvaye tu</s>' (in <s>Ananvaya</s>, however) etc.
Because of the propriety of uniformity between the initial statement and the reference, based on the defining characteristic of sameness of form.

body.translated_text:
Here, in the second occurrence of the words <s>guṇa</s> and <s>kamala</s> (lotus), the difference in purport consists in their becoming a basis for praise etc.
Now, where only the stem and its meaning are repeated, but not the suffix and its meaning — what figure is there? To this he replies: 'here, the lotus-petal...' etc.
'Of the suffix etc.' — For the first word <s>nayana</s> (eye), being used in a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound, takes the gender, number, and case of the other word.
But the second occurrence has its own gender, number, and case.
Therefore there is no repetition of suffix etc. here,
nor is there a loss of the status of <s>Lāṭānuprāsa</s>.
Why? — He answers: 'because of the repetition of most of the words and meanings.'
Thus, <s>Lāṭānuprāsa</s> should be understood as being of two kinds: based on the connection of whole words, and based on stems alone.
He shows the distinction of this figure from <s>Ananvaya</s> (non-correlation simile) — '<s>kāśāḥ kāśā iva</s>' (the <s>kāśa</s> grasses are like <s>kāśa</s> grasses) etc.
For in <s>Ananvaya</s>, one and the same thing serves as both the standard and the object of comparison.
There, although repetition of meaning is the defining characteristic, still repetition of words is also accepted out of fear of the fault.
Because if the principle 'the reference must be exactly as the initial statement' is violated, the fault of variation in synonymous expression and sequence would arise.
But in <s>Lāṭānuprāsa</s>, the repetition of words is also part of the definition itself — this is the distinction.
This is stated: 'mutually dependent...' etc.

children.text: yatra tāveva śabdārthau tātparyaṃ tu vibhidyate /
children.translated_text: Where the words and meanings are the very same but the purport differs,
that repetition is accepted by the teachers as <s>Lāṭānuprāsa</s>.
In <s>Ananvaya</s>, the identity of words exists only out of fear of the fault of repetition;
but in this <s>Lāṭānuprāsa</s>, it is directly part of the definition itself.

body.text: atha paunaruktyanibandhanānāmalaṅkārāṇāṃ niyamanāya sūtram /
body.translated_text: Now, a <s>sūtra</s> to regulate the figures based on repetition:

body.text: tadevaṃ paunaruktye pañcālaṅkārāḥ || 9 ||
body.translated_text: Thus, there are five figures based on repetition. || <s>RuAss</s> 9 ||

body.text:
yathaivaṃ paunaruktyaṃ vyapāśritya vargaśo 'vatiṣṭhante /
tathopamādayo 'pi sādharmyādivyapāśrayeṇa vargaśo 'vasthāyina ityava bodhitaṃ mantavyam /
tadidaṃ nyāyavidāmavagatamevetyabhiprāyeṇāha-nigadavyākhyātamiti /
nigadaśabdoccāraṇaṃ tanmātreṇa pratītārthatvāt vyakhyātakalpamityarthaḥ /
atha citrārthaṃ sūtram /
body.translated_text:
Just as these five figures are established in groups based on repetition,
so too <s>upamā</s> (simile) and other figures are established in groups based on similarity etc. — this should be understood as implied.
This is evident to those versed in logical reasoning — hence he says 'explained by mere statement.'
The word '<s>nigada</s>' (statement) means that its meaning is understood by the mere utterance of the word, so it is as good as explained — this is the meaning.
Now, the <s>sūtra</s> on <s>Citra</s> (visual/pictorial poetry):

body.text: varṇānāṃ khaṅgādyākṛtihetutve citram || 10 ||
body.translated_text: When phonemes (<s>varṇas</s>) cause the shape of a sword etc., it is <s>Citra</s> (pictorial figure). || <s>RuAss</s> 10 ||

children.translated_text: Now, on the petals, two letters each, reading clockwise from the eastern petal.
Entry and exit are in the cardinal-direction petals.

children.text: atrāyaṃ niṣkarṣaḥ- karṇikāyāṃ likhedekaṃ dvau dikṣu vivikṣu ca /
children.translated_text: Here is the summary: one letter should be written in the pericarp, two in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
entry and exit in the cardinal directions — this constitutes the lotus-pattern.

body.translated_text:
He explains the connection — 'in the context of repetition...' etc.
Of phonemes arranged in sequence in specific positions, i.e., in the specific parts forming the sword etc., the repetition in their reading — the description of pictorial compositions like the sword-pattern (<s>khaṅgabandha</s>) etc. which consist of such repetition, fits in the context of the discussion of repetition — this is the meaning.
Now, how is this a sound-figure? Since written phonemes have no denotative capacity — he replies: 'although...' etc.
For the arrangement of sword etc. belongs to written letters only, not to those that inhere in auditory space.
Denotative capacity belongs only to those that inhere in auditory space, not to those in written form.
Thus, although the denotative sound-figure status of those in sword-pattern etc. is not strictly valid, still, because ordinary people perceive denotative capacity even in written letters, the status of denotative sound-figure is figuratively attributed — this is the purport.
Therefore, because it appeals to the unsophisticated mind and because it is outside true denotative sound, poets need not pay regard to it — this should be understood.
He explains the meaning of the word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.) — 'by the word <s>ādi</s>...' etc.
According to derivation and possibility, each word applies respectively.
Therefore, according to derivation and possibility, the lotus-pattern, drum-pattern, cow-urine pattern, and other compositions are admitted — this is to be supplied.
'Shines' — the illustrious assembly, rich in essence, shines through genius.
The word '<s>bata</s>' expresses wonder.
'Rich in <s>rasa</s>' — adorned on all sides with <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment) etc.
'Whose delusion is destroyed' — whose confusion has been eliminated.
'Whose self is cultivated' — who has cultivated the self through those impressions.
'Skilled in debate' — skillful in mere debate, either from the desire to know truth or from the desire to conquer.
Therefore it is like <s>Sudharmā</s>, the assembly hall of the gods — this is the meaning.
Wishing to teach the method of extracting this, he says: 'this is an eight-petaled...' etc.
The petals are four in the cardinal directions and four in the intermediate directions; the first letter is in the pericarp.

children.translated_text: By attributing to written phonemes the status of denotative phonemes through similarity,
the sword-pattern and other <s>Citra</s> (pictorial) compositions are accepted as poetic ornaments.

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.translated_text: Thus ends the section on <s>Śabdālaṅkāra</s> (sound-figures) in the <s>Alaṅkārasarvasvasañjīvanī</s> composed by <s>Śrī Vidyācakravartin</s>.

body.text: || arthārthālaṅkārāḥ || tatra sādṛśyavicchrattiviśeṣaiḥ nānālaṅkārabījabhūtāmupamāmādau lakṣayituṃ sūtram /
body.translated_text: || Figures of Meaning (<s>Arthālaṅkāras</s>) || Now, to define <s>upamā</s> (simile) first, as it is the seed of the various figures based on the varieties of similarity, difference, and distinction — the <s>sūtra</s> states:

body.text: upamānopayayoḥ sādharmye bhedābhedatulyatve upamā || 11 ||
body.translated_text: <s>Upamā</s> (simile) is the equal balance of difference and non-difference in the common property (<s>sādharmya</s>) between the standard of comparison (<s>upamāna</s>) and the object of comparison (<s>upameya</s>). || <s>RuAss</s> 11 ||

children.translated_text: 'This one is a <s>Pāṇḍya</s>'—thus.
Because necklaces, waterfalls, and the like possess qualities, they stand in the relation of original and reflection.
<s>Sādharmya</s> (similarity) is called <s>upamā</s> when it operates through the balance of difference and non-difference.
It attains threefold variety due to the variation of qualifying properties.

body.translated_text: That which is compared, carrying similarity, is the <s>upamāna</s> (standard of comparison)—the non-contextual meaning; and this by rule always possesses superior qualities, because it serves as the substratum of qualities. That to which similarity is carried is the <s>upameya</s> (object of comparison)—the contextual meaning; and this by rule, being the recipient of qualities, always possesses lesser qualities. The aspect of non-difference measured between these two, the relation of common properties, is the figure of <s>upamā</s> (simile)—such is the meaning of the sūtra. Wishing to explain this, to avoid confusion of the topic, he says '<s>arthālaṅkāra</s>' (figure of meaning). Now, similarity exists only between <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>, not between cause and effect and the like. Since these two are established without being exhausted, what is the point of verbal specification?—to address this he says '<s>upamānopameyayor</s>' etc. Since both are well-known, this is a commencement for restricting the scope: only the ornamental quality of well-established <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s> is intended. Therefore, although the relationship of <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s> between Mount <s>Meru</s> and a mustard seed can be conceived through intention, it is not the domain of <s>alaṅkāra</s>—because it is not recognized; this should be kept in mind. To show the distinction by exclusion of '<s>bhedābheda</s>' (difference-and-non-difference), he analyzes the modes of similarity, beginning with '<s>sādharmye yatra</s>' etc. '<s>Vyatirekaval</s>' means 'like <s>vyatireka</s> (contrast).' '<s>Tatra tasyeva</s>'—the suffix '<s>vat</s>' has the same force. The meaning is: 'as in the figure of <s>vyatireka</s>.' '<s>Yathāsyām</s>'—the rest is 'as will be illustrated.' To confirm with authoritative agreement what was stated—that <s>upamā</s> consists in the equality of difference and non-difference—he says '<s>yadāhur</s>' etc. The rest is 'the commentators (<s>bhāṣyakṛt</s>) and others.' '<s>Sāmānya</s>' means similarity. '<s>Viśeṣa</s>' means dissimilarity. <s>Upamā</s>, which is resemblance, operates through the balance of similarity and dissimilarity—such is the purport. He shows the purpose of this figure's primacy in its enumeration: '<s>upamaiva ca</s>' etc.—through the variety of its modes. For example: 'the face is like the moon'—that is <s>upamā</s>. 'The face is like the face itself'—that is <s>ananvaya</s>. 'The face is like the moon, and the moon like the face'—that is <s>upameyopamā</s>. 'Seeing the face, I remember the moon'—that is <s>smaraṇa</s> (remembrance). 'The face is the moon'—that is <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor). 'The heat is cooled by the moon-face'—that is <s>pariṇāma</s> (transformation). 'Is it the moon or the face?'—that is <s>sandeha</s> (doubt). 'The face is the moon, so the <s>cakora</s> birds rejoice'—that is <s>bhrāntimān</s> (delusion). 'It is the moon, not the face'—that is <s>apahnuta</s> (concealment). 'Surely like the moon'—that is <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy). 'Look at the moon [meaning the face]'—that is <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole). 'In this rainy season, the face and the moon's orb both fade'—that is one kind of <s>tulyayogitā</s> (equal connection). 'In autumn both are beautiful'—that is another. 'This and that are beautiful'—that is <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination).

body.text: ananvayaṃ sūtrayati-
body.translated_text: Now he formulates the sūtra on <s>ananvaya</s> (non-correlation)—

body.text: ekasyaivopamānopameyatve ananvayaḥ || 12 ||
body.translated_text: When one and the same thing serves as both <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>, that is <s>ananvaya</s>. (RuAss 12)

body.text:
