'In that'—thus.

children.text: atra hi dhūmaśikhā romāvalivapuḥ pariṇamatītyuktau , na romāvalirapitu dhūmaśikheti pratīyate /
children.translated_text: Here, when it is stated that the smoke-flame transforms into the form of a row of body-hair, the apprehension is: 'not a row of body-hair, but a smoke-flame.'
By this, this [<s>apahnutī</s>] has been shown as also being of the suggested (<s>pratīyamāna</s>) kind.

body.translated_text: Here is the issue: although the twofold division based on the reversal of the order of denial and superimposition does exist, there is no aesthetic wonder (<s>camatkāra</s>). For the mere possibility of division is not the cause for the establishment of a figure; rather, it is the possibility of division accompanied by aesthetic wonder. And aesthetic wonder would arise when there is sentence-division; but in a single sentence, even though the reversal of the order of <s>chadma</s> etc. words may occur, there is no differentiation of apprehension at all—because in its capacity as a verbal qualifier, the primacy of apprehension is fixed with respect to the action. Therefore, with the use of <s>chadma</s> and the like, it is not counted as twofold. To show the absence of variety with examples, he says '<s>tatra apahnave</s>' etc. '<s>Samanantaram</s>'—immediately after, pertaining to the correlate stated here: 'in "<s>udbhrānta ujjhata</s>"' etc. '<s>Jyotsnā bhasma</s>'—'<s>cūraṇā</s>' means 'smearing.' '<s>Antardhāna</s>'—in the night context, it means 'concealment' or 'dissolution'; in the other context, it means 'attainment of invisibility.' '<s>Mudrā</s>' means the alms-bowl; '<s>kapāla</s>' for that purpose is the <s>mudrākapāla</s>. '<s>Parimala</s>' means 'rubbing'; from that, the mark produced is what is indicated. Just as through the use of words like <s>chadma</s>, the meaning is imputed through denial, so too it can occur through another mode—he says '<s>kvacit punar</s>' etc.

children.translated_text: When the contextual is denied and something else is established, that is <s>apahnutī</s> (concealment).
Through the negative particle, words like <s>chadma</s> (guise), and through other words—it is threefold.
There may be a distinctive delight through the balance of difference and non-difference, like <s>upamā</s> etc.
But from <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor), in the aspect of non-difference, because of the dependence on superimposition in the primary sense.

body.text:
tāmeva saṅgatiṃ viśadīkurvan utprekṣāprastāvāyāha-evamabhedaprādhānya ityādi /
āropamūlā rūpakādayo apahnutyantāḥ /
adhyavasāyagarbhāstu utprekṣādayaḥ /
ata eva ṭīkā -tatreti /
adhyavasāyagarbheṣu madhye ityarthaḥ /
atha sūtram -
body.translated_text: Clarifying that very connection, he introduces the topic of <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy), beginning with 'Thus, where non-difference predominates...' Those rooted in superimposition (<s>āropa</s>) are <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) etc., ending with <s>apahṇuti</s> (concealment). But those containing conceptual identification (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) are <s>utprekṣā</s> etc. Hence the commentary [states] 'Among those...' — meaning 'among those containing conceptual identification.' Now the <s>sūtra</s>:

body.text: adhyavasāye vyāpāraprādhānye utprekṣā || 21 ||
body.translated_text: When conceptual identification (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) predominates in operation, it is <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy). // RuAss 21 //

body.text:
adhyavasāyo niścayajñānam /
sa ca loke dvirūpaḥ samyagātmā mithyārūpaśca /
ubhayarūpo 'pyayaṃ nālaṅkāraḥ /
nahi śuktiriti samyagadhyavasāye rajatamiti mithyādhyavasāye vā vicchittiḥ kācit /
ubhaya visakṣaṇāstu jānato 'pyetasmin tadeveti yo 'dhyāsarūpasya ihālaṅkāratvena parigṛṅyate /
tasyaiva alaukikasya vicchittirūpatvāt /
tasya ca dvayī gatiḥ /
kadācidadhyavasāyātmanaḥ svarūpasya prādhānyaṃ, kadācidadhyavasitasya viṣayasya /
itthaṃ ca satyadhyavasāye viṣayabhūte yadā adhyavasānasya prādhānyaṃ tadotprekṣālaṅkāra iti sūtrārthaḥ /
tadetadavayavaśo vyācaṣṭe-viṣayanigaraṇenetyādi /
nigaraṇaṃ nigalanam /
svarūpato 'palāpaityarthaḥ /
viṣayaṃ nigīrṇavato viṣayiṇo viṣayitādātmyena pratītasya ihādhyavasāyo abhimata iti yāvat /
anenālaukikasyaivādhyavasāyasya alaṅkārabījatvaṃ darśitam /
vyāpāraprādhānyagrahaṇasya vyāvartyamuddhāṭayitumāha- sa ca dvividha ityādi /
tatra sādhyasya svarūpamāha-sādhyo yatretyādi /
sādhya - iti yadaikaṃ vākyamākṣiptena tacchabdenārthenābhisaṃbandhaḥ /
uttaravākyagato 'pi yacchabdaḥ pūrvavākyācchabdopādānanirapekṣa eva tadarthena sambandhamīṣṭe /
yatra viṣayiṇo 'satyatayā pratītiḥ sa sādhya ityarthaḥ /
atredamanu sandheyam /
mukhaṃ mukhatvena jānanneva yadā nūnaṃ candra iti saṃbhāvayati tadā viṣayī candro mukhatvenāsatyaḥ pratibhāti tadādhyavasāyaḥ sādhyaḥ /
nanu sādhya evāstu adhyavasāyaḥ siddho vā, abhedapratītau kathamasatyatvaṃ ityata āha- asatyatvaṃ cetyādi /
viṣayigatasya candrādigatasya mādhuryādeḥ dharmasya viṣaye, mukhādāvupanibandhe, nūnaṃ candra ityasyāṃ daśāyāṃ viṣayiṇyeva saṃbhavatyayaṃ viṣathayetu na saṃbhavatīti pratīyamānatvāt /
viṣayaviṣayiṇorabhedasphuraṇe 'pi dharmasyāsatyatāpratītyā na prarohati /
ato 'dhyavasānavyāpārasya sādhyatā /
nanu ko dharmaḥ? kiṃpramāṇā cāsau? tadāśrayasya satyatvāsatyatva pratītirityata āha-dharmo guṇakriyārūpaḥ ityādinā /
guṇakriyārūpa iti dharmasya sākalyakathanāt tadubhayamūlatayā utprekṣāsaṃbhavasmūcitaḥ /
asya hi dharmasya saṃbhavo 'saṃbhavaśca viṣayyāśrayatayā saṃbhavaḥ asaṃbhavastu viṣayāśrayatayā /
itthaṃ ca sati satyatvāsatvapratītirnāprāmāṇikā /
kutaḥ? saṃbhavāśrayasya tatrāvasthāyāṃ paramārthabuddhyanudayāt asatyatvaṃ pratīyate /
yatastaditarasya tu satyatvameva paramārthatvāt /
carcitamarthaṃ niṣkarṣayati-yasyāsatyatvamityādi /
ataśceti /
yata itthamadhyavasāyaḥ sādhyaḥ ataḥ utprekṣāyāmadhyavasāyavyāpārasyaiva prādhānyamityarthaḥ /
atha siddhaṃ vivecayati-siddho yatretyādi /
siddha iti pūrvavadekaṃ vākyam /
sa iti dyotitaḥ ko 'sāvityata āha - yatra viṣayiṇo vastuta ityādi /
yadā tu mukhamuddaśya candro 'pamiti prayogaḥ tadā vastuto 'satyo 'pi viṣayī satyatayā pratīyate /
satyatvapratīterhetumāha-satyatvaṃ cetyādi /
saṃbhavāśrayasya aparamārthatvapratītirasatyatvasya nimittam /
yata itthamataścādhyavasitasyārthasyaiva prādhānyaṃ, tadātiśayoktirvakṣyate /
yadā sādhyatvapratītiḥ tadādhyavasāyasya paryāyān vyutpādayati - tatra sādhyatveti /
carcitalakṣaṇāniṣkarṣaṇam-tadevamityādi /
tasyāḥsāmānyatastāvaddvaividhyamāha-sā ca vācyetyādi /
tatrāpi sāmānyāccāturvidhyaṃ darśayati-sā ca jātikriyetyādi /
adhyavaseyatvena saṃbhavyatvena /
nanvaprakṛtagrahaṇaṃ kim? prakṛte 'pyevaṃ saṃbhavādityata āha-prakṛtasyaitadityādi /
prakṛtaṃ hi lau kikaṃ kavikḷtpa vicchrattividhuratayā na vaicitryāya /
bhedacatuṣṭayamapi dvidhā darśayati-pratyekaṃ ca bhāvābhāvetyādi /
bhāvarūpā saṃbhāvanā abhāvarūpā ceti /
ayaṃ vyāpārabhedādbhedaḥ /
pūrvaṃ vyāpāravadbhedāt vyāpāranimittabhedādāha-bhedāṣṭakasya cetyādi /
bhedaṣoḍaśakamapi nimittopādānānupādānābhyāṃ dviguṇāyati-teṣāṃ cetyādi /
atha saṃbhāvyasya hetvādi rūpatayā punastraividhyamāha-teṣu ca pratyekamityādi /
vā(cyāṃ)nigamayati-eṣā gatirityādi /
tatrāpohya aṃśāyāha- tatrāpi dvavyasyetyādi /
pātanoyāḥ hāpanīyāḥ /
pratīyanāmāṃ vibhaktumāha-pratīyamānāyāścetyādi /
uddeśata etāvanta /
lakṣaṇāparīkṣayostu kṛtayoḥ katicana hīyanta iti bhāvaḥ /
ye hīyante tān prastautitathāpi nimittasyetyādi /
tairiti (nimittā)nupādānanibandhanaiḥ /
ayaṃ prakāra iti pratīyamānotprekṣāprakāraḥ ityarthaḥ /
nimittānupādānaṃ na saṃbhavatīti yatpratijñātaṃ tatpramāṇo na draḍhayati-ivādyanupādāna ityādi /
ivādyanupādānanimittakīrtanayoranyatarābhāve na kiñcitpramāṇāmutprekṣaṇe /
anupāttanimittakā hi yā vācyotprekṣā tasyām ivādyupādānabalādevotprekṣaṇapratītiḥ /
iha punarivādyanupādānavandhyāyāṃ pratīyamānāyāṃ nimittabalādeveti nimittopādānaniyamaḥ /
svarūpotprekṣaṇamapi na saṃbhavatītyāha-prāyaścetyādi /
prāyograhaṇāt paryāyoktanayena svarūpasya kvacitsaṃbhavadapyutprekṣaṇaṃ gamyasyāpibhaṅgyantarābhidhānānna nirāpaṇārhamiti dyotitam /
pratīyamānāṃ nigamayatitadevamiti /
yathāsaṃbhavaṃ saṃbhavamanatikramya /
tathā hi pratīyamānotprekṣā tāvat vācyotprekṣāprakṛtikā /
vācyotprekṣāṣaṇṇāvatidhoddiṣṭā /
yathā jātiguṇakriyādravyāṇām utprekṣyatvena catasra utprekṣāḥ /
jātayaḥ pratisvaṃ caturviśatidhā prathante /
yathā jātyutprekṣā tāvat bhāvābhāvābhimānarūpatayā dvidhā /
dvividhāpi guṇanimittikā, kriyānimittikā ca /
itthaṃ caturdhā /
sācopāttanimittānupāttanimittā cetyaṣṭadhā /
aṣṭavidhāpi hetusvarūpaphalotprekṣārūpatayā trividhā iti caturviśatiprakārā /
anenaiva nayenānyadapyutprekṣātrayaṃ pratyekaṃ caturviśatidhāmantavyam /
tathā ca pratyekaṃ triskandhikā etā hetusvarūpaphalotprekṣaṇatayā skandhatrayamapi pratisvamaṣṭavidham /
tathā hi upāttaguṇanimittā bhāvābhimānarūpiṇī hetujātyutprekṣā /
saivānupāttaguṇanimittā /
tathopāttakriyānimittā, saivānupāttakriyānimittā ceti bhāvābhimānarūpatayā caturdhā /
evamabhāvābhimānarūpatayā caturdheti hetūtprekṣāskandho 'ṣṭavidhaḥ /
anayaivarītyā svarūpotprekṣāskandhaḥ phalotprekṣāskandhaśca pratisvamaṣṭavidheti jātyutprekṣā triskandhatayā caturviśatidhā /
evaṃ guṇakriyādvavyotprekṣāpi pratyekaṃ caturviśatidhā vijñeyā /
tatra dvavyotprekṣāyāṃ hetuphalotprekṣāpāteṣoḍaśakahāniḥ /
ataḥ sthūladṛśā tāvat aśītividhā vācyā /
pratīyamānāyāṃ tu anupāttanimittāyā niravaśeṣaṃ pāte aṣṭacatvāriśaddhāniḥ /
upāttanimittāyāṃ ca svarūpotprekṣāpāte ṣoḍaśakahāniḥ /
ato dvartriṃśadbhedāḥ pratīyamānā mantavyāḥ /
ubhayarūpāyāmapi asya vaicitryāntarāyāha-eṣā cetyādi /
arthāśrayāpi arthālaṅkāro 'pītyarthaḥ /
dharmoguṇakriyātmako viṣayo yasya saḥ /
śliṣṭaśabdaḥ kaściddheturbhavatyasyāḥ /
utprekṣā hyarthālaṅkāraḥ /
śleṣaḥ punarubhayālaṅkāro 'laṅkārāntarabādhakaśca /
tathāpi dharmaviṣayeśliṣṭaśabdahetukā saṃbhavatyeṣā na bādhyate, na cobhayālaṅkāraprātpiriti yāvat /
yathetthaṃ śleṣamutprekṣāṅgaṃ tathopamāpi aṅgamasyāḥ bhavatītyāha-kvacitpadārthānvayetyādi /
padārthasamanvayadaśāyām upamayopakramaḥ /
tathopakrāntāpyupamāvākyārthatātparyaparyālocanamahimnā abhimantuḥsaṃbhāvayiturvyāpāro 'pārohakrameṇasaṃbhāvanavyāpārasya pratītiviśrāntyantaṃ uparyupari prasaraparipāṭyā utprekṣāyāṃ paryavasyati /
atha apahnutiprastāvaḥ /
utprekṣāṅgatvena yadapahnutiḥ pratijñāntā, tasyā ayamavasara ityabhiprāyeṇāha-kvacicchralādi ityādi /
itthaṃye prakārāḥ uktāḥ, ye ca vakṣyante teṣāṃ vaicitryādasyā iyattaiva nāstītyāha-ataścoktavakṣyamāṇetyādi /
nanu yadyānantyaṃ kathamudāharaṇato darśayiṣyate ityata āha-sāmpratantvityādi /
diṅmātreṇetyādi /
yathā diṅmātreṇodāhṛtā api nyāyataḥsākalyena jñātuṃ śakyate, tatheti yāvat /
uddeśakramamāviścikīrṣurāha-tatra jātyutprekṣā yatheti /
sa vaḥ pāyāditi /
kuṭilatvalakṣaṇo guṇo nimittam /
aṅkuraśabdo jātivacanaḥ /
ata upāttaguṇanimittikā bhāvābhimānarūpiṇī jātyutprekṣeyam /
tatra yadyapi svarūpamutprekṣyate na tu hetuphale, athāpyuddeśakramavirodhātsoṃ'śo nodājihīrṣitaḥ /
evamudāharaṇeṣudāhartavyā viśeṣāṃśāḥ svayamanusandheyāḥ /
kramasyāvivakṣaṇāt nāsmābhiḥ pratisvaṃ pratanyante /
atra jātyutprekṣātvaṃ vivicya darśayati-atrāṅkuretyādi /
atha kriyotprekṣā-limpatīvetyādi /
kriyotprekṣātvaṃ vivecayati-atra lepanetyādi /
na ca mantavyaṃ varṣaṇasya nabhaḥkartṛkatvāt na tamogatatvamiti /
nabhaso 'pi tamasādhiṣṭhintasyaiva varṣaṇakartṛkatvasaṃbhavādanena paraṃparāyātāyā api sambhāvanāyā utprekṣātvaṃ dyotitam /
nanūttarārdhānudāharaṇe ko heturityata āha-uttaretvityādi /
upamaiva notprekṣeti /
atraitadupahvaram-upamānāṃśaścellokataḥ siddhastadopamaiva dvayoḥsiddhatvādivaśabdaḥ sādharmyadyotakaḥ /

children.translated_text: But when [the comparison] is imagined by the poet, then it is <s>utprekṣā</s> alone.
Because of the ordinary-world impossibility of the standard of comparison, the word <s>iva</s> indicates imagining (<s>saṃbhāvanā</s>).
Here are subsidiary verses: When the aspect of comparison attains establishment in the ordinary world,
then it is simile alone, for the word <s>iva</s> indicates similarity.

body.translated_text: Conceptual identification (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) is the cognition of certainty. In the ordinary world, it is of two forms: correct and erroneous. Neither form [by itself] constitutes an ornament. For there is no aesthetic charm (<s>vicchitti</s>) in correctly identifying 'This is a shell' or erroneously identifying 'This is silver.' But that which differs from both — when even a knower [perceives] 'This is that very thing' — this superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>) is what is accepted here as the ornament, because it alone, being extraordinary (<s>alaukika</s>), has the nature of aesthetic charm. And it has two possible directions: sometimes the own-nature of the identification predominates, sometimes the object identified with. Thus, when the identification itself predominates while the object identified with [remains subsidiary] — that is the ornament <s>utprekṣā</s>. This is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>. He explains this part by part, beginning with 'By the swallowing of the object...' 'Swallowing' (<s>nigaraṇa</s>) means 'engulfing' — the meaning is: the concealment of [the object's] own nature. Of the subject (<s>viṣayin</s>) who has engulfed the object, the identification here means the one apprehended as identity with the subject — this is the purport. By this, it is shown that only the extraordinary (<s>alaukika</s>) identification is the seed of the ornament. To reveal what is excluded by the qualification 'predominance of operation,' he says beginning with 'And it is of two kinds...' There he states the nature of the <s>sādhya</s> (to-be-established [type]), beginning with '<s>Sādhya</s> is where...' '<s>Sādhya</s>' — this forms one sentence with [the relative pronoun] <s>yatra</s>, connected by the word <s>tat</s> implied in meaning. Even if the <s>yat</s>-word occurs in a subsequent sentence, it seeks connection with the meaning independently of word-borrowing from the previous sentence. Where the subject (<s>viṣayin</s>) is cognized as unreal — that is <s>sādhya</s>. This is the meaning. Here the following should be understood: when one, knowing the face as a face, yet imagines 'This is surely the moon' — then the subject (the moon) appears as unreal in its aspect of being a face, and the identification is <s>sādhya</s>. Now, let the identification be <s>sādhya</s> or <s>siddha</s> (established) — how can there be unreality in the cognition of non-difference? To this he says, beginning with 'And the unreality...' The quality such as sweetness etc. belonging to the subject (the moon etc.), when attributed to the object (the face etc.) — in the state of 'surely [this is] the moon' — [the quality] is possible in the subject alone and not possible in the object. This is what is cognized. Even though non-difference between object and subject flashes forth, the identification does not bloom into fullness because of the cognition of the unreality of the quality. Hence the <s>sādhya</s> nature of the operation of identification. Now, what is this quality? And what is the authority for the cognition of reality and unreality of its locus? To this he says, beginning with 'The quality is in the form of attribute and action...' Since the word 'quality' (<s>dharma</s>) comprehensively refers to [both] attributes (<s>guṇa</s>) and actions (<s>kriyā</s>), the possibility of <s>utprekṣā</s> is indicated as rooted in both. For this quality has possibility and impossibility — possibility by virtue of its locus being the subject, impossibility by virtue of its locus being the object. This being so, the cognition of reality and unreality is not without authority. Why? Because, in the state where one rests in the locus of possibility, the ultimate cognition does not arise — hence unreality is cognized. While for the other [the subject], reality alone [obtains], because it is the ultimate. He draws out the discussed meaning, beginning with 'That whose unreality...' 'Therefore' — since identification is <s>sādhya</s> in this way, therefore in <s>utprekṣā</s>, the operation of identification itself predominates. This is the meaning. Now he analyzes the <s>siddha</s> (established [type]), beginning with '<s>Siddha</s> is where...' '<s>Siddha</s>' forms one sentence as before. [The question arises:] what is indicated by the word <s>sa</s>? To this he says, beginning with 'Where the subject in reality...' But when the expression is 'The moon resembles the face' — then the subject, though in reality unreal [as a face], is cognized as real. He states the reason for the cognition of reality, beginning with 'And the reality...' The non-cognition of the non-ultimate nature of the locus of possibility is the cause of unreality [not being cognized]. Since this is so, therefore the identified object itself predominates — that will be stated as <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole). When there is cognition of <s>sādhya</s> nature, he teaches the synonyms of identification, beginning with 'There, <s>sādhyatva</s>...' The extraction of the discussed definition [is given] beginning with 'That is thus...' He states its general twofold nature, beginning with 'And it is [either] expressed (<s>vācya</s>)...' Even within that, he shows the general fourfold nature, beginning with 'And it [applies to] genus, action...' 'As what is to be identified with, as what is to be imagined as possible.' Now, what is the point of mentioning 'non-primary' (<s>aprakṛta</s>)? Since this is possible even in the primary [subject]? To this he says, beginning with 'Of the primary, this...' For the primary [i.e., real-world identification], being worldly and devoid of the aesthetic charm of poetic invention, does not serve variety. He shows the fourfold division in two ways, beginning with 'And each, through presence and absence...' The positive form of imagining (<s>saṃbhāvanā</s>), and the negative form — this division is based on the difference in operation. Previously, from the difference in what possesses the operation, now from the difference in the cause of the operation, he says beginning with 'And of the eightfold division...' The sixteenfold division is doubled by the inclusion and non-inclusion of the cause, beginning with 'And of those...' Now, he states the further threefold nature of what is imagined, through the forms of cause etc., beginning with 'And in each of those...' He concludes the expressed (<s>vācyā</s>) [type], beginning with 'This is the procedure...' There, he states the portion to be set aside, beginning with 'And there, of substance...' 'To be dropped' means 'to be omitted.' He states [the procedure] for analyzing the suggested (<s>pratīyamānā</s>) [types], beginning with 'And of the suggested...' 'These are [the types] by way of enumeration.' The purport is: when definition and examination are carried out, some are eliminated. He introduces those that are eliminated, beginning with 'Nevertheless, of the cause...' 'By those' means 'based on non-inclusion of the cause.' 'This procedure' means 'the procedure of suggested <s>utprekṣā</s>.' He strengthens with authority the claim that non-inclusion of the cause is not possible, beginning with 'Non-inclusion of <s>iva</s> etc....' When either the non-inclusion of <s>iva</s> (like) etc. or the mention of the cause is absent, there is no authority for imagining. For in expressed <s>utprekṣā</s> that lacks a stated cause, the cognition of imagining arises only by the force of using <s>iva</s> etc. But here, in the suggested [type] where <s>iva</s> etc. are not used, [the cognition arises] only by the force of the cause — hence the restriction that the cause must be included. He says that even the imagining of own-nature is not possible, beginning with 'Generally...' The word 'generally' indicates that even though imagining of own-nature is sometimes possible through the method of <s>paryāyokta</s> (circumlocution) — since the thing to be understood is expressed through another mode — it is not worthy of refutation. He concludes the suggested [type], beginning with 'That is thus...' 'According to possibility' means 'not transgressing what is possible.' For the suggested <s>utprekṣā</s> is indeed based on the expressed <s>utprekṣā</s>. The expressed <s>utprekṣā</s> has been enumerated in ninety-six ways. Thus: four types of <s>utprekṣā</s> according to genus, quality, action, and substance as what is imagined. The genus types individually ramify into twenty-four. Namely: genus-<s>utprekṣā</s> is first twofold through positive and negative imagining. Each twofold [type] is [further divided as] caused by quality and caused by action — thus fourfold. Each fourfold [type], with stated and unstated cause, becomes eightfold. Each eightfold [type], through being cause-imagining, own-nature-imagining, and result-imagining, is threefold — thus twenty-four types. By this same method, the other three types of <s>utprekṣā</s> should each be understood as twenty-four-fold. And thus, each having three divisions through cause, own-nature, and result imagining, each division is individually eightfold. Namely: genus-<s>utprekṣā</s> of the cause-division, positive-imagining form, with stated quality as cause. The same with unstated quality as cause. Similarly, with stated action as cause, and with unstated action as cause — fourfold through positive imagining. Similarly, fourfold through negative imagining — thus the cause-<s>utprekṣā</s> division is eightfold. In the same way, the own-nature-<s>utprekṣā</s> division and the result-<s>utprekṣā</s> division are each individually eightfold. Thus genus-<s>utprekṣā</s>, through three divisions, is twenty-four-fold. Similarly, quality-, action-, and substance-<s>utprekṣā</s> should each be known as twenty-four-fold. Among those, in substance-<s>utprekṣā</s>, the dropping of cause- and result-<s>utprekṣā</s> reduces [it] by sixteen. Thus, roughly speaking, the expressed type has eighty varieties. In the suggested type, with the complete dropping of unstated-cause [varieties], forty-eight are eliminated. And in the stated-cause [variety], with the dropping of own-nature-<s>utprekṣā</s>, sixteen are eliminated. Thus thirty-two varieties of the suggested [type] should be understood. Even in the combined form, he states another variety of this, beginning with 'And this...' 'Even being based on meaning' means 'even being a figure of meaning.' 'Having quality and action as the object of its quality' [means:] the quality whose object is [constituted by] quality and action. A word with double meaning (<s>śliṣṭa</s>) sometimes becomes its cause. For <s>utprekṣā</s> is a figure of meaning, while <s>śleṣa</s> (double meaning) is a figure of both [sound and meaning] and would normally override another figure. Nevertheless, this [<s>utprekṣā</s>] based on a double-meaning word as cause, having its object in a quality, is possible [without being overridden] — it is not overridden, nor does it become a figure of both. This is the purport. He says that just as <s>śleṣa</s> can be an auxiliary of <s>utprekṣā</s>, so too can <s>upamā</s> (simile), beginning with 'Sometimes, in the connection of word-meanings...' In the state of connecting word-meanings, there is an opening through simile. Even though begun as simile, by the power of reflecting on the purport of the sentence-meaning, the operation of the imaginer — through a process of non-obstruction, with the operation of imagining spreading upward and upward until repose of cognition — culminates in <s>utprekṣā</s>. Now [begins] the introduction of <s>apahṇuti</s> (concealment). With the intention that 'This is the occasion for that <s>apahṇuti</s> which was mentioned as an auxiliary of <s>utprekṣā</s>, ending with assertion' — he says beginning with 'Sometimes, beginning with concealment...' The varieties that have been stated and those yet to be stated — because of their variety, there is no limit to this [figure]. He says this beginning with 'Therefore, the stated and to-be-stated...' Now, if it is infinite, how will it be shown through examples? To this he says beginning with 'For the present...' 'By way of mere indication...' — just as [types] exemplified by mere indication can be known in their totality through reasoning, so too [here]. Wishing to reveal the order of enumeration, he says: 'There, genus-<s>utprekṣā</s> is as follows.' '<s>Sa vaḥ pāyāt</s>' (May he protect you) — the quality characterized by crookedness is the cause. The word '<s>aṅkura</s>' (sprout) denotes genus. Therefore, this is a genus-<s>utprekṣā</s> with stated quality as cause, in the form of positive imagining. Although in this [example] the own-nature is imagined and not the cause or result, still, since it would contradict the order of enumeration, that aspect was not intended to be highlighted. Similarly, the specific aspects to be highlighted in the [following] examples should be understood by oneself. Since the order is not intended [to be rigidly specified], we do not elaborate on each individually. Here he demonstrates the genus-<s>utprekṣā</s> nature with discrimination, beginning with 'Here, the sprout...' Now, action-<s>utprekṣā</s>: '<s>limpati iva</s>' (as if anointing) etc. He discriminates the action-<s>utprekṣā</s> nature, beginning with 'Here, anointing...' And one should not think that since rain is caused by clouds, [anointing] cannot belong to darkness. Since it is possible for clouds themselves, being pervaded by darkness, to be the agent of rain — by this, it is shown that even imagining arrived at through a chain [of connections] has the nature of <s>utprekṣā</s>. Now, what is the reason [for citing] the latter half-verse as an example? To this he says, beginning with 'In the latter...' 'It is only simile, not <s>utprekṣā</s>.' Here this should be noted: if the aspect of comparison is established in the ordinary world, then it is simile alone — since both [sides] are established, the word <s>iva</s> indicates similarity.

children.translated_text: But when this [aspect] is not established in the ordinary world and is imagined by the poet,
then it is <s>utprekṣā</s> alone, for the word <s>iva</s> means imagining (<s>saṃbhāvanā</s>).

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus. //

body.text:
atha guṇotprekṣā-saiṣāsthalīti /
iyaṃ pratiṣṭhamānasya dāśaratheḥ sītāṃ pratyuktiḥ /
guṇotprekṣātvaṃ darśayati-duḥkhaṃ guṇaṃ iti /
atha dravyotprekṣā-pātālametaditi /
dravyatvaṃ darśayati-candrasyetyādi /
udāharaṇacatuṣke 'pi anugataṃ viśeṣam uddhāṭayati-etāni bhāvābhimāna ityādi /
athābhāvābhimāne-kapolaphalakāviti /
kaṣṭa kṛcchrāt /
tathāvidhāviti /
svanubhavaikasamadhigamyo ramaṇīyātiśayodyotyate /
kṣāmatāgamanaṃ naisargikam /
parasparadarśanābhāvo hetutvenotprekṣyate /
ata evābhāvābhimānarūpanā /
tadetaddarśayati-atrāpaśyantāvitītyādi /
nyāyasya sujñānatvāt /
sthālīpulākanyāyenodāharaṇamātramiti na vyutkramadoṣaḥ śaṅkanīyaḥ /
kramāpekṣayā tu jātyādyutprekṣāpuraskāreṇodāhartavyam /
tadetadabhisandhāyāha-evaṃ jātyādāvapyūhyamiti /
itthaṃ jātyādi catuṣkam abhāvābhimānarūpatayodāhṛtam /
atha bhedāṣṭakasya guṇakriyānimittatodāhartavyā /
tatra guṇanimittakatvenodājihīrṣurāha-navabisalatetyādi /
tadvivecitacaram /
evaṃ guṇanimittakatvaṃ kriyādyutprekṣātraye sphuṭataratvādudāharaṇanirapekṣanityabhisandhāya kriyānimittakatvenodāharatir-idṛkṣamityādi /
kṣāmatā gamanalakṣaṇakriyāhyadarśanotprekṣāyā nimittam /
iyatā ṣoḍaśakamudāhṛtaṃ mantavyam /
atha nimittopādānānupādānābhyāṃ ṣoḍaśakasya yaddvaividhyaṃ pratijñātaṃ tatra nimittopādānasya samanantarodāharaṇānyevodāharaṇatvena darśayati - ete nimittetyādi /
kuṭikatva kṣāmatāgamanayorupādānādanupādānamapyudāhṛteṣveva darśayati-liṃpatīvetyādi /
atra lepanāditvena saṃbhāvane vyāpanādi nimittaṃ nopāttam /
iyatā dvātriṃśadbhedā udāhṛtāḥ /
atha dvātriṃśaddhetuphalasvarūpātmakatayā tridhodāhartavyā /
tatra heturūpatayodāharati-viśleṣaduḥkhādivetyādi /
atra duḥkhaguṇo hetutvenotprekṣitaḥ /
itthaṃ jātikriye hetutvenāvagantavye /
dravyotprekṣāyāṃ tadabhāvāt tannibandhanam aṣṭakaṃ pātanīyam /
atha svarūpatayodāharati-kuberajuṣṭāmityādi /
juṣṭāṃ sevitām /
kuberajuṣṭā digudīcī, sā pratināyikātvenānusandhīyate /
samaya ekadartuviśeṣaḥ /
anyadātvananyatra gamanalakṣaṇāḥ saṃketaḥ /
dakṣiṇasyāṃ diśi nāyikātvamanusandhīyate /
vyalīkam aparādhaḥ /
atra niśvāsasya svarūpamevotprekṣyaṃ, na tu hetuḥ phalaṃ vā /
itthaṃ guṇotprekṣāditraye svarūpātmakatvaṃ jñeyam /
atha phalavotprekṣā-colasyetyādi /
atra darśanakriyā vipāṭanaphalatvenotprekṣyate /
itthaṃ jātiguṇayorapi phalatvamanusandheyam /
dravyotprekṣāyāṃ hetuphalāsaṃbhavāt tannibandhanaṃ ṣoḍaśakaṃ pātanīyam /
itthamaśītividhāpi vācyotprekṣā sākalyenodāhṛtakalpaiva /

children.translated_text: Concluding this, he says: 'Thus of <s>Vācyotprekṣā</s> (expressible poetic fancy),' and so on.
Now the <s>Pratīyamānā</s> (suggested poetic fancy) is illustrated in order: '<s>Mahilāsahasra</s>' (a thousand women), and so on.
'In your heart, O fortunate one, filled with a thousand women, she, not being loved,
spends the whole day doing nothing else, yet makes even [her] slender body thinner still.'

body.translated_text: Now, <s>Guṇotprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy regarding a quality): '<s>Saiṣā sthalī</s>' (This is the plain). This is the speech of <s>Dāśarathi</s> (<s>Rāma</s>), who is settling down, addressed to <s>Sītā</s>. He shows it to be <s>Guṇotprekṣā</s>: 'Suffering is the quality.' Now, <s>Dravyotprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy regarding a substance): '<s>Pātālam etat</s>' (This is the netherworld). He shows it to be [regarding] substance: 'Of the moon,' and so on. In all four examples, he draws out the common distinguishing feature: 'These [involve] attribution of existence (<s>Bhāvābhimāna</s>),' and so on. Now, [examples of] attribution of non-existence (<s>Abhāvābhimāna</s>): '<s>Kapolaphalakau</s>' (the surfaces of the cheeks). <s>Kaṣṭa</s> means 'with difficulty.' '<s>Tathāvidhau</s>' (of such a kind) — a charming excess, knowable only through one's own experience, is indicated. The coming of emaciation is natural. The absence of seeing each other is fancifully imagined as its cause. Hence it is [an example of] attribution of non-existence. He shows this: 'Here, the two not seeing,' and so on. Because the logical principle is easily understood, and by the principle of '<s>Sthālīpulāka</s>' (judging the pot by one grain of rice), only an example [suffices] — therefore the fault of [departing from proper] order should not be suspected. With regard to the [proper] order, however, one should illustrate with <s>Jāti</s> (universal) and other [types of] <s>Utprekṣā</s> first. Having this in mind, he says: 'Thus, in <s>Jāti</s> and others too, one should infer.' Thus the tetrad of <s>Jāti</s> and others has been illustrated in the form of attribution of non-existence. Now the octad of distinctions should be illustrated with respect to quality, action, and cause. Wishing to illustrate with quality as the cause, he says: '<s>Navabisalatā</s>' (a fresh lotus-stalk), and so on. That has been analyzed in detail. Thus, since the quality-as-cause is clearer in the triad of action and other <s>Utprekṣās</s>, and [hence] does not require [separate] examples — with this intention, he illustrates with action as the cause: '<s>Idṛkṣam</s>' (of this kind), and so on. Emaciation — the action characterized by going away — is the cause of the <s>Utprekṣā</s> of not-seeing. By this much, the set of sixteen should be considered as illustrated. Now, regarding the twofold division of the sixteen through the inclusion and non-inclusion of the cause — which was promised — he shows that the immediately preceding examples themselves serve as examples of inclusion of the cause: 'These, with the cause,' and so on. He shows the non-inclusion [of the cause] regarding crookedness and emaciation-going in the same examples already cited: '<s>Limpatī</s> (it anoints) and so on.' Here, in imagining [something] as anointing and so forth, the cause such as spreading and so on is not included. By this much, thirty-two varieties have been illustrated. Now the thirty-two should be illustrated in three ways — as having the nature of cause, effect, and intrinsic form. He illustrates as having the nature of cause: '<s>Viśleṣaduḥkhāt</s>' (from the pain of separation), and so on. Here, the quality of suffering is fancifully imagined as a cause. Likewise, <s>Jāti</s> (universal) and <s>Kriyā</s> (action) should be understood as [imagined in the form of] cause. In <s>Dravyotprekṣā</s>, since that [causal aspect] is absent, the group of eight based on it should be dropped. Now he illustrates as having intrinsic form: '<s>Kuberajuṣṭām</s>' (favored by <s>Kubera</s>), and so on. <s>Juṣṭā</s> means 'frequented.' The direction frequented by <s>Kubera</s> is the north; it is imagined as the rival heroine (<s>Pratināyikā</s>). <s>Samaya</s> is a particular season. <s>Anyadātva</s> (going elsewhere at another time) is a tryst. In the southern direction, the status of the heroine (<s>Nāyikā</s>) is imagined. <s>Vyalīka</s> means transgression. Here, the intrinsic form of the sigh itself is what is fancifully imagined — not its cause or effect. Thus, in the triad of <s>Guṇotprekṣā</s> and others, the intrinsic-form nature should be understood. Now, <s>Utprekṣā</s> in the form of effect: '<s>Colasya</s>' (of the garment), and so on. Here, the action of seeing is fancifully imagined as having the effect of tearing apart. Likewise, in <s>Jāti</s> and <s>Guṇa</s> too, the aspect of being an effect should be traced. In <s>Dravyotprekṣā</s>, since cause and effect are not possible, the sixteen based on them should be dropped. Thus the eighty varieties of <s>Vācyotprekṣā</s> (expressible poetic fancy) have been illustrated in their near-totality.

divasamityatyantasaṃyoge dvitīyā /

kastūrīti /
rolambābhṛṅgāḥ /
aṅkaḥ paryāntaḥ /
sthāsakaścarcikā /
upamopakramatāmupapādayati-atra yadyapītyādi /

ata utprekṣāyāṃ paryavasānam /

aprapañcane hetumāha- iti tviti /
gatāsu tīramiti /
sasaṃbhramā gatiḥ phenollāsahetuḥ /
atrevaśabdādaṭṭahāsasya saṃbhāvyatā /

adarśanaṃ pratya prakṛtaiva hi kṣāmatā phalaṃ, tatra nimittaṃ hetūtprekṣaṇe prayojakam /

iyamabhāvābhimānarūpakriyālakṣaṇā hetūtprekṣā /

iyaṃ prakriyā sarvatraiva hetūtprekṣāyāmekarūpetyāha-evaṃ sarvatreti /
