avacchekatvāccetyādi /
vyavahārasamāropaḥ na turūpakādvaidharmyamityāha-avacchedakatvāccetyādi /
vyavahārasamāropaḥ na tu rūpasamāropaḥ /
nanu yadā rūpasamāropaḥ tadā kiṃ syādityata āha-rūpasamāropetyādi /
avacchrāditatvena kroḍīkṛtvena /

children.translated_text: Because of being made to have the form of the primary (<s>prakṛta</s>) — that is, being colored by the non-primary form — it is <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) alone.
And this has been discriminated, as appropriate, in [the discussion of] the <s>pariṇāma</s> (transformation) ornament.
Here are subsidiary verses: If the non-primary is understood through similarity of the differentiating aspect alone,
and its activity is superimposed on the primary, [the non-primary] becomes subordinate. Then —

body.translated_text: Where in the qualificand (<s>viśeṣya</s>) portion there is reference only to the primary [subject], and through the similarity of the qualifier, a non-primary [subject] is also understood — that is <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression), because it is expressed in brief (<s>samāsa</s>). Wishing to explain this, he speaks for the purpose of distinguishing the domain, beginning with 'Here, of the primary...' Sometimes both are expressed (<s>vācya</s>) — supplying 'of both.' Sometimes one of them is suggested (<s>gamya</s>) — supplying 'of one.' 'Through the method of <s>śleṣa</s> statement' — the meaning is: when <s>śleṣa</s> (double meaning) is the basis of both the qualifier and qualificand portions, it is not [<s>samāsokti</s>]. 'Through separate employment' — meaning: through separate use of words in the qualifier portion. This twofold division of expressedness (<s>vācyatva</s>) is the domain of the <s>śleṣa</s> ornament. When the suggestion pertains to the primary subject, and through the similarity of the qualifier — then it is <s>prastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the relevant); but when it pertains to the non-primary subject, then it is <s>samāsokti</s> — this is the discrimination. If the non-primary is suggested and there is also similarity in the qualificand, what would [the result] be? To this he says: 'When there is similarity of the qualificand too, <s>śleṣa</s> is obtained.' That is, <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion) based on <s>śleṣa</s> is obtained. Now, the <s>śleṣa</s> ornament, <s>dhvani</s> based on word-power — in all three domains there is the dependence on words with double meaning. When there is <s>śleṣa</s>, both meanings are necessarily expressed. And expressedness is possible thus: when both meanings are contextual, or both non-contextual, then because of the dependence on double-meaning words in both the qualifier and qualificand portions, it is the <s>śleṣa</s> ornament. Since the denotative function (<s>abhidhā</s>) is unrestricted, both meanings are expressed. But when one is contextual and the other non-contextual, then through the force of separate word-employment in the qualificand portion alone, it is the <s>śleṣa</s> ornament. If there is also dependence on double-meaning words in the qualificand portion, then since the denotative function, restricted by context, serves only the contextual meaning, the understanding of the non-contextual meaning would be the domain of the suggestive function (<s>vyañjana</s>) alone. When it is <s>samāsokti</s>: in the qualifier portion there is dependence on words conveying two meanings; in the qualificand portion, reference only to the contextual meaning. Then, because the non-primary is understood through the similarity of the qualifier, it is <s>samāsokti</s> with the stated definition. But when, of the contextual and non-contextual, there is double-meaning even in the qualificand portion, then it is not <s>samāsokti</s> characterized by similarity of the qualifier alone, because the status of <s>śleṣa</s> ornament is also obtained. How? Because the definition there is the very expressedness of both meanings; for the possibility of both being expressed does not hold here, since the denotative function, biased toward the context, has no contact with the non-contextual meaning, since the non-contextual [meaning] is cognized immediately upon construal, and since there would be the consequence of <s>dhvani</s> based on word-power being swallowed up by <s>śleṣa</s>. This is a clear path, [known only] to those who understand the secrets of <s>dhvani</s> theory. Enough of this. Now he discriminates the difference between <s>samāsokti</s> and <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor), beginning with 'Through the similarity of the qualifier...' The word <s>hi</s> indicates reason. Since the non-primary meaning is understood through the similarity of the qualifier, therefore — because of the absence of contact in the qualificand portion — [the non-primary] does not seek to make the qualificand (the primary meaning) endowed with form through its own form; rather, the activity understood through the qualifier portion is superimposed as a delimiting factor upon the primary-meaning activity understood through the qualifier portion. This is what he says: 'The primary is understood as a delimiting factor.' 'Because of being a delimiting factor' etc. — The superimposition of activity, not a difference from <s>rūpaka</s>, he says beginning with 'Because of being a delimiting factor...' It is superimposition of activity, not superimposition of form. Now, when there is superimposition of form, what would result? To this he says, beginning with 'When there is superimposition of form...' 'As something covering' means 'as something encompassing.'

children.translated_text: by superimposing the non-primary narrative, the primary itself
is expressed in brief — therefore this is considered <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression).
If there is similarity in the qualificand aspect too, [the qualificand] being configured in the form of the primary,
the non-primary would be [in] the qualificand [position] — then it is the <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) ornament.

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus. //

body.text:

nanu katham atra nirjñāyate vyavahārasamāropo na rūpasamāropa ityata āha-aparityaktetyādi /
yadi rūpasamāropastadā prakṛtau rūpakanyāyena svaṃ svaṃ rūpamavacchrāditatvena parityajya yadavacchrādakamupamānarūpaṃ tādrūpyamupagṛhṇāti /
iha punarviśeṣyāṃśe niṣpratiyogikatayā jñātayorata evāparityakta sva rūpayoḥ niśāśaśinorviśeṣaṇasāmyāvagamitena nāyakatvadharmeṇa viśiṣṭatayā pratīteḥ /
ato vyavahārasamāropa eva /
tanvīti /
puṣpam ārttavaṃ rajaḥ, prasūnaṃ ca /
iha tanutvādīnāṃ viśeṣaṇānāmubhayatraikārthatāsāmyaṃ na tu śliṣṭatā /
tadetadāha-atra tanutvetyādi /
nanu tanutvādidharmasāmyāt kathaṃ latāvyavahārapratītirityata āha-tatra ca lataiketyādi /
vikāso hi latāyā eva tatsamāropo lolākṣyā latāvyavahārapratīteḥ kāraṇam /
nanu vikāsasya lataikagāmitvātkathaṃ sādhāraṇyamityata āha-vikāsastvityādi /
yathaivaṃ viśeṣaṇasādhāraṇyaṃ dharmasamāropaśca vyavahārasamāropasya kāraṇaṃ tathā kāryasamāropo 'pīti vyutpādayutumāha-evaṃ ca kāryetyādi /
kāryasamāropanibandhano hi bheda iha dharmasamāropanītyā sujñānaḥ upari ca śuddhatvena pṛthagrāśīkariṣyati /
ata iha nodāhṛtaḥ /
evamādau dharmakāryayoranyatarāropamantareṇa aprakṛtārtho nāvagamyate /
prakaraṇaniyantritāyā abhidhāyāḥ prākaraṇikārtha evopakṣayāt /
ato dharmakāryayoranyatarāropa eva vyañjanavyāpārotthā panenāprakṛtārthāvagatihetuḥ /
ito viśeṣaṇasādhāraṇyanibandhanāsamāsoktirnyāyavidāmeva vibhaktaviṣayā /
asphuṭatvāttadidamabhisandhāyāha-iyañcetyādi /
pūrvāpekṣayā śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇanibandhanā samāsoktiḥ pūrvā tadapekṣayetyarthaḥ /
dantaprabhā puṣpaciteti /
atrānapekṣitākhyāne vākye śravaṇa samanantarameva dantaprabhāpuṣpacitatvādinā hetunā hariṇekṣaṇāyāḥ suveṣatā pratīyate /
atastadā suveṣatvalakṣaṇakāryavaśādviśeṣaṇānāṃ dantaprabhāḥ puṣpāṇīvetyupamāsamāsaparatvam /
atha dantaprabhāsadṛśaiḥ puṣpairiti madhyamapadalopi samāsāntarapratyāyitaiḥ puṣpapallavādibhiḥ viśeṣaṇāsāmyadaśāyāṃ latāvyavahārapratītiḥ /
tadetadavabodhayati-atra dantaprabhā ityādinā /
latāvyavahārapratītiriti vadatā rūpakasamāsasyāprātpirāsūcitā /
vyavahārasamārope samāsoktiḥ /
rūpasamārope tu rūpakamiti pratipāditam yataḥ ataḥ pratīto 'pi rūpakasamāsa iha nyāyato na prāpnoti /
nanvevamādau prāgupamāsamāsāsasamāśrayaṇanimittaṃ yadi suveṣatvādinā nopāttaṃ tadā kiṃ syādityata āha-atraiva parītetyādinā /
parītā keśapāśālivṛndena parigatā /
iha dantaprabhāpuṣpāṇīvetyādinā kimupamāsamāsaḥ, uta dantaprabhā eva puṣpāṇītyādiko rūpakasamāsa iti sandehaḥ, upamārūpakayoḥ sādhakabādhakābhāvāt /
ataḥ sandeharūpasaṅkarasamāśrayeṇa pūrvaṃ yojanā /
na ca mantavyaṃ samāsaḥ sandeho papanna iti, sandehasya kavipratibhotthā pitasya vicchrittirūpatvāt /
ataḥsaṅkarasamāśrayeṇādau yojanā /
atha sandehopaśamakāle dantaprabhāsadṛśaiḥ puṣpairityādi pūrvavadeva madhyamapadalopasamāsaḥ latāvyavahārapratītau samāsoktāveva viśrantiḥ /
itthaṃ ca sati upamā samāsagarbhatayā saṅkarasamāsagarbhatayā ca samāsoktibhedo 'yaṃ dvidhā darśito mantavyaḥ /
nanu kevalarūpakasamāsāśrayeṇāpi samāsoktibhedo 'yaṃ kiṃ neṣyata ityata āha-rūpakagarbhatvena tviti /
prāk rūpakasamāse atha tadgarbhatayopamāsamāsāśraye yadyapi viśeṣaṇasāmyaṃ bhavatyeva, tathāpi na tat samāsokteḥ prayojakam /
kutaḥ? ekadeśavivartimukhenaiva latāvyavahārapratītau samāsokteḥ vaiyarthyāt /
nanu upamāsamāse saṅkarasamāse ca samāsoktivaiparthyaṃ kiṃ na syādityāha-na ca prāṅnidarśitetyādi /
eṣa nyāyaḥ samāsoktivaiparthyāpattilakṣaṇaḥ /
tatra hemumāha-upamāsaṅkarayorekadeśavivartinorabhāvāt /
na hyupamālaṅkāraḥ saṅkarāṅkāraśca ekadeśavivartitvena kenacidanuśiṣṭau /
ataḥ svatantrālaṅkāratvasaṃśayānnānyabādhakṣamau /
rūpakaṃ tu ekadeśavivartitayānuśiṣṭamanyabādhakṣamameva /
ata evaṃvidhe viṣaye rūpakaprātpau samāsokte prātpiriti sodāharaṇaṃ darśayitumāha-taccaikadeśavivartītyādi /
nīrakṣya vidyunnayanairiti /
payodo vidyunnayanairniśāyāmabhisārikāyāḥ mukhaṃ nirīkṣya dhārānipātaiḥ saha candro mayā vānta iti dhiyevārtataraṃ rarāsetyarthaḥ /
atrāśliṣṭam ekadeśavivartirūpakaṃ samāsokternāvakāśaṃ dadātīti darśayati-atra nirīkṣaṇetyādi /
nirīkṣaṇaṃ hi puruṣadharmo na payodadharmaḥ /
ataḥ puruṣānusāreṇa yojane vidyuta eva nayanānīti rūpakameva na punarupamā saṅkaro vā /
ataḥ payode draṣṭṛpuruṣarūpaṇamarthāditi ekadeṣavivartitā /
taccedamārtataraṃ rarāseti pratīyamānotprekṣāyā eva nimittaṃ samāsokte raprātpireveti bhāvaḥ /
maganaṇaneti-patrāṇi dalāni tānyeva patrāṇi tāladalāni /
lipayorītayaḥ tā eva lipayo 'kṣara sanniveśāḥ /
kāyastho dehī gaṇakaḥ /
eṣu rūpaṇasāmarthyānmadano mahārājatayā madhuśca śrīkaraṇāgraṇītvena rūpitaḥ pratīyate /
tadetadupadarśayati-atra hi patralipītyādi /
nanu patrāṇīvetyādirupamā kiṃ na syādityata āha-dvirephamaṣītyādi /
maṣīyogo hi madhāvasaṃbhavannupamā samāsaṃbādhitvā gaṇakavṛtteḥ saṃbhavastadanusāreṇa rūpakasamāsaṃ sādhayatīti yāvat /

children.text: nanu samāsoktiprastāve kiṃ sodāharaṇaṃ rūpakabhedapradarśanenetyata āha-asya ca pracura ityādi /
children.translated_text: Now, what is the purpose of showing the varieties of <s>rūpaka</s> with examples in the context of introducing <s>samāsokti</s>? To this he says, beginning with 'And this is abundant...'
This [refers to] the <s>ekadeśavivartin rūpaka</s> (partial transformation metaphor).
Here are subsidiary verses: <s>Samāsokti</s> obtains through a simile-compound when there is certainty;
it obtains through a doubt-compound (<s>saṅkara</s>) when there is doubt [between simile and metaphor].

body.translated_text: To elaborate the specific [sub-types] of this [figure], he says beginning with 'And that similarity of the qualifier...' 'Commonality' (<s>sādhāraṇya</s>) means the possibility of the grounds of application [of a term] in both [subjects]. 'Being pregnant with comparison' (<s>aupamyagarbhatva</s>) means through the adoption of a compound pregnant with that [comparison]. Thus, that similarity of the qualifier is of three kinds — this is the meaning. Therefore <s>samāsokti</s> too is of three kinds. The examples in order: '<s>upoḍharāgeṇa</s>' (with risen passion/redness) — <s>rāga</s> means both the redness of twilight and desire. From '<s>tāraka</s>' (star/pupil), the understanding of both star and the circle within the eye [arises]. '<s>Mukha</s>' means both 'beginning' and 'face.' '<s>Timira</s>' [means both] 'a garment resembling darkness' and 'darkness itself as a garment.' To apply the definition, he says beginning with 'Here, of the night and the moon...' <s>Nāyaka</s> (hero) and <s>nāyikā</s> (heroine) — both are called <s>nāyakau</s> by the rule of single retention for dual forms referring to different genders. The greatness [of this figure] is that the night and moon, qualified by double-meaning attributes like 'having risen passion/redness,' are understood as distinguished by the behavior of hero [and heroine]. Now, how do we ascertain here that it is superimposition of activity, not superimposition of form? To this he says, beginning with 'Without abandoning...' If there were superimposition of form, then, by the method of <s>rūpaka</s>, the primary [subjects] would abandon their own respective forms as something covered and assume the form of the standard of comparison as the covering form. But here, in the qualificand portion, since the night and moon are known without any counterpart [to compare with] — precisely because they have not abandoned their own forms — and since the cognition is of them as distinguished by the hero-attribute conveyed through the similarity of the qualifier, therefore it is superimposition of activity alone. '<s>Tanvī</s>' (slender one) — <s>puṣpa</s> [means both] menses (<s>ārttava rajas</s>) and flower (<s>prasūna</s>). Here the similarity of the qualifiers such as slenderness etc. is one-meaningfulness in both [contexts], not double-meaning (<s>śliṣṭatā</s>). This is what he states, beginning with 'Here, slenderness...' Now, how is the activity of a creeper understood from the similarity of qualities like slenderness? To this he says, beginning with 'There, of a creeper alone...' For blooming (<s>vikāsa</s>) belongs to a creeper alone; its superimposition, being the cause of the understanding of creeper-activity for the side-glancing woman. Now, since blooming belongs to a creeper alone, how is there commonality? To this he says, beginning with 'But blooming...' Just as the commonality of the qualifier and the superimposition of the quality are causes of the superimposition of activity, so too the superimposition of effect — he teaches this, beginning with 'And thus, of effect...' For the distinction based on superimposition of effect is easily known here by the method of quality-superimposition, and will be separately treated in its pure form later. Therefore it is not exemplified here. Thus, at the beginning, without the superimposition of one of quality or effect, the non-primary meaning is not understood — since the denotative function, restricted by context, serves only the contextual meaning. Therefore, the superimposition of one of quality or effect alone is the cause of understanding the non-primary meaning, arising through the operation of the suggestive function. Hence, <s>samāsokti</s> based on commonality of the qualifier has a well-distinguished domain — [known] only to those who understand the principles. Because of its subtlety, keeping this in mind, he says beginning with 'And this...' 'The <s>samāsokti</s> based on double-meaning qualifier [is] prior relative to the first; relative to it [is the present type]' — this is the meaning. '<s>Dantaprabhā puṣpacita</s>' (with teeth-luster and flower-gathering) — here, in a sentence requiring no [further] explanation, immediately upon hearing, the good adornment of the doe-eyed woman is understood through the cause of teeth-luster being flower-gatherings etc. Therefore, at that point, through the effect characterized as good-adornment, the qualifiers have the force of a simile-compound like 'teeth-lusters are like flowers.' Then, through flowers conveyed by a middle-term-elided compound meaning 'flowers resembling teeth-luster,' and through flower-shoots etc. [thus] conveyed — in the state of qualifier-similarity, the understanding of creeper-activity [arises]. He demonstrates this, beginning with 'Here, teeth-luster...' By saying 'understanding of creeper-activity,' the non-obtainment of the <s>rūpaka</s> compound is indicated. In superimposition of activity, it is <s>samāsokti</s>; in superimposition of form, it is <s>rūpaka</s> — since this has been established, therefore the <s>rūpaka</s> compound, even though [apparently] understood, does not properly obtain here by principle. Now, if initially the ground for adopting the simile-compound were not taken up through good-adornment etc., what would result? To this he says beginning with 'Here itself, surrounded...' '<s>Parītā</s>' — surrounded by a mass of tresses (<s>keśapāśa</s>). Here, whether '<s>dantaprabhā puṣpāṇi iva</s>' etc. is a simile-compound, or '<s>dantaprabhā eva puṣpāṇi</s>' etc. is a <s>rūpaka</s>-compound — there is doubt, because there is nothing to establish or refute either simile or <s>rūpaka</s>. Therefore, first the construction is through recourse to the doubtful-type compound (<s>saṅkara</s>). And one should not think 'the compound has become doubtful' [as a fault], because the doubt, arising from poetic intuition, has the nature of aesthetic charm. Therefore, first the construction through recourse to the compound of doubt (<s>saṅkara</s>). Then, when the doubt subsides, [with the understanding] 'with flowers resembling teeth-luster' etc. — the middle-term-elided compound as before — repose [is attained] in <s>samāsokti</s> alone through the understanding of creeper-activity. And this being so, through the pregnancy of simile-compound and through the pregnancy of doubt-compound, this variety of <s>samāsokti</s> has been shown to be twofold — this should be understood. Now, would not a variety of <s>samāsokti</s> through recourse to a pure <s>rūpaka</s>-compound also be intended? To this he says: 'But through being pregnant with <s>rūpaka</s>...' Although in a <s>rūpaka</s>-compound, and previously in a simile-compound adopted as pregnant with it, there is indeed similarity of the qualifier, still that is not the cause of <s>samāsokti</s>. Why? Because through the method of <s>ekadeśavivartin</s> (partial transformation) alone, the understanding of creeper-activity [arises], rendering <s>samāsokti</s> purposeless. Now, would not the purposelessness of <s>samāsokti</s> also obtain in the simile-compound and the doubt-compound? To this he says, beginning with 'But neither in the previously shown...' This is the principle, characterized by the consequence of purposelessness of <s>samāsokti</s>. He states the reason: because simile and doubt (<s>saṅkara</s>) are not [a type of] <s>ekadeśavivartin</s>. For the simile-ornament and the doubt-ornament have not been taught by anyone as being of the <s>ekadeśavivartin</s> type. Therefore, because of the doubt regarding their being independent ornaments, they cannot override another [ornament]. But <s>rūpaka</s>, being taught as <s>ekadeśavivartin</s>, is indeed capable of overriding another [ornament]. Hence, in such a domain, when <s>rūpaka</s> is obtained, <s>samāsokti</s> has no scope — to show this with examples, he says beginning with 'And that <s>ekadeśavivartin</s>...' '<s>Nīrakṣya vidyunnayanaiḥ</s>' (having gazed with lightning-eyes) — the cloud, having gazed with lightning-eyes at the face of the <s>abhisārikā</s> (woman going to a tryst) in the night, cried out most piteously along with the shower of rain, as if [saying] 'The moon has been swallowed by me' — this is the meaning. Here he shows that the non-double-meaning <s>ekadeśavivartin rūpaka</s> leaves no room for <s>samāsokti</s>, beginning with 'Here, the act of gazing...' For gazing is a quality of a person, not of a cloud. Therefore, when constructing [the meaning] following the person-analogy, 'the lightnings themselves are the eyes' — it is <s>rūpaka</s> alone, not simile or doubt. Therefore, the configuration of the cloud as a seeing person follows implicitly — hence the <s>ekadeśavivartin</s> nature. And this '<s>ārtataraṃ rarāsa</s>' (cried out most piteously) is the ground for the suggested <s>utprekṣā</s> alone, and <s>samāsokti</s> simply has no scope here — this is the purport. '<s>Maganaṇana</s>' — <s>patrāṇi</s> means leaves, which are also palm-leaves (<s>tāladalāni</s>). <s>Lipayaḥ</s> means scripts, which are also letter-arrangements. <s>Kāyastha</s> means embodied one, [and also] an accountant. Among these, through the power of figuration, <s>Madana</s> (the Love-god) is understood as configured as a great king, and Spring (<s>Madhu</s>) as the chief of the revenue office. He demonstrates this, beginning with 'Here, indeed, leaf-scripts...' Now, would not '<s>patrāṇi iva</s>' (like leaves) etc. be a simile? To this he says, beginning with '<s>Dvirephа</s> (bee) [and] ink...' For the combination with ink, being impossible in spring, refutes the simile and — since the activity of an accountant is possible — establishes the <s>rūpaka</s>-compound following that [analogy].

children.translated_text: When a <s>rūpaka</s>-compound is obtained, this [<s>samāsokti</s>] does not operate —
because the meaning is accomplished through the <s>ekadeśavivartin</s> <s>rūpaka</s> [alone].

body.text:
ataḥ prabhedāntaraprathanāya uktabhedān saṃcaṣṭe-tadevamityādi /
iyaṃ khalu śliṣṭātsādhāraṇādaupamyagarbhācyeti viśeṣaṇavaicitryāt tridhoddiṣṭā /
tatra śliṣṭādviśeṣaṇādekavidhā /
sādhāraṇātpunardharmasamāropakāryasamāropābhyāṃ dvidhā /
aupamyagarbhādapi upamāsamāsena saṅkarasamāsena ceti dvidhā /
śliṣṭāśliṣṭatayā tu rūpakasamāsadvayamasyā na viṣayaḥ /
ataḥ pañca prakārāḥ /
itthaṃ viśeṣaṇasāmyātpañcaprakāratvasiddhā vavāntaraṃ viśeṣasahitāmimāṃ punastrirāśikatayā saṃcaṣṭe-itthaṃ śuddhakāryetyādinā /
kāryasya śuddhatvaṃ nāma nirūpita viśeṣaṇasāmyā saṃkīrṇatā /
prathamaṃ viśeṣaṇasāmyanibandhanabhedodayāvarvāgityarthaḥ /
atraitadākūtam-viśeṣaṇa sāmyādaprastutasya gamyatve hi samāsoktiḥ /
tacca viśeṣaṇasāmyaṃ śuddhakāryasamārope satyupacaritaṃ, yathā vilikhatītyādāvudāhariṣyamāṇepadye sa eko rāśiḥ , yadā punaridamanupacaritaṃ tadā pañcadhodāhṛtam prāk sa dvitīyaḥ /
ubhayamayatve tu tṛtīyo rāṣiḥ /
anupacaritaviśeṣaṇasāmyanibandhanasya nyāyanirbharatvena prāk pradarśanaṃ pañcavidhatvena kṛtamiti /
atha tadeva prāk pradarśanamanusmārayati-viśeṣaṇāsāmyaṃ ceti /
nanu śuddhakāryasamārope viśeṣaṇasānyamupacaritam , anyadātvanupacaritaṃ anugatamekarūpaṃ tu prayojanaṃ nānupaśyāma ityata āha-sarvatra cātretyādi /
evakāreṇa tadekaprāṇatāṃ samāsokterabhaipraiti /
tasya cāturvidhyaṃ darśayati-sa ca laukika ityādi /
vastujātiguṇādi /
anena ca vyavahārasamāropacāturvidhyena rāśitrayamapi pratyekaṃ caturdhā prathate /
ataḥsamāsoktiḥ prapañcacavatītyāha-tadevaṃ bahuprapañceti /
tatrādyaṃ rāśimudājihīrṣarāha-tatra śaddhakāryeti /
vilikhatīti /
uccairvilekha(na)(?)gāḍhaṃ kacagrahaḥ patrāvalyāmasāmañjasyamaṃśukavikarṣaśceceti haṭhakā (mu)kakāryam /
haṭhāditi vikarṣathaṇa kriyāviśeṣaṇam /
atropacaritatvādaprastutāvagatau viśeṣaṇasāmyaṃ nātibaddhabharam api tu śuddhakāryasamāropa eva ityāha-atra patrāvalītyādi /
khadire 'tyasaṃbhavāt patrāvalīgrahaḥ /
vyutkramoktānāṃ kramasvārasyāyānusmārayativiśeṣaṇasamyeneti /
viśeṣaṇasāmyaṃ hi yadā śliṣṭatā tadobhayārthatā /
yadā sādhāraṇyaṃ tadobhayatra pravṛttinimittasaṃbhavaḥ /
yadaupamyagarbhaviśeṣaṇatā tadā samāsabheda iti /
viśeṣamasāmyavaśādeva aprastutāvagatiriti jñeyam /
athobhayamayatvenodāharatilirlūnānīti /
nīrasaiḥ śuṣkai rahṛdayaiśca /
kaṇṭakibhiḥ kṣudraśaṅkumadbhiḥ ghātakajanayogibhiśca /
ubhayamayatāṃ yojayati-atra kaṇṭakibhiriti /
eṣitriṣu rāśiṣu vyavahārasamāropa vaicitryanibandhanāt bhedānupadarśayitukāma āha-vyavahārasamāropetyādi /
dyāmāliliṅgeti /
ambaraṃ nabho vāsaśca /
nimagracarapuṣpa śaratvaṃ dāhena /
taruṇaḥ prabalo yuvā ca /
atra ambarakarataruṇeṣu viśeṣaṇa sāmyam /
anyatra kāryasamāropaḥ /
atra laukikavastuni laukikavyavahārasamāropaḥ /
pradarśitodāharaṇeṣu ca /
tatra laukikaṃ vastu vividhamityāha-laukikaṃ ceti /
yairiti /
ekarūpamavikṛtaṃ /
vṛttiṣu jāgaritādiṣu /
avyayaṃ sauṣu(ptyā)diṣu sthagitam /
ata evāsaṅkhyatayā pravṛttam /
jāgare viśvaḥ prathamaḥ , svapne taijaso dvitīyaḥ, sauṣupte prājñastṛtīya iti /
saṅkhyayā vastuto rahitaṃ turīyasya sarvānusyūtatvāt /
uktaṃ hi śrīmadgauḍapādauḥ-"māyā saṅkhyā turīyami"ti /
yairīdṛśaṃ tvāṃpaśyadbhiḥ paratvajuṣo vibhakterlopaḥ kṛtaḥ /
asmātparamastīti vibhāgo lutpaḥ /
taistava sakṣaṇaṃ kṛtaṃ (manye)parameśvarasya hi sarvavṛttiṣvakatvaṃ rūpamavyayatvaṃ asaṃkhyatā na kutaścidapideśakālāderbheda iti idameva lakṣaṇam /
idamāgamaśāstraprasiddhaṃ vastu /
atha sarvāsu kārikādivṛttiṣvekatvādisaṃkhyārahitamavyaye hi syāditi pratiyogyekatvaṃ nāsti kiṃ tvabhedaikatvamevar /
idṛśamavyayaṃ paśyadbhiḥ paratvajuṣaḥ prakṛteḥ paratvalakṣaṇāyāḥ vibhakteḥ prathamāderlopaḥ kṛtaḥ /
idamavyayalakṣaṇaṃ"sadṛśaṃ triṣu liṅgeṣvi"tyādinā pratipāditam /
idaṃ vyākaraṇāprasiddhaṃ vastu /
atra viśeṣaṇāsāmyameva /
sīmānamiti /

children.translated_text: 'Having entered another <s>utprekṣā</s>' — thereby simultaneity is indicated.
He concludes that such variety should be traced: 'thus this...' etc.
'Through the similarity of the qualifying aspect, the understanding of the non-contextual meaning —'
'That is considered <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression), by which the meaning is expressed in abbreviated form.'

body.translated_text: Therefore, to manifest further subdivisions, he surveys the stated varieties: '<s>tad evam</s>' etc. This [<s>samāsokti</s>] has been indicated as threefold by the variety of qualifiers: arising from <s>śliṣṭa</s> (compounded), <s>sādhāraṇa</s> (common), and <s>aupamyagarbha</s> (simile-containing) qualifiers. Among these, from the <s>śliṣṭa</s> qualifier, it is of one kind. From the <s>sādhāraṇa</s>, it is of two kinds: through the superimposition of properties and through the superimposition of effects. From the <s>aupamyagarbha</s>, it is also of two kinds: through simile-compound and through mixed compound. But the two types of metaphorical compound, being either compounded or uncompounded, are not its domain. Hence there are five modes. Having thus established the fivefold nature through similarity of qualifiers, he further surveys this, with its additional particulars, as a threefold grouping: '<s>itthaṃ śuddhakārya</s>' etc. 'Purity of the effect' means its being unmixed with the established similarity of qualifiers. 'First' means prior to the arising of the varieties based on the similarity of qualifiers—such is the meaning. The intent here is this: when the irrelevant is understood through the similarity of qualifiers, that is <s>samāsokti</s>. And that similarity of qualifiers, when there is pure superimposition of effect, is figurative (<s>upacarita</s>), as in the verse to be illustrated beginning with '<s>vilikhatī</s>'—that is the first grouping. But when this is non-figurative, then it was illustrated in five ways earlier—that is the second grouping. When it partakes of both, that is the third grouping. The prior demonstration in fivefold form was made because the one founded on non-figurative similarity of qualifiers is full of logical rigor. Now he reminds of that prior demonstration: '<s>viśeṣaṇasāmyaṃ ca</s>' etc. Now, in pure superimposition of effect the similarity of qualifiers is figurative, and at other times non-figurative—but we do not see a common, uniform purpose—to address this he says '<s>sarvatra cātra</s>' etc. By the particle '<s>eva</s>' he proclaims that as the vital principle of <s>samāsokti</s>. He shows its fourfold nature: '<s>sa ca laukika</s>' etc. Worldly things, universals, qualities, etc. And through this fourfold variety of conventional superimposition, even each of the three groupings manifests in four ways. Therefore <s>samāsokti</s> is elaborate—he says '<s>tad evaṃ bahuprapañca</s>' etc. Wishing to illustrate the first grouping, he says '<s>tatra śuddhakārya</s>' etc. '<s>Vilikhatī</s>'—vigorous scratching, firm hair-grasping, impropriety regarding the ornamental leaf-design, and pulling of the garment—these are the effects of forceful love-play. '<s>Haṭhāt</s>' is an adverbial modifier of the action of pulling. Here, because of the figurative nature, in the understanding of the irrelevant, the similarity of qualifiers does not bear much weight; rather, it is purely the superimposition of effect—he says '<s>atra patrāvalī</s>' etc. Because of the impossibility regarding the <s>khadira</s> tree, the leaf-design is grasped [as figurative]. He reminds of the natural sequence of things stated in reversed order: '<s>viśeṣaṇasāmyena</s>' etc. For when the similarity of qualifiers is <s>śliṣṭa</s> (compounded), then there is double meaning. When it is <s>sādhāraṇa</s> (common), then there is the possibility of the ground of application in both. When there is <s>aupamyagarbha</s> (simile-containing) qualifier-hood, then there is the distinction of compounds. The understanding of the irrelevant arises only from the force of the similarity of qualifiers—this should be known. Now he illustrates the case partaking of both: '<s>lirlūnāni</s>' etc. '<s>Nīrasai</s>' means dry and heartless. '<s>Kaṇṭakibhiḥ</s>' means having small thorns and being associated with harmful people. He applies the partaking of both: '<s>atra kaṇṭakibhir</s>' etc. Wishing to show the varieties in these three groupings based on the variety of conventional superimposition, he says '<s>vyavahārasamāropa</s>' etc. '<s>Dyām āliliṅga</s>' etc. '<s>Ambara</s>' means both sky and garment. The submerged lotus acquires autumn-nature through burning. '<s>Taruṇa</s>' means both powerful and young. Here the similarity of qualifiers is in '<s>ambara</s>,' '<s>kara</s>,' '<s>taruṇa</s>.' Elsewhere it is superimposition of effect. Here it is conventional superimposition of worldly things upon worldly things. And in the examples shown. He states the variety of worldly things: '<s>laukikaṃ ca</s>' etc. '<s>Yair</s>'—uniform, unchanged. In the states of waking etc. '<s>Avyaya</s>' (undeclinable/imperishable)—covered in deep sleep etc. Hence engaged without number. In waking, <s>Viśva</s> (the Universal) is the first; in dreaming, <s>Taijasa</s> (the Luminous) is the second; in deep sleep, <s>Prājña</s> (the Wise) is the third. Actually devoid of number, because the <s>Turīya</s> (Fourth) pervades all. As the illustrious <s>Gauḍapāda</s> has said: 'The <s>Turīya</s> is beyond <s>māyā</s> and number.' By those who perceive you thus—they who are devoted to transcendence have abolished the division (<s>vibhakti</s>)—the division that 'there is something beyond this' has been removed. By them your true characteristic has been determined. For the true nature of the Supreme Lord is: uniformity in all states, imperishability, innumerability, and no differentiation from any place, time, or the like—this alone is the defining characteristic. This is the subject matter well known from the <s>Āgama</s> scriptures. Now, in all grammatical functions, being devoid of number such as unity etc.—for in the undeclinable there would be [no number]—the correlative unity does not exist; rather, there is only the unity of non-difference. Those who perceive this undeclinable nature have abolished the <s>vibhakti</s> (case-ending/division) characterized by transcendence from <s>Prakṛti</s>. This characteristic of the undeclinable has been established by the rule 'alike in all three genders' etc. This is the subject matter known from grammar. Here the similarity of qualifiers is operative. '<s>Sīmānam</s>' etc. Here, by transgressing the boundary of the eyes, the domain of direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) is exceeded. By the absence of invariable connection with anything else, inference (<s>anumāna</s>) is also inapplicable. By the absence of contact with words, ordinary verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) is inapplicable. By the nature of unprecedented testimony, analogy (<s>upamāna</s>) is inapplicable. Because meaning does not arise spontaneously, presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>) is inapplicable. And even when no means of knowledge has been stated, in reality, upon such beauty, there is the superimposition of entities known from <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> and other scriptures, such as <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit). Because the means of knowledge whose sole characteristic is injunction (<s>codanā</s>) has no contact with other means of knowledge, the similarity of qualifiers here is uncommon. He shows the variety of scriptural subject matter: '<s>evaṃ tarke</s>' etc. '<s>Svapakṣa</s>'—<s>pakṣa</s> is both wing and the thesis-locus qualified by the property to be proved. '<s>Heti</s>'—both weapon and reason/logical mark. '<s>Viśeṣa</s>'—both excellence and the particular category of entities. '<s>Māna</s>'—both amorous anger and means of knowledge. '<s>Mandāgni</s>' etc. Here, the manifestation of weak digestive fire, swelling, darkness, and disease [can be understood] when the lord of herbs (the moon/physician) is absent. Here, since similarity exists even in the qualified element, another example should be sought. Alternatively, since '<s>candramasa</s>' (of the moon) can be supplied as the qualified, '<s>oṣadhipati</s>' (lord of herbs) should be intended as a qualifier. '<s>Prasarpat tātparyair</s>' etc. Those who know the purport and those who relish inference—by them too, he is unknowable; he does not relinquish his measurelessness; he cannot be spoken of nor characterized. But, O revered teacher! Your assemblage of qualities, residing in the hearts of the sensitive, has been ascertained by the wise as an operation that surpasses the operations of other assemblages of qualities through unprecedented operations. Here, upon the assemblage of qualities, the conventional usage of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment) and other <s>rasas</s> has been superimposed—he says '<s>atra bharata</s>' etc. For <s>rasa</s> is traditionally ascribed to <s>Bharata</s>'s origination. Because of the doctrine that <s>rasa</s> arises from the conjunction of <s>vibhāva</s> (determinants), <s>anubhāva</s> (consequents), and <s>vyabhicārin</s> (transient states). He substantiates that conventional usage: '<s>tathā hy atra</s>' etc. 'Not knowable through the power of purport (<s>tātparya</s>)'—for <s>tātparya</s> is, in the doctrine of <s>abhihitānvaya</s>, the syntactic-connection power that transcends denotation; <s>rasa</s>, whose cognition rests solely in the syntactic connection, is not knowable through this power, which arises immediately after syntactic construal. Because of the absence of invariable connection with <s>vibhāvas</s>, <s>anubhāvas</s>, and <s>vyabhicāri</s> states, it is not the object of inference either. Because it is not directly the object of convention, it is not denoted. Because there is no failure of primary meaning etc., it is not the object of <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) either. Rather, being unlimited because it overflows from other knowable objects, being beyond denotation, <s>lakṣaṇā</s>, and <s>tātparya</s>, it is objectified by the unprecedented operation called <s>vyañjanā</s> (suggestion), which belongs exclusively to poetry and is unknown to other disciplines. Being worldly, therefore to be imitated; because it removes the effort of gestural representation, setting aside the imitator, it resides exclusively in the hearts of the sensitive—so the wise have determined. This is but an outline; the elaboration is in the investigation of <s>rasa</s>. Since it is not relevant to the present topic, it is not undertaken. It has been treated at length in the <s>Saṃpradāyaprakāśinī</s>, the commentary on the <s>Kāvyaprakāśa</s>; it should be ascertained from there—enough. The superimposition of astronomical and other subject matter should be understood in this manner—he says '<s>evam anyad</s>' etc. '<s>Paśyantī</s>' etc. Here the intent is this: the goddess of Speech is measured in four stages: <s>Parā</s> (transcendent), <s>Paśyantī</s> (visionary), <s>Madhyamā</s> (intermediate), and <s>Vaikharī</s> (articulate). Among these, having withdrawn into herself the phenomenal world consisting of name and form, shining with the light of her own nature, transcending the three abodes of waking etc., she is <s>Parā</s>. Assuming the identity of the initial vital stirring for the purpose of manifesting the phenomenal expansion of name and form, dwelling in the <s>kanda</s> (bulb center), extending to the <s>maṇipūraka</s> (navel center), having attained the seed-state consisting of undifferentiated phonemes, facing toward the universe, being in the deep-sleep state, she is <s>Paśyantī</s>. Having arisen from <s>Parā</s>, from the <s>maṇipūraka</s> up to the <s>anāhata</s> (heart center), assuming the identity of the intellect-modification stirred by the vital vibration, having taken on phonemes and words, being in the form of inner speech, having the nature of <s>Paśyantī</s>'s power, being in the dream state, she is <s>Madhyamā</s>. Extending from the <s>anāhata</s> to the cavity of the mouth, being in the form of external speech, gross, arising from <s>Madhyamā</s>, being in the waking state, she is <s>Vaikharī</s>. The etymological and other particulars of these names have been elaborated in the commentary on the first verse. Now, at the time of dissolution, preceded by the dissolution of waking, <s>Vaikharī</s> dissolves into <s>Madhyamā</s>. <s>Madhyamā</s>, preceded by the dissolution of dream, dissolves into <s>Paśyantī</s>. She, preceded by the dissolution of deep sleep, dissolves into <s>Parā</s>. <s>Parā</s>, being of the nature of the <s>Turīya</s> (Fourth) stage, is called the <s>samādhi</s> state. Thus, the empowered Self is in <s>Parā</s> as <s>Turīya</s>; in <s>Paśyantī</s> as <s>Prājña</s>; in <s>Madhyamā</s> as <s>Taijasa</s>; in <s>Vaikharī</s> as <s>Viśva</s>—this is the outline of the scriptural meaning. Now we analyze according to the verbal connection. 'O Lord! Through the mastery of the senses, in the firm embrace of play with your supreme Goddess, when such <s>samādhi</s> unity arises effortlessly, how can external speech extend the restlessness of uttering sweet words, with the activity of manifest palate and lip openings—there is simply no possibility of such restlessness'—such is the meaning. Why is there none?—to address this he says: the inner <s>Paśyantī</s>, concealing herself out of modesty—being more interior than <s>Madhyamā</s>, she does not wish to reveal herself. In the <s>Turīya</s> stage, because breath does not arise, even <s>Madhyamā</s> breaks off from the taste of desiring to issue forth sweet sound. She does not uproot the sweet sound that is in the form of inner speech—such is the meaning. Where in the <s>samādhi</s> of <s>Parā</s> there is the non-arising of <s>Paśyantī</s> and <s>Madhyamā</s>—there how can <s>Vaikharī</s> operate?—such is the purport. Here, upon a subject matter established in the <s>Āgama</s> scriptures, conventional worldly usage of the <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic) type has been superimposed. Just as when the firm embrace of play with <s>Parā</s>, the supreme Goddess, the chief queen, is taking place, some other inner one, being inner by nature, seeing the embrace of you two, conceals herself out of modesty. <s>Madhyamā</s> too—neither inner nor outer—the intermediate-state sweet sound, as it might be, breaks off from the taste of desiring to emerge. She, wishing to come out, desists out of curiosity. There the external one, a courtesan of the retinue, how can she extend the restlessness of uttering sweet words?—such is the purport. He applies the definition: '<s>atra āgama</s>' etc. He reminds of the variety of worldly subject matter useful for poetry: '<s>laukikavastu</s>' etc. Now, similarity of qualifiers has been stated as the definition of <s>samāsokti</s>. But in pure superimposition of effect, that is not all-pervading—to address this he says '<s>tatra śuddhakārya</s>' etc. For in pure superimposition of effect, in '<s>vilikhati kucāv</s>' etc., although the forceful love-play effects like breast-scratching do not primarily possess the qualifier-status regarding <s>khadira</s> etc., still through figurative usage, the qualification is made; therefore the definition should somehow be applied. Now, why resort to figurative usage?—to address this he says '<s>pūrvaśāstrānusāreṇa</s>' etc. Now, where there is impropriety for <s>samāsokti</s>, to rectify it through logical procedure, he says '<s>iha tu</s>' etc. '<s>Aindraṃ dhanur</s>'—bearing <s>Indra</s>'s bow (rainbow) resembling fresh nail-scratches, having a pallid cloud, propitiating the blemished moon, she made autumn surpass the sun's heat. '<s>Payodhara</s>' means both cloud and breast. Because of the prominence of the blemish exceeding grace, the statement of being blemished serves to reveal the paramour's nature. Autumn's heat is greater relative to the rainy season. Here the discussion: '<s>asti tāvad</s>' etc. Having asserted that the apprehension of hero-hood exists, he objects to it: '<s>na ca atra</s>' etc. The meaning is that in the apprehension of hero-hood through suggestiveness, there is no reason. Anticipating the existence of a reason, he refutes: '<s>prasādayantī</s>' etc. If you think that from the similarity of qualifiers in the form of propitiating the blemished one, first the heroine-hood of autumn is understood, and subordinate to that, the hero-hood of the moon and sun is understood—this is not sustainable. Why? Because of the dissimilarity of the qualifier '<s>ārdranakhakṣatābham aindraṃ dhanuḥ</s>' (rainbow resembling fresh nail-scratches). <s>Indra</s>'s bow is a qualifier of autumn alone, not of the heroine. Now, if through the simile-containing qualifier '<s>ārdranakhakṣatābham</s>' there is a partial simile (<s>ekadeśavivartinī upamā</s>) in autumn, and by its force the hero-hood of the moon and sun might be understood—to address this he says '<s>na ca ekadeśa</s>' etc. If a partial simile had been stated by someone, then by its force, the hero-hood of these two would follow. But this has not been stated by anyone. Therefore, how can the establishment of hero-hood for these two follow from its force? Wishing to resolve this, he says '<s>ucyata</s>' etc. '<s>Ekadeśavivartinī</s>' etc. Although it has not been explicitly stated, there is no prohibition of it either. Now, in the absence of both statement and prohibition, how is it possible?—to address this he says '<s>sāmānyalakṣaṇa</s>' etc. Now, if a partial simile is possible here, then it would be the figure of <s>upamā</s> alone that obtains, not <s>samāsokti</s>—to address this he says '<s>atha atra</s>' etc. '<s>Atha</s>' marks the governing rule. If some hero were understood as the <s>upamāna</s> (standard of comparison), the figure of <s>upamā</s> would obtain. But no hero is understood here as the governing subject. Rather, the conventional usage of hero-hood applies to the sun and moon alone—because the conventional usage of hero-hood is attributed to them in this autumn. Thus, when <s>samāsokti</s> obtains, the verbal arrangement should follow accordingly—he says '<s>tad atra</s>' etc. The <s>upamāna</s> status, though established by verbal proximity in the nail-scratches, should be transferred to <s>Indra</s>'s bow. Why? Through the consideration of the subject matter. He clarifies that consideration of the subject matter: '<s>indracāpābham</s>' etc. The apprehension proceeds from the conventional usage of another word. Where has the transfer of a property belonging to one thing to another been seen?—to address this he says '<s>yathā dadhna</s>' etc. In '<s>dadhnā juhoti</s>' (he offers with curds), the injunction understood as pertaining to the offering is already established in '<s>agnihotraṃ juhoti</s>' (he offers the fire-oblation). Through the consideration of the subject matter, just as it is transferred in the case of curds, so too here it should be investigated—such is the purport. Therefore, he concludes that this is <s>samāsokti</s> alone: '<s>evam upamānuprāṇita</s>' etc. Because the <s>upameya</s> status of <s>Indra</s>'s bow is fashioned into <s>upamāna</s> status, the enlivening by <s>upamā</s> is intentional. Now, where by logical reasoning <s>samāsokti</s> is removed and only the partial simile obtains, he shows that domain: '<s>iha punar</s>' etc. '<s>Netrair iva</s>' etc. He investigates the cause for the apprehension of heroine-hood in the beauty of the lake: '<s>saraḥśriyam</s>' etc. The apprehension of heroine-hood through similarity of qualifiers—not by <s>samāsokti</s>. Therefore, the superimposition of conventional usage also does not apply—he says '<s>tasmāt nāyikā</s>' etc. The heroine here functions as the <s>upamāna</s> (standard) for the beauty of the lake, not through superimposition of conventional usage as a property of the lake's beauty. Therefore, in such a domain, in the absence of any alternative, the partial simile alone should be accepted. Though unstated, how can it be accepted?—to address this he says '<s>yais tu</s>' etc. By us, at least, it has been stated with reasoning. By those who have not stated it, in the absence of any alternative, it should be enumerated—such is the meaning. Now, previously the partial simile was rejected, and now it is being established—is this not a contradiction?—to address this he says '<s>yatra tu keśapāśa</s>' etc. When a simile has been stated in compound form, like 'the radiance of teeth is like flowers,' even then by the force of another compound, the similarity of qualifiers is established. There, <s>samāsokti</s> raised by the simile-containing qualifier is appropriate. But presently, in '<s>netrair iva</s>,' in the absence of any alternative, only the partial simile is established—hence there is no contradiction; all is clear. Now he states another variety when this is empowered by <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s> (corroboration by a general statement): '<s>sā ca</s>' etc. '<s>Samarthya</s>' is the contextual meaning; '<s>samarthaka</s>' is the non-contextual. '<s>Atha upagūḍha</s>'—'embraced'; '<s>yayau</s>'—'departed.' Here it pertains to the contextual meaning. '<s>Asamāpta</s>'—here it pertains to the corroborating meaning. He applies both: '<s>atra upagūḍhatvena</s>' etc. The embrace and the cessation of sidelong lightning-glances serve as the similarity of qualifiers; by the <s>samāsokti</s> raised thereby, the conventional usage of hero is understood. That being so, the particular meaning embraced by <s>samāsokti</s> is corroborated by the general meaning through <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s>. And the arising of the corroborating general form: through the force of <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia) in '<s>paribhraṣṭapayodharāṇām</s>' (of those whose clouds/breasts have fallen away), the qualifier '<s>upagūḍha</s>' (embraced) is clearly common. '<s>Śāntataṭid</s>' (with calmed lightning)—this was earlier simile-containing. '<s>Taṭitaḥ kaṭākṣā iva</s>' (whose sidelong glances are like lightning). Now, the corroborating meaning in the general form '<s>taṭitsadṛśakaṭākṣa</s>' (one whose glances resemble lightning)—through the <s>samāsokti</s> raised by the effect in the form of enjoyment, contained in the gender-variation of feminine and masculine designation, the particular autumn-narrative with superimposed hero-convention is corroborated. He states the variety due to <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy): '<s>ākṛṣṭivega</s>' etc. '<s>Veṣṭanā</s>'—whose wrapping is <s>Mandara</s> mountain; '<s>pāda</s>' means both the foot-hill and the foot. Here, to show the simultaneity of <s>samāsokti</s> and <s>utprekṣā</s>, he says '<s>atra nirmoka</s>' etc. By the wrapping in the slough-silk, through the narration of <s>Mandākinī</s>, through the denial of that, the superimposition of <s>Mandākinī</s>; and its being wrapped by the bordering mountain is determined as being wrapped at the base of the foot—through the <s>atiśayokti</s> of the type 'non-difference in difference' arising from the paronomasia of the word '<s>pāda</s>.' And what is thus determined, '<s>manthavya</s>' etc., raises a fancy regarding the result. And that [fancy], depending on the conventional usage of husband and wife regarding the ocean and <s>Mandākinī</s>, raises <s>samāsokti</s> simultaneously with itself—thus the two are simultaneous. He shows this in other examples too: '<s>evaṃ nakhakṣata</s>' etc.

children.translated_text: 'In the superimposition of pure form, the similarity would be figurative.'
'The superimposition of behavior is the direct cause in this [<s>samāsokti</s>].'
'If there is similarity of qualifiers, due to the dissolution of another compound,'
'Simile, operating in one part only, does not obstruct this [<s>samāsokti</s>].'
'In <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s> (corroboration) one sees [the matter]; and in <s>samarthya</s> (capability), the enabler;'
'And this [<s>samāsokti</s>] sometimes becomes conjoined with <s>utprekṣā</s>, and sometimes simultaneous.'

body.text: parikaraṃ lakṣayati-
body.translated_text: He defines <s>parikara</s> (attendant qualification) —

body.text: viśeṣaṇasābhiprāyatvaṃ parikaraḥ || 32 ||
body.translated_text: The purposefulness of qualifiers is <s>parikara</s> (attendant qualification). || <s>RuAss</s> 32 ||

body.text: saṅgatimāha-viśeṣaṇavaicitryeti /

children.translated_text: He explains: 'the name "qualifier"...' etc.

children.text: prasannagaṃbhīratvaṃ nāma padānāṃ vyāṅgyārthagarbhīkāra eva na tu vyaṅgyasya vācyātiśāyitā /
children.translated_text: 'Lucid profundity' (<s>prasannagāmbhīratva</s>) means precisely the impregnation of words with suggested meaning — not the surpassing of the expressed by the suggested.
To explain, he says: 'thus...' etc.
'Facing toward the expressed' means subordination to the expressed meaning.

body.translated_text: He states the connection: 'the variety of qualifiers...' etc.

body.text:
rājñaḥ iti /
rājño na tu yādṛśatādṛśasya /
tatrāpi mānadhanasya na tvavamānasahasya /
kārmukabhṛto na nirāyudhasya /
duryodhanasya na tu śakyayodhanasya /
agrato na tvasamakṣyam /
kurubāndhavasya miṣataḥ karṇasya śalyasya ca na niḥsahāyasya /
sarvaiveya-"manādare ṣaṣṭhī" /
itthaṃ miṣato duryodhanakarṇaśalyānanādṛtyetyarthaḥ /
duḥśāsanasyetyanuktvātasya pāṇḍavavadhūkeśāmbarākarṣiṇa ityuktiḥ hantavyatvaprasiddhyai /
jīvatā eva na tu mūrcchitasya mṛtasya vā /
tīkṣṇākarajakṣuṇṇāda sṛgvakṣasaḥ na tvāyudhavidāritāt /
koṣṇaṃ na tuparyuṣitam /
mayādya pītamiti bhīmasenoktiḥ /

children.translated_text: He shows the purposefulness: 'here...' etc.
He shows [purposefulness] in a sentence as well: 'thus, the king of <s>Aṅga</s>...' etc.
'The impregnation of qualifiers with suggested meaning —'
'That purposefulness with sarcasm (<s>utprāsa</s>) is <s>parikara</s>; because <s>parikara</s> is suggested.'

body.translated_text:
'Of the king' — [means] of [a particular] king, not of just any [king].
Moreover, one who is rich in honor, not one who endures dishonor.
One who bears a bow, not one who is unarmed.
Of <s>Duryodhana</s>, not of one who can be easily fought.
Before [him], not out of sight.
Of the kinsman of the <s>Kurus</s>, while <s>Karṇa</s> and <s>Śalya</s> looked on, not of one without allies.
All these [genitives follow the rule]: 'the sixth case-ending is used to express disrespect.'
Thus, the meaning is: disregarding <s>Duryodhana</s>, <s>Karṇa</s>, and <s>Śalya</s> who were looking on.
'Of <s>Duḥśāsana</s>' — by saying not his name but 'the one who dragged the hair and garment of the wife of the <s>Pāṇḍavas</s>,' [the intention is] to establish that he deserves to be killed.
'While still alive' — not while unconscious or dead.
'From the chest torn by sharp nail-tips' — not torn by weapons.
'Warm' — not stale.
'Drunk by me today' — this is the statement of <s>Bhīmasena</s>.

body.text: śleṣaṃ lakṣayati-
body.translated_text: He defines <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia/double-meaning) —

body.text: viśeṣyasyāpi sāmye dvayorvopādāne śleṣaḥ || 33 ||
body.translated_text: When even the qualified noun has similarity [of meaning], or when both [qualifier and qualified] are adopted, that is <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia). || <s>RuAss</s> 33 ||

body.text:
arthadvayasya yadā prākaraṇikatvamaprākaraṇikatvameva vā tadā viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyayoḥ śabdasāmye śleṣaḥ /
yadā tūbhayamayatvaṃ arthadvayasya tadā viśeṣyāṃśe pṛthagupādāne śleṣa iti sūtrārthaḥ /
saṅgatimāha-kevalaviśeṣaṇeti /
idamiti vacanaviśeṣaṇam /
vyācaṣṭe-tatra dvayorityādi /
viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyasāmya eveti /
ubhayatra śabdasāmye satyevetyarthaḥ /

ādye tu prakāradvaye niyamahetvabhāvāt dvāvapi vācyau /

śliṣṭaprakāradvayeti /
ādyaṃ prakāradvayaṃ śliṣṭaṃ viśeṣyāṃśe 'pi śleṣārthatvāt /
yena dhvasteti /
anaḥśākaṭam /
abhavena asaṃsāreṇa balidaityajitkāyaḥ purāmṛtasaṃvibhāgakāle strīkṛtaḥ strībhāvaṃ nītaḥ /
yaśca udvṛttakāliyādibhujaṅgaghātīti /
aravalayavān aravalayaṃ cakram /
agaṃ govardhanaṃ gāṃ mahīṃ ca yaḥ kṛṣṇaḥ varāhāvatāre adhārayat /
yasya ca stutyaṃ nāma amaraḥ śaśimacchirohara ityāhuḥ /
śaśimadrāhuḥ śaśinaṃ mathnātīti /

sa mādhavastvāṃ sarvadā pāyāt /
atha yena dhvastamanobhavena nāśitamanmathena balijitkāyaḥ viṣṇorvapuḥ purāṇāṃ saṃharaṇe astrīkṛtaḥ /
yaścedvṛndrakalāvat stutyaṃ ca nāma hara ityāhuḥ /
andhakāsurakṣayakaraḥ umādhavo gaurīpatiḥsarvadā tvāṃ pāyāt /
atra hariharayordvayorapi prākaraṇikatā /
nītānāmiti /
lubdhairmadhulaṃpaṭaiḥ vyādhaiśca bhūriti kriyāviśeṣaṇam ekadā śilīmukhairbhramaraiḥ anyadā bhūribāṇaiḥ /
vanaṃ jalaṃ vipinaṃ ca /
kamalānāṃ padmānāṃ mṛgāṇāṃ ca /
atra padmamṛgayoraprākaraṇikatā /
sveccheti /
viṣayo deśakośādistryādiśca /
dehīti vitareti dehavāniti ca /
mārgaṇaśatairyācakasārthaiḥ /
vaktuṃ na yātītyekadā mārgaṇaśataiḥ prayogabhedān (t)śatasaṅkhyairbāṇaiḥ duḥkhaṃ dadātītyanyadā /
jīvitaṃ jīvikā jīvaścar /
iśvaraḥ durvidagdhaḥ /
prabhuratra prākaraṇikataḥ, aprākaraṇiko manobhavaḥṣa atra viśeṣyayordvayorupādānam /
udāharaṇatraye 'pi yojanāyāha-atra hariharetyādi /
punastraividhyāyāha-eṣa ca śabdārtheti /
udāttādīti /
laukikaśabdeṣvapi svarabhedādevārthāvagatiḥ /
tālvoṣṭhādivyāpāraḥ prayatnaḥ ayaṃ śabdānyatve hetuḥ /
śabdaśleṣe liṅgāntaramāha-yatra prāyeṇeti /
arthaśleṣastu anyathetyāha-ata eveti /
ubhayaśleṣamāha-saṅkalanayeti /
ubhayaśleṣamudāharati-raktacchadatvamiti /
chadodalaṃvāsāśca /
vikacāḥ vikasvarāḥ, kacarahitāśca /
jalaiḥsaṅgataṃ nālamādadhānāḥ jaḍajanaiḥsakhyamalaṃ nādadhānāḥ /
puṣpeṣu kusumānatareṣu ruciṃ śobhāṃ puṣpabāṇapriyatāṃ ca /
ubhayaśleṣatāṃ darśayati-atraraktetyādi /
pṛthaganudāharaṇe hetumāha-granthagauraveti /
athāsya sāvakāśaniravakāśādicarcām ārabhate-eṣa cetyādinā /

body.translated_text:
'Of the punning qualifier' —
In <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression), however, since when it is based on a punning qualifier the qualified portion is suggested, <s>samāsokti</s> itself is the overriding figure.
For in <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia), the defining characteristic is precisely the expressed status (<s>vācyatva</s>).
Therefore, being deficient in the defining characteristic, even when the pun is manifest in the qualifiers, it is overridden.
To show the overriding power of <s>śleṣa</s> in another qualifier too, he says: 'here, however...' etc.
<s>Vivasvān</s> (the Sun), though renowned in the worlds as pervaded by the three <s>Vedas</s>, went toward <s>Vāruṇī</s>.
<s>Vāruṇī</s> means both the western direction and liquor.
Therefore he has fallen from the sunset mountain.
'Falling' means contact with a lower place; and the degradation itself being due to the fall — for purification he entered the midst of the submarine fire (<s>baḍavāgni</s>) — this is the meaning.
He explains: 'of <s>Vivasvān</s>, in actual fact...' etc.
Of him, who is in reality pervaded by the three Vedas, the falling and the entry — resulting from contact with <s>Vāruṇī</s> — through an <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole) based on <s>śleṣa</s>, both actions of <s>Vivasvān</s> are determined.
This is the hyperbole called <s>tatkriyāyoga</s> (conjunction of that action).
Although it is one and the same action, differentiated by the difference of agents, determined as non-different despite real difference — that is <s>tatkriyāyoga</s>; the <s>atiśayokti</s> is caused by it.
Here, regarding the <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) —
The figure of <s>virodha</s> (contradiction), which is referred to by the pronoun 'therefore' and has the form of the semblance of contradictory conduct — the meaning adorned by it is fancied as having the cause in the form of falling.
And 'for purification' is fancied as the effect.
Therefore there is both <s>hetūtprekṣā</s> (causal fancy) and <s>phalotprekṣā</s> (fancy of result).
The figure of <s>virodha</s> too fulfills its definition — he says: 'and of the <s>virodha</s> figure...' etc.
Therefore, <s>virodha</s> and <s>utprekṣā</s> are simultaneous — forming one episode; but the subsiding of the contradiction comes later — this is the order of cognition.
Thus, <s>śleṣa</s>, being the overrider of all, overrides the <s>virodha</s> figure and establishes it as a mere semblance.
And when <s>virodha</s> is overridden, the overriding of the <s>utprekṣā</s> caused by it is automatically established — this is the purport.
Therefore this is <s>śleṣa</s> alone.
But where in drama etc. there is the function of <s>sūcakatva</s> (suggestiveness), characterized by seed-planting in the form of introducing future events — regarding that, he discusses: 'but where...' etc.
Even when the expressed meaning is the principal and pertains to the present —
'the introduction of an alternative meaning' —
'introduction' (<s>upakṣepa</s>) is its name.
As has been said: 'seed-planting is introduction.'
'Of dual meaning' — there, the dual meaning is not intended as connected at the level of expression.
Rather, one meaning is expressed and contextual.
The future meaning, however, is suggested.
Therefore this is not <s>śleṣa</s>.
For in <s>śleṣa</s>, the necessity is that both meanings be expressed.

rājanniti /

children.text: arthāntaranyāse hi sāmānyaviśeṣyayoḥ kāryakāraṇayośca vācyatvaṃ(dṛṣṭānte tu)sarūpayoḥ vācyatvam /
children.translated_text: In <s>Arthāntaranyāsa</s> (Corroboration), the general and particular, or cause and effect, are expressed [at the literal level]. In <s>Dṛṣṭānta</s>, two similar [propositions] are expressed.
In every case, when the subject matter is understood through the statement of something not the subject, it is precisely <s>Aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (Description of the Irrelevant).
[Definition:] <s>Aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> is the understanding of the subject matter from something other [than the subject].
It is considered to be fivefold, through the varieties of general-particular and so on.

body.translated_text: This has been explained previously. He shows the cognition of the particular from the general: 'Here, <s>Prahasta</s>,' and so on. 'This much of his' — this much from his mouth. The meaning is: in comparison to the dullness to be mentioned next, his dullness is slight — [hence] the word 'this.' What is it? That which — taking a drop of water on a lotus petal for a pearl, he believed [it to be so]. Such a believer is not excessively dull — this is the meaning. But he who is truly dull is the one who, when that water-drop — believed to be a pearl — is being picked up and dissolves at the touch of his fingertip, does not sleep at night from inner grief [thinking]: 'My gem has flown away!' He shows the cognition of the general from the particular: 'Here, of the dull ones,' and so on. '<s>Paśyāma</s>' (let us see): this is the hero's speech in the form of narrating the heroine's behavior to a friend. [He says:] 'Let us see what she will do' — with this thought, I adopted firmness in the form of avoiding conversation and such. But she adopted anger, [thinking:] 'This deceitful one does not speak to me at all.' Thus, at that juncture — with both artfully displaying mutual bewilderment — I laughed with a stratagem, and she too shed tears that robbed [her of] composure. When she was overcome with tears, her composure itself was abandoned — this is the meaning. He shows the cognition of the effect from the cause: 'Here, thus, mounted on the stream [of tears].' When the effect — the cessation of the love-quarrel — is the subject at hand, the tears that are mentioned should be understood as unintended [i.e., as a vehicle for the subject]. '<s>Indira</s>': by 'as if smeared with moon-ointment' — the beauty of the face [is suggested]; by 'the glances of doe-eyed women are frozen' — the captivating movement of the eyes; by 'the petal of coral seems to have faded in redness' — the radiance of the lips; by 'in the throats of cuckoo-wives, the effect is blackness, which is indeed the subject' — the mellifluous quality of the throat; and by 'the peacock feathers seem to be objects of reproach' — the abundance of the hair is suggested. He shows the cognition of the cause from the effect: 'Here, by those being imagined,' and so on. '<s>Saṃbhāvyamānaiḥ</s>' means 'by those being fancifully imagined.' He anticipates an objection of over-extension: 'But from the effect,' and so on. '<s>Yena lambālakaḥ</s>' (by whom [he has] hanging locks): here, through the effect — the hanging locks and such — the cause, namely the slaying of the elephant-demon, is cognized. '<s>Cakrābhighāta</s>' (the blow of the discus): here, from the variety of effects — the embrace of <s>Rati</s> being rendered fruitless and only the kiss remaining — the cause, the severing of <s>Rāhu</s>'s head, [is cognized]. He shows the over-extension: 'Here, indeed,' and so on. He resolves [the objection]: 'This is not a flaw.' When both [cause and effect] are the subject matter, the vivid description of the effect in relation to the cause — being aesthetically striking — falls within the domain of <s>Paryāyokta</s> (Indirect Expression) as the medium for conveying the cause. When the effect is not the subject matter, it is <s>Aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (Description of the Irrelevant) — this is the distinction. He concludes by [showing] the distinct domains: 'Thus, wherever,' and so on. '<s>Tādṛśam</s>' means 'of such a kind' — that which is the subject matter itself. '<s>Āgūrayati</s>' means 'brings by [its own] force.' This being so, he says again, to make it clear that when the subject matter itself draws in another subject matter for its own embellishment, it is precisely <s>Paryāyokta</s>: 'And therefore, by this,' and so on. '<s>Rājan</s>': the <s>Kubjā</s> (hunchback woman) is appointed to feed the parrot. '<s>Kumāra</s>' is a form of address. 'Its ministers' means those in charge of its meals. '<s>Rājaśuka</s>' means 'the chief parrot.' Here, since even the behavior of the royal parrot is the subject matter as ancillary to the hero's glory, it should be understood as <s>Paryāyokta</s>. He states the view of others: 'Others, however.' Of the cause in the form of the enemy's flight. In such a subject, even if others consider it <s>Aprastutapraśaṃsā</s>, there is no contradiction. When both [subject and non-subject] are the subject matter, it is <s>Paryāyokta</s>; when the effect is not the subject matter, it is <s>Aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> — since the distinction is unshakeable, with this intention he says: 'In every case.' Now he says these should be understood as examples with similarity: 'These, with similarity,' and so on. With dissimilarity, they should be inferred. He illustrates with dissimilarity, since the distinction based on resemblance is easily understood through this method with similarity: '<s>Dhanyā</s>' (blessed). He shows the dissimilarity: 'Here, the winds,' and so on. When the expressible [meaning] is possible, [examples] need not be given separately — he says: 'The expressible,' and so on. '<s>Kas tvaṃ bhoḥ</s>' (Who are you, sir?): when asked 'Who are you?', the <s>Śākoṭaka</s> tree says: 'Sir, I shall tell you,' and so on. Then another question: 'Will you speak from detachment, as it were?' The reply: 'Well understood.' Then in response to 'Why is this so?', the remaining answer [follows]. He shows the impossibility: 'Here, by the inanimate [tree],' and so on. But if such impossibility is already established? — to this he says: 'The subject is understood.' Since the superimposition of the <s>Śākoṭaka</s>'s behavior is cognized at the very outset, the impossibility is proper — because the expressible [literal] meaning is completely concealed through <s>Jahatsvārthalakṣaṇā</s> (abandonment of the primary meaning). '<s>Antaśchridrāṇi</s>': '<s>Chridrāṇi</s>' means holes and also gateways to misfortune. '<s>Kaṇṭakāḥ</s>' means thorns and also horripilation and also troublemakers. Here, in the expressible meaning, 'holes' being the cause for the weakening of qualities — this has a dual nature. Since the understanding follows the purport of the subject matter, the superimposition of that is fitting. He states this: 'Here, the expressible,' and so on. The same should be observed when <s>Śleṣa</s> (paronomasia) is embedded — since 'holes,' 'thorns,' and 'qualities' have punning meanings — he says: 'This same [principle] also.' He shows the distinction of domain from <s>Arthāntaranyāsa</s> and <s>Dṛṣṭānta</s>: 'There, in this [context],' and so on.

children.translated_text: It is again twofold, through the employment of similarity and dissimilarity.
And again threefold, through the division of the expressible [meaning] — into possible, impossible, and both.
It is distinguished from <s>Paryāyokta</s> (Indirect Expression) by the fact that the subject matter is [itself] understood [there, not through another].
This [<s>Aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> is also distinguished] from the figure of <s>Arthāntaranyāsa</s> (Corroboration) and from <s>Dṛṣṭānta</s> (Illustrative Example).

body.text:
arthāntaranyāsārthaṃ saṅgatimāha-uktanayeneti /
sāmānyaviseṣādisambandhayogata ukto nayaḥ /
tatra sūtram-
body.translated_text: He states the connection for <s>Arthāntaranyāsa</s>: 'By the stated method.' The stated method is through the relations of general-particular and so on. The definition:

body.text: sāmānyaviśeṣakāryakāraṇābhāvābhyāṃ nirdiṣṭaprakṛtasamarthanamarthāntaranyāsaḥ || 35 ||
body.translated_text: <s>Arthāntaranyāsa</s> (Corroboration) is the substantiation of a stated subject by means of the relations of general-particular, cause-effect, or [their] absence. // <s>RuAss</s>_35 //

body.text:
ābhyāṃ sambandhābhyāṃ samarthyatvena nirdiṣṭasya prakṛtasya samarthanamarthāntaranyāsa ityarthaḥ /
vyācaṣṭe-nirdiṣṭasyetyādi /
samarthanārhasya na tu samarthananirvyapekṣasya /
samarthakātpūrvaṃ paścādveti pūrvapaścādbhāve kāmacāra uktaḥ /
na tvapūrvatveneti /
nirdiṣṭatvenaiva pratītirnatvapūrvatvena /
apūrvatve ko doṣaḥ ityata āha-anumānarūpeti /
tathā pratītāvanumānarūpatvameva prasajedityarthaḥ /
bhedān saṃcaṣṭe - tatra sāmānyamityādi /
saṃbhavato 'pi vaicitryavirahiṇo bhedānapohati-hiśabdetyādi /
uṭṭaṅkitaṃ niṣṭaṅkitam /
anantaratneti-sannipāto bahūnāṃ saṅghātaḥ /
atra guṇasannipāte doṣanimajjanalakṣaṇaṃ sāmānyaṃ sādharmyeṇa viśeṣasamarthakam /
lokottaramiti /
puṃsāṃ lokottaraṃ caritameva pratiṣṭhām arpayati audāryaṃ pratiṣṭhāpayatītyarthaḥ /
na tu kulamiha nimittam /
vātāpitāpano 'gastyaḥ /
kalaśaḥ kulasthānīyastasya samudrapāne ko 'dhikāraḥ /
līlāyitaṃ caritasthānīyam /
atra agastyavṛttalakṣaṇo viśeṣaḥ sādharmyeṇa sāmānyasamarthakaḥ /
sahaseti-kriyā dhyavasāyaḥ sahasāvidhānarūpo hyāvivekaḥ āpadāṃ padam anenāpatpadatvarūpaṃ kāryaṃ sahasā vidhānābhāvarūpasya kāraṇasya vaidharmyeṇa samarthakam /
vimṛśyakāriṇāṃ sampado (vṛṇata)iti /
sahasāvidhānābhāvātmano vimṛśyakāritvasya kāraṇasya sampadvaraṇaṃ kāryaṃ sādharmyeṇa /
atra sādharmyasya prāthamikatvāt uttarārdhārthapuraskāreṇa yojayati-atra sahasāvidhānetyādi /
vimṛśyakāritvarūpasya kāraṇasyeti śeṣaḥ /
tasyaiva kāraṇasyetyarthaḥ /
pṛthvīti-dvitayaṃ pṛthvī bhujaṅgarūpaṃ tat tritaye kūrmarāja yuktadvitayātmani /
didhīrṣā dhārayitumicchā /
atrātatajyīkaraṇaṃ kāraṇaṃ sthirībhāvādikārye sādharmyeṇa samarthakam /
tadidaṃ yojayati- atra harakārmuketi /
aho hīti-āyuṣā bahvaparāddhaṃ hi suhyadaḥ parābhavaṃ dṛṣṭvā ridṛśamapriyaṃ vaktavyatvenāpatitaṃ yataḥ /
ta evara hidhanyā, suhṛtparābhavamaṭṭaṣṭvā ye kṣayaṃ gatāḥ /
atra sāmānyasya vaidharmyeṇa samarthakatvam /
yojayati-atrāyuḥ kartṛketi /
āyuḥ kartṛkeṇa hi aparādhenādhanyatvaṃ ākṣitpam /
āyurviruddhakṣayagamanaprayuktaṃ yaddhanyatvaṃ tadvaidharmyeṇa samarthakaṃ sāmānyamuktam /

children.translated_text: He reminds: 'When [the relationship] is of cause and effect.'
He reveals the indifference toward the rejected [varieties]: 'The word <s>hi</s> (indeed),' and so on.

children.text: samarthyatve na nirdiṣṭaḥ prakṛto yaḥ samarthyate /
children.translated_text: That which is stated in order to be substantiated — the subject matter that is substantiated —
this is <s>Arthāntaranyāsa</s> (Corroboration), eightfold through [the relations of] general, particular, and so on.

body.translated_text: The meaning is: the substantiation of a stated subject — stated as that which is to be substantiated — through these [two] relations, is <s>Arthāntaranyāsa</s>. He explains: 'Of the stated,' and so on. 'Deserving substantiation' — not one that is independent of substantiation. The order — the substantiating [statement] before or after [the substantiated] — is optional. 'Not by [virtue of] being unprecedented' — the cognition [arises] by virtue of being stated, not by being unprecedented. What is the fault in being unprecedented? — to this he says: 'In the form of inference.' [If unprecedented,] the cognition would amount to having the character of inference — this is the meaning. He explains the varieties: 'There, the general,' and so on. He removes [from consideration] varieties that, though possible, lack aesthetic variety: 'The word <s>hi</s> (indeed),' and so on. '<s>Uṭṭaṅkitam</s>' means 'stamped/proclaimed.' '<s>Anantaratna</s>': '<s>Sannipāta</s>' means the concourse of many. Here, the general — characterized by [the principle that] defects are submerged in a concentration of good qualities — substantiates the particular through similarity. '<s>Lokottaram</s>' (extraordinary): the extraordinary conduct of men alone confers distinction — it establishes magnanimity. Not lineage here. <s>Agastya</s> is the scorcher of <s>Vātāpi</s>. The pot (<s>Kalaśa</s>), standing for [humble] birth — what authority has it for the drinking of the ocean? The playful [act of drinking the ocean] stands for [extraordinary] conduct. Here, the particular characterized by the behavior of <s>Agastya</s> substantiates the general through similarity. '<s>Sahasā</s>' (hastily): action, namely resolution — haste in the form of acting without deliberation is the seat of calamities. By this, the effect — being a seat of calamities — substantiates the cause — absence of hasty action — through dissimilarity. 'The fortunes attend upon (<s>vṛṇate</s>) those who act with deliberation.' The effect — fortunes attending — [substantiates] the cause — deliberate action as the absence of hasty action — through similarity. Here, since the similarity is primary, he connects it with the meaning of the latter half [of the verse] first: 'Here, hasty action,' and so on. The remainder is: 'of the cause in the form of deliberate action.' [It means:] of that very cause. '<s>Pṛthvī</s>' (Earth): the pair [of things] — the Earth and the serpent-form — in the trio of the Tortoise-king, united with the pair. '<s>Didhīrṣā</s>' means the desire to support. Here, the stringing of the bow is the cause, substantiating the effect — stability and such — through similarity. He connects this: 'Here, the bow of <s>Hara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>),' and so on. '<s>Aho hī</s>' (Ah, indeed): 'Much has been transgressed by life, for upon seeing the defeat of a friend, such an unpleasant thing must be said.' Rather, blessed are they who, having [merely] heard of the friend's defeat, passed away. Here, the general substantiates through dissimilarity. He connects: 'Here, life as the agent,' and so on. For by the transgression whose agent is life, wretchedness is implied. The blessedness arising from the passing away that is contrary to [continued] life — that, stated as the general, substantiates through dissimilarity.

body.text:
paryāyoktārthasaṅgatiṃ śodhayati-evaṃ aprastuteti /
gamyaprastuveti /
pratīyamānārthaprastāvo hi vartate /
tatra sūtram-
body.translated_text: He clarifies the connection with <s>Paryāyokta</s> (Indirect Expression): 'Thus, of the irrelevant.' '<s>Gamyaprastuta</s>': for what is presented is a suggested meaning. The definition:

body.text: gamyasyāpi bhaṅgyantareṇābhidhānaṃ paryāyoktam || 36 ||
body.translated_text: <s>Paryāyokta</s> (Indirect Expression) is the expression of what is understood [as the subject], through an indirect mode. // <s>RuAss</s>_36 //

body.text:
pratīyamānasyāpi kāryādimukhena prakārānyacareṇābhidhānaṃ paryāyoktam /
vyācaṣṭe-yadevetyādi /
gamyasya sato 'bhidhānamākṣipyopapādayati-gamyasyaiveti /
bhaṅgyantareṇetyetadvivṛṇoti-na hītyādi /
nanu kāryādyabhidhāne gamyasya kathamabhidhānamityata āhakāryāderapīti /
aprastutapraśaṃsāto bhedaṃ nirūpitacaramanusmārayati-etacceti /
spṛṣṭāstā iti /
vyākhyātaṃ prāk /

children.translated_text: He connects: 'Here, of <s>Hayagrīva</s> (the horse-headed demon),' and so on.
The effect is the touching of the flower-clusters.
<s>Paryāyokta</s> (Indirect Expression) is the description of what is understood, through the medium of effect and such.
It is distinguished from <s>Aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> by the fact that the expressible [meaning] is the subject matter [itself].

body.translated_text: The expression of what is suggested too, through an alternative mode such as effect and so on, is <s>Paryāyokta</s>. He explains: 'That which,' and so on. He implies and establishes the expression of what is [already] understood: 'Of what is understood itself.' He explains '<s>bhaṅgyantareṇa</s>' (through an indirect mode): 'For not,' and so on. But when the effect and such are expressed, how is the [subject that is] understood expressed? — to this he says: 'Of the effect and such too.' He reminds [the reader] of the previously determined distinction from <s>Aprastutapraśaṃsā</s>: 'And this,' and so on. '<s>Spṛṣṭāstā</s>': this has been explained previously.

body.text:
vyājastuteḥsaṅgatimāha-gamyatveti /
sūtram-
body.translated_text: He states the connection for <s>Vyājastuti</s> (Ironic Praise): 'The fact of being understood,' and so on. The definition:

body.text: stutinindābhyāṃ nindāstutyorgamyatve vyājastutiḥ || 37 ||
body.translated_text: <s>Vyājastuti</s> (Ironic Praise) is when, through [apparent] praise or blame, the opposite — blame or praise — is understood. // <s>RuAss</s>_37 //

body.text:
stutyā nindāyā gamyatve ekā nindayā stutestvanyā /
ato vyājarūpāstutiḥ vyājena stutiriti ca vigrahaḥ /
vyācaṣṭe-yatra stutirityādi /
pramāṇāntarāt ābhāsīkaraṇakṣamāt /
anugamena arthānvayena dvitīyā tu nindāvyājena stutiriti āha-yatrāpīti /
ato yogavibhāgāt vyājastudidvayam /
nanu stutinindayorgamyāṃśasya prastutatvāda prastutapraśaṃsātaḥ ko bheda ityata āha-stutinindeti /
he heleti /
bodhisattvo jīmūtavāhanaḥ /
sa hi kadācideva parasya hitamādhāt tvaṃ tu ye yāvantastṛṣyanti, tebhyaḥsarvebhya eva vaimukhyalabdhānāmayaśobhārāṇaṃ prodvahane maroḥsāhāyarkaṃ karoṣi /
ato helājitabodhisattve tvayi stutivacovistaro(na)paryāpnotītyarthaḥ /
stuternindāgamakatvaṃ darśayati - atra viparīteti /
indorlakṣmeti /
urvīvalayatilaka indulakṣmādiṣu śyāmaleṣu satsu tvadyaśobhirnakiñciddhavalitaṃ iti stutirgamyate /
tadetadāha-atra dhavalatveti /
anavakḷtpiḥ aparyātpiḥ /
yatra tu gamyāṃśasya nyagbhāvastatra nāsyāḥsāmañjasyamiti darśayitumāha-kiṃ vṛttāntairiti /

children.text: atra vallabhā bhramati hantetyuktyā nindāyāḥsutiparyavasāyitvaṃ na sphuṭībhāvati, anaucityāditi kliṣṭatā /
children.translated_text: Here, by the statement 'the beloved wanders, alas!' — the culmination of blame in praise does not clearly emerge, and from the impropriety, there is awkwardness (<s>Kliṣṭatā</s>).
He states this: 'Here, even though commenced.'
<s>Vyājastuti</s> (Ironic Praise) is twofold: praise through a pretext, or praise that is itself pretextual.
It is distinguished from <s>Aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> by having the nature of praise and blame.

body.translated_text: One type: when blame is understood through [apparent] praise. Another: when praise is [understood] through [apparent] blame. Hence the analysis: 'praise that is in the form of a pretext (<s>Vyāja</s>)' or 'praise through a pretext.' He explains: 'Where praise,' and so on. 'From another means of valid knowledge, capable of rendering [the statement] a mere semblance.' 'Through logical connection, through the connection of meaning' — the second type, praise through the pretext of blame, is stated: 'Where also,' and so on. Hence, through the division of the combination, <s>Vyājastuti</s> is twofold. But since the understood aspect of praise and blame is the subject matter, what is the difference from <s>Aprastutapraśaṃsā</s>? — to this he says: 'Praise and blame,' and so on. '<s>He hele</s>' (O, hey!): the <s>Bodhisattva</s> is <s>Jīmūtavāhana</s>. For he bestowed benefit on another at one time; but you — for all who are thirsty, you render assistance to Death in carrying the burden of ill-fame gained through aversion to all. Therefore, the profusion of words of praise cannot encompass you, who have conquered the <s>Bodhisattva</s> through contempt — this is the meaning. He shows that praise conveys blame: 'Here, the opposite.' '<s>Indorlakṣmī</s>' (the beauty of the Moon): when the moon's beauty-marks and such are dark, 'your fame has not made [them] at all white' — praise is understood. He states this: 'Here, whiteness,' and so on. '<s>Anavakḷptiḥ</s>' means insufficiency. But where the understood aspect is subordinated, this [figure] is not appropriate — to show this he says: '<s>Kiṃ vṛttāntaiḥ</s>' (What is the point of stories?).

body.translated_text: He states the connection for <s>Ākṣepa</s> (Apparent Denial): 'The very fact of being understood.' '<s>Viśeṣa</s>' means excellence. The meaning is: [something] whose domain is the understanding of a special excellence. The definition:

body.text: uktavakṣyamāṇayoḥ prākaraṇikayoḥ viśeṣapratītyarthaṃ niṣedhābhāsa ākṣepaḥ || 38 ||
body.translated_text: <s>Ākṣepa</s> (Apparent Denial) is an apparent negation aimed at the cognition of the special excellence of two contextual things — one already stated and one about to be stated. // <s>RuAss</s>_38 //
