children.translated_text: Here he says that the relationship of type and exemplar is based on the general-particular relation, independent of meaning: 'Similarity of words...'
'<s>Bāla</s> (Young one)...' —

children.text: bālaka! nāhaṃ dūti tasyāḥ priyo 'sīti nāsmākaṃ vyāpāraḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Young one! I am not her messenger — [I know that] you are her beloved, this is not our business.'
'She is dying — this is your disgrace. We are speaking only this much in defense.'

body.translated_text: The apparent prohibition of a contextual [subject], whether already stated or about to be stated, for the purpose of [conveying] a specific understanding — that is <s>ākṣepa</s> (objection). This pair of <s>ākṣepas</s> should be known as heterogeneous. He explains, beginning with 'Here, contextual...' 'Of such a kind' means 'of the intended [subject].' Therefore, the predicate (<s>vidheya</s>) is 'made to operate in an improper domain' — this is the meaning. And therefore, its own nature being negated, it becomes merely apparent. Now, what is the point of this effort? To this he says: 'Of this, by that...' 'Otherwise' means: in the absence of the purpose of specific understanding, it would merely amount to a bath of an elephant — since [the result] would end up as a mere [futile] positive statement. For an elephant, having bathed, immediately becomes grey with dust again. He states its twofold nature: 'And that...' 'As being in the nature of a commenced statement' means 'as having begun to state.' As to which type belongs to which domain, he says beginning with 'As pertaining to the stated...' '<s>Kaimarthakya</s>' means purposelessness. '<s>Āgūraṇa</s>' means accomplishment through implication. Therefore the heterogeneity — he says beginning with 'And thus...' He states that the aspect to be negated differs in both cases: 'There, the stated...' Therefore the difference — he says: 'Hence, here...' 'Following the words' — because [the figure] depends on the force of the apparent negation, it follows the words. 'Pertaining to the stated' — the twofold nature arises from the negation of the thing [itself] and the negation of the statement of the thing. 'Pertaining to the about-to-be-stated' — since the thing has not [yet] been stated, only the statement is negated. There he states a different twofold [division]: 'There, general...' Thus the fourfold [nature].

children.translated_text: 'Therefore, I do not know what is proper to say.'
'<s>Subhaga</s> (O fortunate one)...' —
'O fortunate one! Wait a moment — while this heart, anxious with separation, [composes itself].'
'Having steadied [my heart], I shall speak — or rather, go on your way! What shall I say?'

body.translated_text: 'Be appeased...' — If I were to say 'Be appeased,' in the absence of anger, this speech would not be appropriate. If I were to say 'I shall not do this again,' then that would be an admission of something that exists [i.e., the offense]. If I were to say 'I have no fault,' you would then consider this speech denying fault to be false.

children.translated_text: He demonstrates this, beginning with 'For here, of the courtesan...'
He shows what is not in the domain even in the suggested [type]: 'But that is not to be said...'
That apparent negation in the delimitation of the ocean [of meaning], which is <s>ākṣepa</s> for the accomplishment of the desired [understanding] of the primary [subject] —
that, in the stated domain, pertains to the thing [itself] and to the statement of the thing.

body.translated_text: 'Having steadied my heart anxious with separation, I shall speak' — by this, the agitation in the form of danger to life is commenced [as a topic]. 'Or rather, go on your way — what shall I say' — but because that [death] is more imminent, the inability to speak [is conveyed]. '<s>Jyotsnā</s>' (moonlight) — here, through the force of the pain of separation, moonlight, the cuckoo's call, and such things take on the form of saw-of-darkness etc., hence the endlessness [of suffering]. Therefore, 'She is surely [near death]' — by this half-statement, the state of danger to life is hinted at. 'Ah! What then — what use is life?' — by this, the renunciation of life even before that calamity [arrives]. He constructs [the examples] in order, beginning with 'The first...' 'I am not a messenger' is the negation of a thing — the thing being the status of messenger. 'What is proper to say about this' is the negation of the statement. Both of these pertain to the already-stated domain. He reveals the specific [aspect] indicated by the apparent negation in both cases: 'And there...' 'Being a speaker of things as they are' means 'speaking truths.' The specific [understanding] is to be supplied — 'is understood.' 'What is being stated' — '<s>Prasīda</s>' (be appeased). 'Of what is being uttered' — 'this is not appropriate' — through the very face of negation. 'In the latter' — 'What shall I say' — through the general channel, what one wishes to say — the danger to life etc. — the negation of speaking about the own-nature itself — [here] the drawing in (<s>āgūraṇa</s>) [of meaning] is through the force of the content. 'She is surely [near death]' — through the poignant utterance — 'I cannot live' — the drawing in of another aspect through the negation of speaking about the own-nature. He reveals the specific [understanding] indicated in both cases: 'And there...' The fact that it generates extreme anger — from the determination to depart. He extracts the factors here: 'And thus...' Therefore he says the nature of <s>ākṣepa</s> is such: 'Hence...' Now, would not negation-<s>ākṣepa</s> [suffice]? To this he says: 'But through injunction...' 'Through injunction' means 'through apparent injunction' — this is the meaning. Supplying: 'It will be stated through another <s>sūtra</s>.' Since this is how <s>ākṣepa</s> works through negation of injunction, in such a domain no other ornament [applies] — to this he says: 'And therefore...' Since self-imagining [occurs], therefore the statement of suitability is not proper — hence the negation of the statement. Similarly, in 'Not befitting affection,' the negation is of going [away]. Therefore this is <s>ākṣepa</s> pertaining to the stated domain. He shows what is not in the domain: 'But merely...' For here, the inability to be abandoned etc., due to youth, is not actually negating but rather establishing [the point] — so the understanding of <s>ākṣepa</s> should not be applied. Rather, he shows through a specific contradiction with a prefatory challenge: 'Of whom then?...' Here, a verse for the extraction: 'Therefore, of the desired...' Therefore, the apparent negation of the desired [subject] is the cause of <s>ākṣepa</s>-utterance — for the easy achievement of the specific [understanding] — not an actual identity with negation. Therefore, where the negation is real, there is no <s>ākṣepa</s> — he shows this with examples, beginning with 'But here...' In the first verse here, poetry-thieves, like <s>Daityas</s> (demons), gear up for plundering; therefore 'Protect the nectar of poetry!' — protection is enjoined. But in the second verse, 'Let everyone take as they wish — there is no loss in the world either' — the previously enjoined protection of poetry is directly negated. Similarly, for imprisoning the wind, the placing of stone shutters in caves is enjoined; in the second verse, 'Such worry-like wretchedness is false; the <s>Kirātas</s> do not wish enmity with the wind over imprisonment' — the placing of shutters is directly negated. Therefore this pair of verse-pairs is not an example of <s>ākṣepa</s>. In the absence of <s>ākṣepa</s>, he states another reason: 'Not even aesthetic wonder (<s>camatkāra</s>)...' He shows the possibility of this [figure] as suggested (<s>vyaṅgya</s>): 'And this...' '<s>Gaṇikāsu</s>' (among courtesans) — since courtesans, being devoted to wealth, do everything that is improper, therefore 'You should not trust [her]' — in the very statement about the courtesan, the negation of trust is merely apparent. Because [the understanding is:] 'Through her indifference to wealth, this one is a vessel of pure affection.' Therefore this is <s>ākṣepa</s> pertaining to the stated domain, as suggested.

children.translated_text: But the about-to-be-stated [type] is another, to be known as having the nature of drawing-in (<s>āgūraṇa</s>).
And it is twofold: through the general aspect and through the specific aspect.
The negation of the desired, the obstruction of it, the suggestion of excess —
this fourfold [set] should be known as combining to form the cause of <s>ākṣepa</s>.

'Because of having the same principle' — the purport is that a thing that exists in states of presence and absence has a principle (<s>nyāya</s>) that is the same, inasmuch as it exists in [both] states of presence and absence. There, the <s>sūtra</s>:

children.translated_text: He concludes: 'Therefore...'
'Through novelty, not being encountered by others.'
The indication of an unstated negation through an apparent injunction —
this is understood as <s>ākṣepa</s>, pertaining solely to the about-to-be-stated domain.

body.translated_text: 'For the purpose of specific understanding of the contextual [subject]' continues [from before], but not 'of two contextual [subjects],' since [this type] pertains to a single domain — the about-to-be-stated. As previously, the apparent negation of the desired is <s>ākṣepa</s>. Similarly, for the purpose of specific understanding, the apparent injunction of the undesired is also <s>ākṣepa</s>. He explains, beginning with 'Of the desired...' 'Just as' — by the relative pronoun, he recalls the previously analyzed final <s>ākṣepa</s> to establish the sameness of principle. 'Thus' etc. pertains to the present topic. 'Having a stumbling form' means [it arises] from operation in an improper domain. 'This is through injunction' — since this injunction, appearing [as a real command], is the instrument through which the negation to be suggested is conveyed, therefore this negation, being analyzed through apparent injunction as the suggestive [device], — this is the meaning. And this, culminating in the specific [understanding of] the undesired, is the <s>ākṣepa</s> ornament — this is the construction. Now, <s>ākṣepa</s> has been shown as twofold: in the stated domain, through purposelessness; in the domain to be stated, through the nature of drawing-in. But which [type] is this? To this he says: 'From the drawing-in of negation...' For the negation, unstated here, is drawn in through the apparent injunction. Therefore this should be known as pertaining solely to the about-to-be-stated domain. For it has been said: '<s>Ākṣepa</s> is the drawing-in, in the form of bringing forth, pertaining to the about-to-be-stated domain.' '<s>Gaccha</s>' (Go!) — by '<s>gacchasi cet</s>' (if you go), it is understood: 'If you have a desire to go, I do not refuse.' But in '<s>gaccha</s>' (Go!), the injunction put forward through that [permission] — [the meaning is] 'May my course also be to that same [place]' — but through the revelation of hopelessness regarding life, the negation is conveyed. He constructs [the meaning]: 'Here, by someone...' 'Through the face of non-refusal' — by this, the semantic following of '<s>gacchasi cet</s>' is shown. 'The stumbling form' here is the non-entry directly into the sentence. He also shows the result in the form of specific understanding: 'And the result here...' The result is the utter avoidability of going. What is the cause there? He says: '<s>Asaṃvijñāna</s>' (non-understanding). That by which the meaning is not properly understood — that is non-understanding. The word '<s>cet</s>' (if) is a particle. When '<s>gacchasi cet</s>' is said, the understanding arises: 'What is the use of going there if I am not understood?' etc. This very meaning-conveying particle <s>cet</s> is the basis for [understanding] the utter avoidability — this is the meaning. Now, by what is this utter avoidability established? To this he says: 'And this...' To show the removal of negation in another way, he says: 'As indeed...' 'Nothing at all' — the mature ones, even without being told, know the meaning to be told. '<s>Śithila</s>' (loose/relaxed) — for a swan, being loose-limbed, is especially charming, because of the revelation of inner whiteness. Waves having a similar luster — [thus marking] the ultimate degree of purity. He constructs [the meaning]: 'Here, the unintended...' Of the unintended going, 'there is nothing at all to be said' — directly at the outset, the acceptance is understood. And this being so, this injunction, appearing as undesired, is an auxiliary of <s>ākṣepa</s> having the nature of drawing-in of negation. By 'should be remembered,' the negation is more abundantly indicated — since in the remembrance of such waves, even the topic of going has no place.

body.translated_text: Now, wishing to take up the aesthetic charm of contradiction (<s>virodha</s>), he says beginning with '<s>Ākṣepa</s>, of the desired...' For in the <s>ākṣepa</s> ornament, contradiction is inherent — since in the two <s>sūtras</s> operating through the support of negation of the desired and through the support of injunction of the undesired, there is the presence of non-conformity — this is the meaning. 'We take up this present contradiction' — he says: 'In this connection...' Even among those [figures], he first takes up the <s>virodha</s> (contradiction) ornament as the foundation, because of its primacy: 'Even there...' The <s>sūtra</s>:

body.text: viruddhābhāsatvaṃ virodhaḥ || 40 ||
body.translated_text: The appearance of contradiction is <s>virodha</s> (contradiction). // RuAss 40 //

children.translated_text: When the contradiction pertains to a single domain, it is the <s>virodha</s> ornament.
But when the domains differ, <s>asaṅgati</s> (incongruity) etc. will be stated [later].

body.translated_text: Because a resolution (<s>samādhāna</s>) exists [for the contradiction], it is merely an appearance — [and this apparent] contradiction is the <s>virodha</s> ornament. He explains, beginning with 'Here, of genus etc...' From genus [comes] genus — the same genus is homogeneous; another is heterogeneous. Similarly, quality of quality, etc. He enumerates the varieties: 'And there...' Of genus-contradiction — contradiction based on genus. '<s>Pariccheda</s>' (delimitation) — the unlimited one is beyond the range of all words. 'Here, in this birth, thus experienced' — '<s>manas</s>' (mind) — not in terms of the prior limit — meaning 'not as before.' By the darkness of delusion accumulated especially from the destruction of discrimination, some indescribable modification of separation both numbs and burns from within. He constructs [the meaning]: 'Here, the numbing...' Separation is the [primary] unattainment; and this contradiction of opposed actions caused by it — this is the meaning. '<s>Ayaṃ vārām</s>' (this [ocean] of waters) — thirst (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) means both literal thirst and desire for jewels, as well as longing. Who knows this? No one can imagine this — this is the meaning. He constructs: 'Here, the ocean...' Another variety is easily understood — he says: 'Thus...' What happens when <s>śleṣa</s> (double meaning) is involved here? To this he says: 'Distinct...' Since it is seen in the previously cited examples that the domain is distinct from <s>śleṣa</s>. Therefore, when <s>śleṣa</s> is involved, <s>śleṣa</s> overrides [<s>virodha</s>] — according to those who follow <s>Udbhaṭa</s>'s view; but for others, it is a compound [figure] (<s>saṅkara</s>). An example: '<s>Sannihita</s>' (nearby) — '<s>bālāndhakāra</s>' means both the darkness of tresses and fresh darkness. '<s>Bhāsvanmūrti</s>' means both the form of the radiant one (sun) [and a radiant body]. This [is an example] where both contradictory [terms] have double meanings. '<s>Kupati</s>' — one [term only having double meaning]: 'lord of the earth' and 'having a base husband.' Here he states the specific [distinction]: 'In a single domain...'

children.translated_text: In "kajjala" etc., he connects the meaning—"here of kajjala and so forth."
Through <s>śruti</s> (verbal expression), the connection pertains to the aggregate.
"When the correlation of those previously stated with those not yet stated is threefold,"

children.text: yathāsaṃkhyaṃ tathā śābdam ārthaṃ ceti dvidhā matam" //
children.translated_text: "<s>Yathāsaṃkhya</s> (correlation) is thus considered twofold: verbal (<s>śābda</s>) and semantic (<s>ārtha</s>)."

body.translated_text: The correlation in order of those mentioned earlier with those mentioned later is the figure <s>yathāsaṃkhya</s> (correlation). He explains with "ūrdhvam" etc. The meaning of "ūrdhvam" is "before" (prāk).

body.text: paryāyārthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> for <s>paryāya</s> (alternation):

body.text: eka manekasminanekamekasmin vā krameṇa paryāyaḥ || 60 ||
body.translated_text: One in many, or many in one, in sequence, is <s>paryāya</s> (alternation). // RuAss 60 //

body.text:
ekasyānekādhāratve ekaḥ paryāyaḥ /
anekasyaikādhāratve dvitīyaḥ /
sasaṅgatikaṃ vyācaṣṭe-kramaprastāvādityādi /
kramagrahaṇasya prayojanāyāha-nanvekamityādi /
ekasyānekagocaratvalakṣaṇaviśeṣālaṅkāravyāvṛttyai amagrahaṇāmityarthaḥ /
evaṃ tarhi viśeṣālaṅkāre yaugapadyagrahaṇaṃ kiṃ na kṛtamityata āha-iha ceti /
iha amapratipādanāttatra yaugapadyaṃ lakṣaṇatvena arthāt siddhyati ityarthaḥ /
ato viviktaviṣayatayā dvitīyamāha-tathā ekasminniti /

vakṣyamāṇe samuccaye yaugapadyaṃ lakṣaṇatvena gṛhīṣyata ityāha-ata eva guṇeti /
lakṣyapadaṃ nirvakti-ata eva krameti /
paryāyasya amātmakatvāt parivṛttyalaṅkārato vaidharmyāyāha-vinimayeti /
asya cāturvidhyaṃ darśayati-tatrāneka iti /
iha yo 'yamanekārthaḥ sa pṛthavṛttiḥ saṅghatātmā ca /
dvividho 'pyādhārādheyaśceti catvāro bhedāḥ /
nanvāśrayeti /
re kālakūṭa! tavāśrayeṣuvṛttiḥ uttarottaraviśiṣṭapadanyāsā kenopadiṣṭā yataḥ prāk hṛdaye, aya tadapekṣayoparikaṇṭhe vātsīḥ /
samprati tu kaṇṭhādapyuparitanyāṃ vāci vasasi /

visṛṣṭarāgāditi /
atrādhara[kandu]kau karādhārau nivṛttikriyāṃ prati apādānatvena saṃhatau /
nivṛtteranekatvenāvivakṣaṇāt-niśāsviti /
saṃcaraḥ saṃcārādhiṣṭhānam /
atrābhisārikāśivārūpaṃ anekamādheyaṃ pṛthagvṛttiḥ /

children.translated_text: Here, qualities such as naivety and so forth, and states such as wifehood and so forth, are the many things attributed.

children.text: vargatvāvasthā iti saṅghāta vṛtticatuṣṭaye 'pi yojayati-atra kālakūṭamityādi /
children.translated_text: He applies the group-condition to the fourfold mode of collective functioning with "atra kālakūṭam" etc.
<s>Paryāya</s> (alternation) is also stated as "one in many, many in one."
These two are not <s>viśeṣa</s> (specification) or <s>samuccaya</s> (conjunction), due to the distinguishing characteristics.

body.translated_text: When one entity has many substrates, that is the first type of <s>paryāya</s>. When many entities have one substrate, that is the second type. He explains with context—"kramaprastāvāt" etc. The word "krama" (sequence)—

children.translated_text: This is not <s>parivṛtti</s> (exchange) due to the absence of interchange; the distinctions here are:
Four varieties, because the manifold entity operates both individually and collectively.
Due to operating individually and collectively, the manifold meaning is twofold; and that,
standing in the relation of <s>ādhāra</s> (substrate) and <s>ādheya</s> (superstratum), has four varieties accordingly.

body.text: parivṛttarthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> for <s>parivṛtti</s> (exchange):

body.text: samanyūnādhikānāṃ samādhikanyūnaiḥ vinimayaḥ parivṛttiḥ || 61 ||
body.translated_text: The interchange of equals, lessers, and greaters with equals, greaters, and lessers is <s>parivṛtti</s> (exchange). // RuAss 61 //

samasya samena saha vinimayaḥ ekā parivṛttiḥ /

vyācaṣṭe-vinimayo 'treti /
saṅgatimāha-kramapratibhāseti /
uro datveti-hiraṇyākṣavadhādyeṣu yuddheṣu uro datvā daityānāṃ yaśo gṛhītam /
yojayati-atra ura iti /

tasyahīti /
pravayastvāt svargamupeyuṣo na śocyaṃ kiñcit /
yojayati-atra kalevareṇeti /
dvairūpyeṇādāharati-tatveti /

children.translated_text: The equality of sight and life-breath.
The inferiority of the battle-drum compared to the mind.
He connects—"atrādya" etc.
"<s>Parivṛtti</s> (exchange) is interchange, threefold, with equals and so forth."

body.translated_text: The interchange of an equal with an equal is the first type of <s>parivṛtti</s>; of a lesser with a greater is the second; of a greater with a lesser is the third. He explains—"vinimayo" etc.

body.text: " parisaṅkhyārthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> for <s>parisaṅkhyā</s> (restriction):

body.text: ekasyānekaprātpavekatra niyamanaṃ parisaṅkhthā || 62 ||
body.translated_text: The restriction of one having applicability in many places to a single place is <s>parisaṅkhyā</s> (restriction). // RuAss 62 //

sasaṅgatikaṃ vyācaṣṭe-ekāneketyādi /
asaṃbhāvye sthūladṛśā saṃbhāvayituṃ aśakye /
nirvakti-parīti /
parītyupasargovarjanavṛttirityarthaḥ /

kimāsevyamiti /
yadāsaktyā dyusaridādisamāsaṅgena /

bhaktirbhava iti /
yuvatirūpe kāmāstre /
iyam apraśrā śābdavarjyā /
kauṭilyamiti /

alaukikasya prasiddheḥ kvacitpraśro 'nyathā ceti cāturvidhyam /
śleṣabhittikatayā, darśayati-vilaṅghayantīti /

vikrimā arālatā dauḥśīlya ca /
citrakarmastiti-varṇā valakṣāyadayo dvijātayaśca /
daṇḍoyaṣṭiḥ śāstiśca /

alaukikatāṃ darśayitumāha-atra ceti /
pākṣikatvaniyama anekatra yugapatprātpau parisaṅghyeti hi vākyavitprasiddhaṃ lakṣaṇam /

children.translated_text: For the distinction from that, the common substrate of restriction is stated, because—

children.text: itthamataḥ pākṣikaprātpirūpaṃ niyamalakṣaṇamapi svīkriyata iti yugapatsaṃbhāvanātmakaṃ parisaṅkhyālakṣaṇāmiha[prāyikam] /
children.translated_text: Thus, the definition of restriction in the form of partial applicability is also accepted; hence what is in the nature of simultaneous possibility is generally the definition of <s>parisaṅkhyā</s> here.
<s>Parisaṅkhyā</s> (restriction) is the constraining to one place of that which has applicability in many.
It is considered fourfold based on the presence and absence of question and exclusion.

body.translated_text: <s>Parisaṅkhyā</s> (restriction) is the constraining to one place of that which has applicability in many, by excluding one place and enumerating in another. He explains with context—

children.translated_text: Not only simultaneous applicability, but applicability in an alternative case is also intended.
Therefore, in <s>parisaṅkhyā</s> (restriction) and <s>niyama</s> (regulation), the situation here is extraordinary.

body.text: arthāpattyarthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> for <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption):

body.text: daṇḍapūpikayā arthāntarāpatanaṃ arthāpattiḥ || 63 ||
body.translated_text: The arriving at another meaning by the method of the staff and the cake is <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption). // RuAss 63 //

svasaṃmatimāha-aparetviti /

paśupatiriti-utkaḥ unmanāḥ /
viprakuryuḥ bādhaṃ vikuryuḥ /
amī bhāvā vanitādayaḥ /

dhṛtadhanuṣīti /
sthirā apiprahvī bhavanti, loleṣu kā kathā? atra prākaraṇikārthāpātaḥ /
vicchittyanyarāyāha-kvacittviti /
alaṅkāra iti /
śaṅkākaraṃ kimayaṃ sevya uta neti śaṅkājanakam /

children.translated_text: <s>Vidhura</s> means the moon; <s>vidhi</s> means fate (<s>diṣṭa</s>).
Through <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia), he states the contextual implication—"atra vidhau" etc.
<s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption) is considered the implication of another meaning through a fortiori reasoning.
And this is considered twofold based on whether the implication relates to what is under discussion or what is not under discussion.

body.translated_text: Just as eating a cake follows a fortiori from eating a staff, so the arriving at another meaning is <s>arthāpatti</s>. He explains—"daṇḍāpūpayoḥ" etc.

body.text: vikalpārthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> for <s>vikalpa</s> (alternative):

body.text: tulyabalaviridho vikalpaḥ || 64 ||
body.translated_text: A contradiction between things of equal force is <s>vikalpa</s> (alternative). // RuAss 64 //

body.text:
viruddhyoḥ tulya bavayoryugapatprātpau vikalpaḥ /
vyācaṣṭe-viruddhayoriti /
tulyapramāṇa viśiṣṭatvaṃ tulyabalatve hetuḥ /
vailakṣaṇyaṃ darśayati-aupamyagarbhatvāditi /
laukika vikalpasyā tathātvāt /
namantviti -sandhau śirasāṃ natiḥ vigrahe dhanuṣām /
evamājñāmaurvyoḥ karṇapūrikaraṇamapi /
vyacaṣṭe-atra pratirājeti /
namanamiha pratirājānāṃ kāryam /
tatra śirāṃsi dhanīṣi ca sandhivigrahapramāṇatayā tulyabalāni viruddhatvādyugapatprāptyayoge 'pi prāpnuvanti /
ataḥsādhanabādhanādirupagatyantarābhāvāt vikalpaḥ /
vaidharmyaṃ yojayati-namanakṛtamiti /
evaṃ karṇapūrīkaraṇe 'pi /
vaicitryāntarāyāha-aupamyeti /
bhaktiprahveti-praṇāyinīspardhinītyādau prathamādvivacanaikavacanayoḥ napuṃsakastrīliṅgayośca śleṣaḥ /
nītehiteti nītār ihiteti ca padabhaṅgaḥ /
nidhī iti nidhiriti ca /
yojayati-atra netre tanuriti /
samuccayabhramo mā bhūdityāha-na ceti /
anuśāsanāt gatisaṃbhave 'pi kaviprayogābhāvānna samuccayaḥ /
aprayuktadoṣāpatterlakṣaṇe nyūnatāmāśaṅkatenanviti /
pariharati-naitaditi /
netre athaveti /
vikalpasvarūponmīlita śleśānugamam uddhāṭayati-sa cātreti /

children.translated_text: He concludes—"tasmāt" etc.
He states this is his own original contribution—"pūrvaiḥ" etc.
<s>Vikalpa</s> (alternative) occurs when two contradictories of equal force come together.
It is described as twofold based on whether it rests on the absence or presence of <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia).

body.translated_text: When two contradictory things of equal force are simultaneously applicable, that is <s>vikalpa</s>. He explains—"viruddhayoḥ" etc. Being distinguished by equal authority is the cause of equal force.

body.text: samuccayārthaṃ sūtram
body.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> for <s>samuccaya</s> (conjunction):

body.text: guṇākriyāyaugapadyaṃ samuccayaḥ || 65 ||
body.translated_text: The simultaneity of qualities and actions is <s>samuccaya</s> (conjunction). // RuAss 65 //

body.text:
guṇānāṃ kriyāṇāṃ ca yaugapadyaṃ samuccayaḥ /
vyācaṣṭe-guṇānāmiti /
vikalpeti saṅgatikathanam /
vidaliteti /
pra(kha)lamukhāni durdāntapracurāṇ /
atra vaimalyamālinyayoḥ samuccayaḥ /
ayamiti /
ekapade yugapadbhavitavyaṃ bhūtamityarthaḥ /
atra upamatibhūtikriyayoḥ /
vaicitryāntarāyāha-etadvibhinneti /
bibhrāṇeti /
śalyabharaṇaṃ śayanādikriyāhetuḥ /
atra śayanādīnāṃ ekādhikaraṇatayā samuccayaḥ /
guṇasamuccayo 'pi sujñāna ityāha-evamiti /
guṇakriyayoḥ saṃbhṛtayorapi saṃbhavatīti darśayati-keciditi /
nyañcaditi-cakṣuriha cakṣurvikāraḥ /
ekaikaṃ cakṣuranyakriyaṃ bhinnavyāpāraṃ vartate /
ato heto rasavaśāt /
rasa iha śṛṅgāraḥṣad dagvikārāṇāmeṣāṃ tadekaniṣṭhatvāt kathaṃ bhinnakriyaṃ nyañcitamityarthaḥ /
yadapāṅge nyañcati /

children.translated_text: For I have stated in the <s>Bharatasaṃgraha</s>—"syānnayañcitannayañcadapāṅgabhāva" etc.
"The <s>apāṅga</s> (side-glance) contracted and curved would be <s>unmukha</s> (upward-looking)"—this is the definition of <s>udañcita</s> (uplifted glance).
<s>Udañcita</s> is the upward movement of the side-glance, without blinking, with smiling laughter,
suggestive, containing anticipated emotion, squinting, with pupils moving sideways.

body.translated_text: The simultaneity of qualities and of actions is <s>samuccaya</s>. He explains—"guṇānām" etc. "Vikalpa" etc. states the contextual connection. "Vidalita" etc.—

body.text:
vyāvṛttaṃ vilitam /
"tiryaṅnivṛttaṃ valitaṃ vilokya premṇā sudūraṃ parivalga[duktam]" /
prasādi prasannam /
"sabhrūvilāsaṃ smayate prasannaṃ saṃmīlyamānaṃ mukulaṃ vadanti /
" saprema premagarbham /
"syātpremagarbhaṃ asau dravāya (?)" /

children.translated_text: with trembling, having quivering eyelashes;
steady, with its object placed far away;
<s>Udbhrū</s>—with raised brow, having upward-moving eyebrows.
would be <s>bhrānta</s> (bewildered), sluggish with intoxication.

body.translated_text: <s>Vyāvṛtta</s> means <s>valita</s> (turned). "Turned sideways, seeing from afar with love, vigorously spoken." <s>Prasādi</s> means serene.

body.text:
apāṅgavṛtti vikṣepi /
vikṣepi pārśve yadapāṅgavṛtti /
[vikacaṇ] vikāsi /
vikāsi dṛśye saviśeṣalakṣam /
majjannihāñcitam /
nāsāgraniṣṭhāntunihañcitākhyam /
taraṅkottaraṃ taraṅgitam /
"taraṅgitaṃ yadyutirurmikalpā /
" sāśru utkaṇṭhitam /
"utkaṇṭhitaṃ rāganibaddhabāṣpam /
" yojayati-atrākekaretyādi /
nanvākūtaprasādapremṇāṃ guṇavacanatve 'pi samāsataddhitādyarthaistirodhānamityata āha-prasādisapremetyādi /
samāsādayo hi sambandhābhidhāyinaḥ /
sambandhaśca siddharūpo guṇātmā /
na guṇāvacanānāṃ svabhāvaṃ bhinatti /
sākūtaṃ satprema iti samāsaḥ /
prasādītitaddhitaḥ /
nigamayati-evamayamiti /
vyastatvena ubhau samastatvena eketi tridhā /
"guṇakriyāyaugapadye trividhaḥsyātsamuccayaḥ "/
samuccayāntarāyāha-ekamiti /
sūtram -
body.translated_text:
<s>Apāṅgavṛtti</s> is <s>vikṣepi</s> (glancing aside).
<s>Vikṣepi</s> is when the sidelong glance moves to the side.
<s>Vikacaṇ</s> is <s>vikāsi</s> (blooming).
<s>Vikāsi</s> is a glance with a distinctive mark.
<s>Majjan nihāñcita</s> (sinking-bent) —
is called that which sinks toward and is bent at the tip of the nose.
<s>Taraṅkottara</s> is <s>taraṅgita</s> (undulating).
'<s>Taraṅgita</s> is that whose luster is wave-like.'
With tears, it is <s>utkaṇṭhita</s> (yearning).
'<s>Utkaṇṭhita</s> is that with tears bound by passion.'
He construes: 'here, <s>ākekara</s>...' etc.
Now, even though <s>ākūta</s> (intention), <s>prasāda</s> (grace), and <s>prema</s> (love) are quality-denoting words, their concealment by compound-formation, secondary suffixes, etc. — to address this he says: '<s>prasādi</s>, <s>saprema</s>...' etc.
For compounds and the like denote relations.
And a relation, being an established form, is of the nature of a quality.
It does not alter the essential nature of quality-denoting words.
<s>Sākūta</s> and <s>satprema</s> are compounds.
<s>Prasādin</s> takes a secondary suffix.
He concludes: 'thus this...' etc.
Separately the two, combined as one — thus threefold.
'When quality and action are simultaneous, <s>samuccaya</s> (accumulation) is threefold.'
For yet another type of <s>samuccaya</s>, he says: 'of one...' etc.
The <s>sūtra</s> —

body.text: ekasya siddhihetau anyasya tatkaratvaṃ ca || 66 ||
body.translated_text: When one thing serves as the cause of accomplishment, and another also does the same — that too is [<s>samuccaya</s>]. || <s>RuAss</s> 66 ||

body.text:
ekasmin kasyacit siddhihetau spardhayā anyasyāpi tatkaratvaṃ samuccayaḥ /
vyācaṣṭe-samuccaya ityādi /
ityevetyanuṣaṅgakathanam /
samādhivaidharmyāyāha-na cāyamiti /
ekaḥ paryātpaḥ sādhakaḥ /
anyaḥ kākatālīyavṛttyā cetsamādhiḥ /
yathā khale kapottāḥ spardhayā pratisvaṃ ahamahamikayāvataranti /
tathā bhāve samuccayaḥ iti mahān bhedaḥ /
khale kapotā asyāṃ santi nītāviti khalekapotikā /
matvarthīyaḥ ṣṭhan /
nanu kākatālīyaṃ iti kathamucyate /
kākasyāgamanaṃ yādṛcchikaṃ tālasya ca pātaḥ /
tena patatā kākasya vadhaḥ /
evaṃ devadattasya āgamanaṃ dasyīnāñcacopanipātastaiśca tasya vadhaḥ /
tatra devadattatasyusamāgamaḥ kākatālasamāgama iveti eka upamārthaḥ /
tadvadhaḥ kākavadha iveti dvitīyaḥ /
ādyaḥ samāsārthaḥ kākatālamiti /
dvitīyastadvitārthaḥ kākatālīyamiti /
samāsaścāyam /
asmādeva jñāpakāt "samāsācca tadviṣayā"dākasmika ivārthecchro bhavatīti /
tadviṣayādivārthaviṣayādityarthaḥ /
evamardhajaratīyaṃ ajākṛpāṇīyaṃ ghuṇākṣarīyamityādausamāsataddhitau jñeyau /
bhedānāha-eṣa iti /
kulamiti /
yairjano darpaṃ vrajati, ta eva tavāṅkuśāḥ unmārganivārakāḥ /
yojayati-atrāmālinyeti /
amālinyaṃ śobhanatvahetuḥ /
ekaikaṃ caitanyasya tatkaratvaṃ darśayati-durvārā iti /
manmathasuhṛdvasantādiḥ śaṭho vañcakaḥ /
yojayati-atra smareti /
navavayaḥ prabhṛteḥ kathamaśobhanatvam ityata āha-navavaya ityādi /
śaśīti-śaśyādi viśeṣyaṃ śobhanaṃ dhūsaratvādi viśeṣaṇavaśādaśobhanamiti viśiṣṭasya dvairūpyam /
tatra tathāvidhaiḥ kāminyādibhiḥsamuñcīyate /
yojayati-atra śaśina ityādi /
anyathā tu na yojanīyamityata āha-na tvatreti /
na vyakhyeyastathā /
sadasadyogavivakṣaṇāditi śeṣaḥ /
atrākṣipati-nanu nṛpeti /
nṛpāṅgaṇa khalayordvayorapyaśobhanatvādanye śobhanā iti katham /
na tathā samuccayaḥ /
pariharati-naitaditi /
viśiṣṭasya dvairūpyaprakrame dvayoraśobhanatvam /
prakramabhedo vākyadoṣaḥ /
prakramabhedā valambena cānyairdeṣāntaraṃ udbhāvitamityāha-ata eveti /
viśeṣyāntaraṃ śobhanaṃ khalatvarūpaṃ tvaśobhanamiti sahacarabhinnor'thaḥ /
ata itthaṃ vivakṣiṇīyamityāha-prakṛte tviti /
tathāpi na doṣanivṛttirityāha-evamapīti /
pūrvodāharaṇe sadasadyogamāśaṅkate-nanu durvārā iti /
smaramārgaṇādīnāṃ śobhanatvaṃ durvāratvādīnāmaśobhanatvamiti pratīteḥ /
pariharati-naitaditi /
vivakṣābhede gamakamāha-ata eveti /
sundaratvenāntaḥ praviṣṭānāmapi śaśyādīnāṃ dhūsaratvādinā vaiyarthyahetutvamupasaṃhṛtam /

children.text: durvāretyatratvitthaṃ "śaṭhaḥ kathaṃ soḍhavya" iti sarvathā kaṣṭatvamevopasaṃhṛtam /
children.translated_text: In '<s>durvāra</s>' (irresistible), thus — 'how is the deceitful one to be endured?' — utter wretchedness alone has been concluded.
He concludes: 'therefore...' etc.
When one action is being performed and another also performs an action — that is another type of <s>samuccaya</s> (accumulation).
With the combination of good-and-bad duality, together with the previous, it is threefold.

body.translated_text:
When one thing serves as the cause of accomplishment for someone, and another also does the same through rivalry — that is <s>samuccaya</s> (accumulation).
He explains: '<s>samuccaya</s>...' etc.
'Indeed' — this is a statement of continuation.
To show the distinction from <s>samādhi</s>, he says: 'and not this...' etc.
One is sufficient as an accomplisher.
The other, if by mere coincidence — that would be <s>samādhi</s>.
Just as pigeons in a threshing floor descend in rivalry, each competing 'I first, I first' —
so in this case it is <s>samuccaya</s> — this is the great distinction.
<s>Khalekapotikā</s> ('threshing-floor-pigeon-like') — they are in this threshing floor, in this policy — thus <s>khalekapotikā</s>.
The possessive suffix <s>ṣṭhan</s> is applied.
Now, how can <s>kākatālīya</s> (coincidental, lit. 'crow-and-palm') be said?
The crow's arrival is accidental, and the palm-fruit's falling too.
By that falling, the crow is killed.
Likewise, <s>Devadatta</s>'s arrival and the robbers' attack — by them his killing.
There, the meeting of <s>Devadatta</s> and the robbers is like the meeting of crow and palm — that is the first simile-meaning.
His killing is like the crow's killing — that is the second.
The first is the compound-meaning: <s>kākatāla</s>.
The second is the secondary-derivative meaning: <s>kākatālīya</s>.
And this is a compound.
From this very indicatory sign, 'from compounds and in that domain' — it becomes like <s>ākasmika</s> (accidental) in meaning — the sense of 'accidental' is intended.
'In that domain' means 'in the domain of such meaning.'
Likewise in <s>ardhajaratīya</s> (half-old-woman-like), <s>ajākṛpāṇīya</s> (goat-and-knife-like), <s>ghuṇākṣarīya</s> (worm-letter-like), etc. — both compound and secondary derivative should be understood.
He states the varieties: 'this...' etc.
'Of the family' — those very things through which people become proud are your goads, preventers of wrong paths.
He construes: 'here, <s>amālinya</s>...' etc.
<s>Amālinya</s> (purity/nobility) is the cause of excellence.
He shows the doing-the-same by each individually: '<s>durvāra</s>...' etc.
The friend of <s>Manmatha</s> (Love), <s>Vasanta</s> (Spring), etc. — <s>śaṭha</s> means 'deceitful.'
He construes: 'here, <s>Smara</s> (Love)...' etc.
Since youth is of a new age, how can it be unbecoming? — To address this he says: '<s>navavayaḥ</s>...' etc.
'The moon' — the qualified object like the moon etc. is beautiful, but through the qualifier of duskiness etc. it is unbecoming — thus the dual nature of the qualified entity.
There, by such things as the beloved woman etc., it is accumulated.
He construes: 'here, of the moon...' etc.
Otherwise it should not be construed — to address this he says: 'but not here...' etc.
It should not be explained that way.
'Because the intention is to express the combination of good and bad' — this is to be supplied.
Here he raises an objection: 'now, the king...' etc.
Since both the royal courtyard and the rogue are unbecoming, how can the others be called beautiful?
Not so — that is not <s>samuccaya</s>.
He resolves: 'not this...' etc.
In the procedure of the dual nature of the qualified entity, the unbecomingness of both is established.
The change of procedure would be a fault of the sentence.
From the change of procedure and delay, another defect has been pointed out by others — he says: 'therefore...' etc.
The other qualified entity is beautiful; the roguishness is unbecoming — thus the meaning differs with the associate.
Therefore it should be intended thus — he says: 'in the present case, however...' etc.
Even so, the fault is not removed — he says: 'even so...' etc.
In the previous example, he suspects the combination of good and bad: 'now, <s>durvāra</s>...' etc.
Because there is the perception that <s>Smara</s>'s arrows etc. are beautiful, while irresistibility etc. is unbecoming.
He resolves: 'not this...' etc.
He states the indicator of the difference in intention: 'therefore...' etc.
Even of the moon etc., which have entered as beautiful, the causing of futility through duskiness etc. has been concluded.

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: samādhyarthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> for the purpose of <s>samādhi</s> (adjustment) —

body.text: kāraṇāntarayogāt kāryasukaratvaṃ samādhiḥ || 67 ||
body.translated_text: The facilitation of an effect through the conjunction of an additional cause is <s>Samādhi</s> (adjustment). || <s>RuAss</s> 67 ||

body.text:
ārabdhasya kāryasya kāraṇāntarayogāt samyagādhānaṃ samādhiḥ /
vyācaṣṭe-kenaciditi /
samuccayeti saṅgatyuktiḥ /
samuccayavaidharmyaṃ smārayati-tadvailakṣaṇyamiti /
mānamiti /
pādapatane kāraṇe garjitaṃ kāraṇāntaram /
yojayati-mānanirākaraṇa iti /
upakāpareti saukaryaprakāśanam /
samādhiḥsamyagādhānaṃ kāraṇāntarayogataḥ /
saṅgatyarāyāha-evaṃ vākyeti /
pratyanīkārthaṃ sūtram /
body.translated_text:
The proper settling (<s>samyag ādhāna</s>) of an effect already begun, through the conjunction of an additional cause, is <s>samādhi</s> (adjustment).
He explains: 'by some...' etc.
'<s>Samuccaya</s>' — this is a statement of connection.
He reminds of the distinction from <s>samuccaya</s>: 'its distinctiveness...' etc.
'Pride' — when falling at the feet is one cause, thunder is an additional cause.
He construes: 'in the removal of pride...' etc.
'Assistance' — this is a manifestation of facilitation.
<s>Samādhi</s> is proper settling, arising from the conjunction of an additional cause.
For the connection, he says: 'thus, of the sentence...' etc.
The <s>sūtra</s> for the purpose of <s>pratyanīka</s> (confrontation) —

body.text: pratipakṣatiraḥsākāśaktau tadīyatiraskāraḥ pratyanīkam || 68 ||
body.translated_text: When one is unable to directly oppose the adversary, the opposing of what belongs to that adversary is <s>Pratyanīka</s> (confrontation). || <s>RuAss</s> 68 ||

body.text:
balavataḥ tiraskārāśaktau tadīyatiraskāraḥ pratyanīkam /
vyācaṣṭe-yatra balavadityādi /
tatsambandhinaḥ balavatsambandhinaḥ /
taṃ bādhituṃ balavantaṃ bādhitum /
atra dṛṣṭāntamāha-yathā anīka ityādi /
prayojanamāha-pratipakṣeti /
yasya kiñciditi /
yasya kṛṣṇasya /
vigrahaḥ kalahaḥ /
kāntena bakreṇa sadṛśākṛtiḥ /
yojayati-atra rāhoriti /
tattiraskārāditi prayojanoktiḥ /
tadīyasya tiraskāraḥ pratyanīkamaśaktitaḥ /
pratīpārthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text:
When one is unable to oppose the powerful one directly, the opposing of what belongs to that powerful one is <s>pratyanīka</s> (confrontation).
He explains: 'where the powerful one...' etc.
'Of that one's associate' means of the powerful one's associate.
'To defeat that one' means to defeat the powerful one.
Here he states an illustration: 'just as, the army...' etc.
He states the purpose: 'of the adversary...' etc.
'Of a certain one' — of <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>.
<s>Vigraha</s> means 'quarrel.'
'<s>Kānta</s>' means having an appearance similar to <s>Vakra</s> (the crooked one, i.e., <s>Rāhu</s>).
He construes: 'here, of <s>Rāhu</s>...' etc.
'By opposing what belongs to that one' — this is a statement of the purpose.
The opposing of what belongs to that one, from inability — that is <s>pratyanīka</s>.
The <s>sūtra</s> for the purpose of <s>pratīpa</s> (reversed simile) —

body.text: upamānasyākṣepa upameyatākalpanaṃ vā pratīpam || 69 ||
body.translated_text: The rejection of the standard of comparison, or the imagining of the object of comparison as the standard — that is <s>Pratīpa</s> (reversed simile). || <s>RuAss</s> 69 ||

body.text:
upameyasyaiva puṣkalaguṇatvavivakṣaṇenopamānasya kaimarthakyaṃ prātikūlyādekaṃ pratīpam /
yañcopamānāntarārthaṃ prasiddhopamānasyopameyatvakḷtpiranādarāt dadvadvitīyam /
vyācaṣṭe-upameyasyaivetyādi /
yatra ceti /
cakṣuṣa eva muṇḍamālātvamiti kuvalayadāmno nairarthakyam /
alaṅkārāntarasaṃbhedenāparamudāharati-lāvaṇyeti /
lāvaṇyaukastvādiguṇānāmupameya eva pauṣkalyādindvādyupamānānāṃ kaimarthakyam /
saṃbhedamanusmārayati-atra yathāsaṅkhyamapīti /

children.translated_text: '<s>E</s>, come!' —
'<s>E</s>' is a form of address.

children.text: ayi ehi tāvatsundari karṇāṃ dattvā śṛṇu vacanīyam /
children.translated_text: O beautiful one, come here, lend your ear and hear what is to be said.

children.text: tatava mukhena kṛśodari candra upamīyate janena //
children.translated_text: For by your face, O slender-waisted one, the moon is measured by people.

body.translated_text:
When one intends to express the abundance of qualities in the object of comparison itself, the purposelessness of the standard of comparison through contrariness — that is the first type of <s>pratīpa</s> (reversed simile).
And when the well-known standard of comparison is imagined as an object of comparison, for the purpose of another standard — that is the second type, arising from disregard.
He explains: 'of the object of comparison itself...' etc.
'And where...' etc.
The eyes themselves being a garland of skulls — thus the purposelessness of the garland of blue lotuses.
To illustrate with a combination of another figure, he gives: '<s>lāvaṇya</s> (charm)...' etc.
Because of the abundance of qualities like charm etc. in the object of comparison itself, the purposelessness of standards of comparison like the moon etc.
He reminds of the combination: 'here, <s>yathāsaṅkhya</s> (sequential correlation) also...' etc.

body.text:
candrasyopamānatvaṃ vacanīyamiti kathanāt candrasya nikṛṣṭatvenopameyatvena kalpanam /
prayojanaṃ tu mukhasyopamānatā /
yojayati-atropamānatveneti /
kvacit upamānasya sataḥ upamānatvameva nyakkaraṇādalaṅkāraṃ samutthāpayatītyāha-kvacitpunariti /
garvamitir /
idṛśāni nīla nalināni santīti upamānāvirbhāvaḥ /
evaṃ niḥsāmānyasya locanayugalasya nyakkāraḥ /
yojayati-atrotkarṣeti /
yathātropameyasya upamānāsahatvaṃ, tathaiva atiprakarṣādupamāna bhūmimapyatipatate /
upamānatvakḷtpirapi pratīpamityāha-aneneti /
ahameveti /

children.translated_text: Of <s>hālāhala</s> (deadly poison) — harsh, wooden-barked — the imagining as a standard of comparison for the speech of wicked people, for the purpose of belittlement.
He construes this: 'here, the <s>hālāhala</s>-nature...' etc.
From the purposelessness of the standard of comparison, and from imagining it as the object of comparison,
<s>pratīpa</s> (reversed simile) is thus twofold — from the former and also from the standard-of-comparison status.

body.translated_text:
Because the statement 'what is to be said' declares the moon's status as a standard of comparison, the moon is imagined as inferior, i.e., as an object of comparison.
But the purpose is the standard-of-comparison status of the face.
He construes: 'here, as a standard of comparison...' etc.
In some cases, the very standard-of-comparison status of an existing standard produces a figure through belittlement — he says: 'but in some cases...' etc.
'Pride' —
That such blue lotuses exist — this is the appearance of a standard of comparison.
Thus, the belittlement of the incomparable pair of eyes.
He construes: 'here, the excellence...' etc.
Just as here the object of comparison cannot tolerate the standard of comparison, similarly, due to extreme superiority, it surpasses even the status of standard of comparison.
The imagining of standard-of-comparison status is also <s>pratīpa</s> — he says: 'by this...' etc.
'I myself' —

body.text: nimīlitārthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> for the purpose of <s>nimīlita</s> (concealment) —

body.text: vastunā vastvantaranigūhanaṃ nimīlitam || 70 ||
body.translated_text: The concealment of one thing by another thing is <s>Nimīlita</s> (concealment). || <s>RuAss</s> 70 ||

body.text:
vastu vastvantaraṃ sahajena lakṣmaṇā yannigūhayati āgantukena vā tannigūhitatvānnimīlitam /
vyācaṣṭe-sahajenetyādi /
sāmānyato bhedamāha-na cāyamiti /
tasya hi guṇasādhāraṇyādbhedānupalakṣaṇam /
asya punarutkṛṣṭena guṇena nikṛṣṭasya sthaganam /
apāṅgeti /
aṅgelīlayā iti sphuritam itthaṃ līlayā prasasāretyarthaḥ /
dṛktāralyā dinā sahajena lakṣaṇena līlā madodayahetukaṃ dṛktāralyādi tirodadhāti /
yojayati-atra dṛktāralyeti /
ye kandarāsviti /
tvatpādaśaṅkitadhiyaḥ tvadā pātaśaṅkācakitāḥ /

children.text: atra himamā gantikalakṣaṇābhyāṃ kamparomāñcābhyāṃ bhayakṛtau kamparomāñcau sthagayati /
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>Himālaya</s>, by its characteristics of cold and movement, conceals the trembling and horripilation caused by fear.
He construes: 'here, of the <s>Himālaya</s>...' etc.
The concealment of another thing by either an innate or an adventitious characteristic —
the figure called <s>nimīlita</s> (concealment) has been shown to be of two kinds.

body.translated_text:
When a thing conceals another thing by an innate characteristic or an adventitious one — that, being concealed, is <s>nimīlita</s> (concealment).
He explains: 'by an innate one...' etc.
He states the general distinction: 'and this is not...' etc.
For in that [other figure], because of the commonality of qualities, the distinction is not perceived.
But in this one, the concealment of the inferior by a superior quality.
'<s>Apāṅga</s>' — '<s>aṅgelīlayā</s>' means '<s>sphurita</s>' (flashing); thus, 'spread playfully' is the meaning.
The coquettish movement of the sidelong glance — by that innate characteristic — playfulness caused by the onset of intoxication, the coquettish movement of the sidelong glance etc., is concealed.
He construes: 'here, the coquettish movement of the sidelong glance...' etc.
'Those who are in caves' — 'frightened by the thought of your feet' means 'startled by the apprehension of your attack.'

body.text: sāmānyārthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> for the purpose of <s>sāmānya</s> (generality) —

body.text: prastutasyānyena guṇāsāmyādaikātmyaṃ sāmānyam || 71 ||
body.translated_text: The identity of the contextual subject with another, due to similarity of qualities, is <s>Sāmānya</s> (generality). || <s>RuAss</s> 71 ||

body.text:
prastutasya aprastutena guṇasāmyādekarūpatvaṃ sāmānyayogātsāmānyālaṅkāraḥ /
vyācaṣṭe-yatra prastutasyetyādi /
apahnuterbhedāyāha-na ceyamiti /
apahnutau hi prakṛtaniṣedhenāprakṛtapratiṣṭhāpanam ihatu na tathā /
kiṃ tarhi? aikātmyam /
malayajaraseti /
dantapatraṃ karidaśanatāṭaṅkam /
avibhāvyatā gatiraikātmyaliṅgam /
yojayati-atra malayajeti /
prastutasyānyatādātmyaṃ sāmānyaṃ guṇasāmyataḥ /
taduṇārthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text:
The oneness of form of the contextual subject with the non-contextual, due to similarity of qualities — by the connection of generality — is the figure of <s>sāmānya</s> (generality).
He explains: 'where, of the contextual subject...' etc.
To show the distinction from <s>apahnuti</s> (denial), he says: 'and this is not...' etc.
For in <s>apahnuti</s>, the contextual is denied and the non-contextual is established; but here it is not so.
Rather, what? — Identity.
'<s>Malayaja</s> (sandalwood) paste...' etc.
<s>Dantapatra</s> means an ornament made from elephant tusk.
The imperceptibility of distinction is the mark of identity.
He construes: 'here, the sandalwood...' etc.
The identity of the contextual with another is <s>sāmānya</s>, arising from similarity of qualities.
The <s>sūtra</s> for the purpose of <s>tadguṇa</s> (acquiring another's quality) —

body.text: svaguṇātyāgādatyutkṛṣṭaguṇāsvīkārastadguṇaḥ || 72 ||
body.translated_text: Without abandoning one's own qualities, the acquisition of exceedingly superior qualities — that is <s>Tadguṇa</s> (acquiring another's quality). || <s>RuAss</s> 72 ||

body.text:
parimitaguṇasya vastuno 'tyutkṛṣṭaguṇasvīkārastadguṇaḥ /
vyācaṣṭe-yatreti /
nirvakti-tasyeti /
nimīlitādbhādamāha-na ceti tatra hi vastvantaranigūhanam /
iha tvanigūhitasya tadguṇenoparāgaḥ /
vibhinneti /
aruṇena varṇābhedaṃ nītā rathavāhā yatra vaṃśāṅkuranīlairmarakataratnaiḥ prabhayā punaḥ svāṃ prabhāṃ āninyire /
atrāśvānāmāruṇye tadguṇatā /
āruṇyasya ca hārityena /
yojayati-atra ravīti /
tadguṇāḥsvaguṇatyāgādutkṛṣṭasya guṇagrahaḥ /
body.translated_text:
The acquisition of exceedingly superior qualities by a thing of limited qualities is <s>tadguṇa</s> (acquiring another's quality).
He explains: 'where...' etc.
He etymologizes: 'of that...' etc.
To show the distinction from <s>nimīlita</s> (concealment), he says: 'not so...' etc. — for there, another thing is concealed.
But here, the coloring of the unconcealed by that quality.
'<s>Vibhinna</s>' (variegated) — the chariot-horses, brought to a state of redness by the dawn (<s>Aruṇa</s>), then by the green bamboo-shoot-colored emerald gems, brought back their own radiance.
Here, the redness of the horses is <s>tadguṇa</s> (acquiring that quality).
And the redness in turn by the greenness.
He construes: 'here, of the sun...' etc.
<s>Tadguṇa</s> is the acquisition of a superior quality without abandoning one's own quality.

body.text: sati hetau tadrūpānanuhāro 'tadguṇāḥ || 73 ||
body.translated_text: When a cause exists but the form of that [superior quality] is not imitated — that is <s>Atadguṇa</s> (not acquiring another's quality). || <s>RuAss</s> 73 ||

body.text:
tadruṇaviparīto 'tadguṇaḥ /
saṅgatiṃ vyācaṣṭe-tadguṇeti /
utkṛṣṭaguṇavastupratyāsaktau hi nyānaguṇasya tadguṇasvīkāro nyāyopapannaḥ /
prasyāsattā vapyananuharaṇamatadguṇālaṅkāraḥ /
nirvakti-tasyotkṛṣṭasyeti /
yadi veti /
niruktyantaramanuharaṇāhetau satyapi ananuharaṇāt atadguṇaḥ /

children.translated_text: Here he analyzes: 'of that one' means 'of the contextual subject.'
Thus this is twofold.

children.text: dhavalo 'sīti- dhavalo 'si yadyapi sundara! tathāpi tvayā mama rañjitaṃ hṛdayam /
children.translated_text: 'You are white' — O beautiful one, though you are white, yet by you my heart has been colored.

children.text: rāgabharite 'pi hṛdaye subhaga! nihito na rakto 'si //
children.translated_text: O fortunate one, though placed in a heart filled with passion, you are not colored.

body.translated_text:
The opposite of <s>tadguṇa</s> is <s>atadguṇa</s> (not acquiring another's quality).
He explains the connection: '<s>tadguṇa</s>...' etc.
For when there is proximity to a thing of superior qualities, the acquisition of that quality by one of lesser qualities is logically warranted.
But non-imitation despite proximity is the figure of <s>atadguṇa</s>.
He etymologizes: 'of that superior one...' etc.
'Or alternatively' — another etymology: even when the cause of imitation exists, because of non-imitation — it is <s>atadguṇa</s>.

body.text:
dhavalo yuvā valakṣaśca /
rāgabharitahṛdayanidhāne 'pyaraktatvamatadruṇāḥ /
gāṅgamiti /
aṅgeti sambodhanam /
cīyate upacīyate /
atra aprakṛtarūpānanuhāraḥ /
ubhayatra yojayati-pūrvatretyādi /
prathamārdhe ko 'laṅkāra ityata āha-dhavalo 'sīti /
dhavalasyāpi rañjane atadruṇatvaṃ sphuṭameva /
yataḥ kāryakāraṇeti /
viṣamavaidharmyaṃ vyaktam /
na tadruṇe 'nuhārastu guṇatādrūpyayordvidhā /
uttarārthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text:
<s>Dhavala</s> means 'young man' and also 'fair-complexioned.'
Being uncolored despite being placed in a passion-filled heart — that is <s>atadguṇa</s>.
'<s>Gāṅga</s>' — '<s>aṅga</s>' is a form of address.
<s>Cīyate</s> means 'is heaped up, is augmented.'
Here there is non-imitation of the non-contextual form.
He construes both: 'in the first...' etc.
What figure is in the first half? — To address this he says: 'you are white...' etc.
Even in the coloring of the white one, the <s>atadguṇa</s> nature is quite evident.
Because cause and effect — the incompatible distinction is manifest.
Non-imitation of the quality — <s>atadguṇa</s> is twofold, in quality-nature and form-nature.
The <s>sūtra</s> for the purpose of <s>uttara</s> (rejoinder) —

body.text: uttarātprakṣonnayanamasakṛdasambhāvyamuttaraṃ cottaram || 74 ||
body.translated_text: A reply that repeatedly surpasses the previous statement, each time with something deemed impossible — that is <s>Uttara</s> (rejoinder). || <s>RuAss</s> 74 ||

body.text:
praśrānupādāne 'pyuttarā dunnayanamekamuttaram upāttasya ca praśrasya yadasambhāvyamasakṛduttaraṃ taddvitīyam /
vyācaṣṭe-yatrānupanibadhyamāna ityādi /
ativyātpiṃ pariharati-na cedamiti /
trairūpyanirdeśo hyanumānalakṣaṇam /
dvitīyasya svarūpamāha-yatra ceti /
tatra niyamamāha-tacceti /
atra ativyātpiṃ pariharati-na ceyamiti /
parisaṃkhyāyāṃ vyavacchredyavyavacchedakabhāvaḥ vivakṣyaḥ /
atra svavivakṣā /
ekākinīti-kiṃ yācase vāsayācanena kimityarthaḥ /
kā visameti /
kā viṣamā daivagatiḥ kiṃ (labdhaṃ)yajjano guṇagrāhī /
kiṃ saukhyaṃ sukalatraṃ kiṃ duḥkhaṃ yat khalo lokaḥ /
yatra daivagatyādi gūḍhatvādapratisambhāvyam /
uttaraṃ yojayati-pūrvatretyādi /
asakṛditi /
nānātvaniyamoddhāṭanam /
"uttaraṃ praśrapiśunaṃ asambhāvyottaraṃ dvidhā /
" saṅgatyantarāyāha-itaḥ prabhṛtīti /
sūkṣmārthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: Even when the question is not included, the bringing out of a single answer is the first [type]; and when the answer to an included question is inconceivable and given repeatedly, that is the second [type]. He explains: 'Where, without being connected [to an explicit question],' and so on. He removes the objection of over-extension: 'This is not,' and so on. For the statement of the triple characteristic is the definition of inference [not of this figure]. He states the nature of the second [type]: 'And where.' He states the restriction for that: 'And that.' He removes the over-extension here: 'And this is not.' In a restrictive enumeration (<s>Parisaṃkhyā</s>), the relation of the excluded and the excluder is intended. Here, one's own intention [determines the figure]. '<s>Ekākinī</s>' (alone): 'Why do you beg? What is the use of begging?' — this is the meaning. '<s>Kā visamā</s>': 'What is adverse fate? — The fact that people appreciate good qualities. What is happiness? — A good wife. What is sorrow? — That the world is wicked.' Where the [answers to] fate and such are inconceivable due to being hidden. He connects the answer: 'In the former,' and so on. '<s>Asakṛt</s>' (repeatedly): this reveals the restriction of multiplicity. '[The figure of] unexpected answer is twofold: one revealing the question and one with an inconceivable answer.' He states the connection for the next [figure]: 'From this point on.' The definition for <s>Sūkṣma</s> (the Subtle):

body.text: saṃlakṣitasūkṣmārthaṃprakāśanaṃ sūkṣmam || 75 ||
body.translated_text: <s>Sūkṣma</s> (the Subtle) is the revealing of a subtle meaning that has been observed [through gestures and signs]. // <s>RuAss</s>_75 //

body.text:
iṅgitādibhiḥsaṃlakṣitasya sūkṣmārthasya vidagdhāya prakāśanaṃ sūkṣmam /
vyācaṣṭe-iha sūkṣma ityādi /

children.translated_text: '<s>Kuśāgravat</s>' (like the tip of a blade of <s>Kuśa</s> grass) means sharp — that is, <s>Kuśāgrīya</s> (extremely acute).
Hence this [figure] is twofold, through <s>Iṅgita</s> (gesture) and <s>Ākāra</s> (expression).
Bodily movements that manifest inner intention are called <s>Iṅgita</s> (gesture) — they are produced by the intellect.
<s>Ākāras</s> (expressions), on the other hand, are traditionally defined as those very same [movements] that are not produced by the intellect [but are involuntary].

body.translated_text: The revealing to a discerning person of a subtle meaning observed through gestures (<s>Iṅgita</s>) and such is <s>Sūkṣma</s>. He explains: 'Here, subtle,' and so on.

children.translated_text: For example: 'The changes in the widened pupils of the eyes, the bitten brow, and such are known as <s>Iṅgita</s> (gesture).'
'<s>Ākāras</s> are involuntary emotional states (<s>Sattvaja Bhāvas</s>) — the former are produced by intellect, the latter arise otherwise.'

body.text:
saṅketeti-kālamanasaṃ kālaṃ jñātumanasamityarthaḥ /
netrārpitākūtaṃ netrābhivyañjitabhāvamityarthaḥ /
saṅketakālamanaso jñānaṃ bhrūkaṭākṣādi /
tadīyeṅgitena jñātveti sūkṣmārthaṃ salakṣaṇam /
padmanimīlanaṃ tu prakāśanam /
yojayati /
atra saṅketeti /

children.text: vaktrasyantīti-svedena ākārastena kuṅkumabhedāt puruṣāyitajñānaṃ sūkṣmārthaṃsaṃlakṣaṇam khaṅgalekhastu tatprakāśanam /
children.translated_text: '<s>Vaktrasya</s>' (of the face): through perspiration — the expression — through the breaking of the saffron [cosmetic], the knowledge of the <s>Puruṣāyita</s> (woman-on-top position) is the observation of the subtle meaning. The scratch-mark, however, is its revealing.
He connects: 'Here, perspiration,' and so on.

children.text: sūkṣmaṃ tu sūkṣmaṃ saṃlakṣya vidagdheṣu prakāśanam /
children.translated_text: [Definition verse:] <s>Sūkṣma</s> (the Subtle) is the revealing to discerning persons of what has been subtly observed.
It is twofold, through the subtle observation by <s>Iṅgita</s> (gesture) or <s>Ākāra</s> (expression).

body.translated_text: '<s>Saṅketa</s>' (assignation): '<s>Kālamanasam</s>' means 'wishing to know the time' — this is the meaning. '<s>Netrārpitākūtam</s>' means 'intention expressed through the eyes.' The knowledge of the time of the assignation [comes through] the brow-glance and such. Having known [the time] through her gestures — this is the observation of the subtle meaning. The closing of the lotus, however, is the revealing [of that subtle meaning]. He connects: 'Here, the assignation,' and so on.

body.text: vyājoktyai sūtram-
body.translated_text: The definition for <s>Vyājokti</s> (Pretextual Speech):

body.text: udbhinnavastunigūhanaṃ vyājoktiḥ || 76 ||
body.translated_text: <s>Vyājokti</s> (Pretextual Speech) is the concealment of a matter that has become manifest. // <s>RuAss</s>_76 //

body.text:
kutaścinnimittāt prakāśyāsyagūḍhavastuno vyājavacasā nigūhanaṃ vyājoktiḥ /
vyācaṣṭe-yatra nigūḍhamityādi /
vaḥsvantaraprakṣepeti niruktiḥ /
śailendreti /
pratipādyamānā dīyamānā /
ādiśabdāt stambhavepathū /
vidhivyasaṅgaḥ kriyāśaktiḥ /
śailāntaḥpureṇa mātṛmaṇḍalena gāṇaiśca dṛṣṭaḥ /
yojayati-atra romāñceti /
asāmañjasyaṃ śamayitumāha-yadyapītyādi /
apalāpamātraṃ cintayeti sasmitasvakathanāt punaḥ prakāśanaṃ lakṣaṇatayāna cintanīyamiti bhāvaḥ /
ullekha uṭṭaṅkanam /
avyāsimāśaṅkate-nanvapahnutīti /
uttaraḥ prakāraḥ apahvavāya sādṛśyaṃ ityevamātmakaḥ /
pariharati-satyamiti /
tatra tathoktiḥ udbhaṭasiddhāntāśrayeṇa /
tanmate vyajostyanupavarṇānāt tathāpahnutisambhavaḥ /

children.text: iha tu vyājoktyupavarṇanāt so 'pahnuti prakāra eva nāstītyekaivāpahnutaḥ /
children.translated_text: But here, since the description follows <s>Vyājokti</s> (pretextual speech), that type of <s>Apahnuti</s> simply does not exist — hence <s>Apahnuti</s> is only one [type, not two].
Therefore this is precisely <s>Vyājokti</s>.
<s>Vyājokti</s> (Pretextual Speech) is the concealment of what has become manifest through a pretextual utterance.
Since the similarity for the purpose of denial is accepted [only in another system], <s>Apahnuti</s> does not [apply here].

body.translated_text: The concealment through a pretextual utterance of a matter that has become evident for some reason, though [previously] hidden — that is <s>Vyājokti</s>. He explains: 'Where the concealed,' and so on. '<s>Vah-svantara-prakṣepa</s>' (casting another matter in between) is the etymology. '<s>Śailendra</s>' (king of mountains): '<s>Pratipādyamānā</s>' means 'being given [in marriage].' The word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.) [implies] trembling and shaking. '<s>Vidhivyasaṅga</s>' means 'capacity for action.' [She is] seen by the mountain's inner quarters — the circle of mothers — and by the attendants. He connects: 'Here, the horripilation,' and so on. To resolve the impropriety, he says: 'Although,' and so on. 'Mere denial is [the intent]' — the meaning is that since the [subsequent] smiling self-confession again reveals [the truth], the concealment should not be considered [as a separate figure] from the perspective of <s>Lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary meaning). '<s>Ullekha</s>' means proclamation. He anticipates an over-extension: 'But is this not <s>Apahnuti</s> (Denial)?' The other type, 'similarity for the purpose of denial' — is of that nature. He resolves: 'True,' and so on. 'There, <s>Tathokti</s> (Such-saying)' follows the doctrine of <s>Udbhaṭa</s>. In that view, since a pretextual description is not described, such a [type of] <s>Apahnuti</s> is possible.

body.text: vakroktyarthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: The definition for <s>Vakrokti</s> (Oblique Speech):

body.text: anyathoktasya vākyasya kākuśleṣābhyāṃ anyathā yojanaṃ vakroktiḥ || 77 ||
body.translated_text: <s>Vakrokti</s> (Oblique Speech) is the reinterpretation of a statement uttered [with one intention] in another way, through <s>Kāku</s> (tonal intonation) or <s>Śleṣa</s> (paronomasia). // <s>RuAss</s>_77 //

body.text:
ekābhiprāyeṇoktasya vākyasya kākuśleṣābhyāṃ anyathābhiprāyeṇa yojanaṃ vakroktiḥ /
sasaṅgatikaṃ vyācaṣṭe-uktivyapadeśeti /
guruparatatreti /
dūrataraṃ gantumudyata iti nāyikoktirasau /
guruparatantratayā asau guruparatā samaye 'smin naiṣyati na neṣyatīti kākugarbhasakhyuktiḥ /
yojayati-etadvākyamiti /
nanu gamanavidhiniṣedhau śābdau /
tasmādramananiṣedhavidhiryojitau /
ata āha-kākuvaśetir /
idṛśi viṣaye kākorniṣedhadyotakatvāt viparītārthasaṃkrāntiḥ /
aho keneti-dāruṇā ghorā kāṣṭhena ca /
yojayati-atreti /
tvaṃ hālāhaleti /
hālāhalavān mūrchrāṃ karoṣīti devī /

children.translated_text: <s>Pāśakāḥ</s> means dice.

children.text: nanu vicchittirūpatvāt sarva evālaṅkāro vakroktirityata āha-vakroktīti /
children.translated_text: Since every figure has the nature of aesthetic charm (<s>Vicchitti</s>), all figures would be <s>Vakrokti</s> — to prevent this [objection], he says: '<s>Vakrokti</s>,' and so on.
<s>Vakrokti</s> (Oblique Speech) is defined as the reinterpretation of a sentence in another way.
And it should be known as being of two types, through recourse to <s>Kāku</s> (tonal intonation) or <s>Śleṣa</s> (paronomasia).

body.translated_text: The reinterpretation of a sentence uttered with one intention, [now understood] with another intention, through <s>Kāku</s> (tonal intonation) or <s>Śleṣa</s> (paronomasia), is <s>Vakrokti</s>. He explains with the connection: '<s>Uktivyapadeśa</s>' (under the pretext of speech). '<s>Guruparatantra</s>' (dependent on the guru/elder): 'She has set out to go far away' — this is the heroine's statement. 'Being dependent on the elder, she will not come in this occasion' — this is the friend's statement, pregnant with <s>Kāku</s> (tonal irony). He connects: 'This sentence,' and so on. But the injunction and prohibition of going are verbal [i.e., literal]. Therefore the prohibition and injunction of enjoyment are [also literally] conjoined. To this he says: 'Through the force of <s>Kāku</s>.' In such a domain, since <s>Kāku</s> (intonation) indicates the opposite [of negation], there is a transfer to the opposite meaning. '<s>Aho kena</s>' (Oh, by whom!): '<s>Dāruṇā</s>' means both 'terrible' and 'made of wood (<s>Kāṣṭha</s>).' He connects: 'Here,' and so on. '<s>Tvaṃ hālāhala</s>' (You are <s>Hālāhala</s> [poison]!): 'You who possess <s>Hālāhala</s>, you cause swooning!' — says the Goddess. But the God [replies]: 'I do not bear <s>Hālā</s> (liquor) nor <s>Hala</s> (a plough). What is this talk of <s>Hala</s>-possession? You are a ploughman (<s>Hālika</s>)!' — the Goddess [retorts] again. 'For one capable of driving oxen, being a ploughman is indeed true!' Here, '<s>Hālāhala</s>' involves a <s>Śleṣa</s> (pun) with word-division. '<s>Vijaya</s>' (Victory): the sentence is in <s>Kulaka</s> (linked verse) form. '<s>Vijaye</s>' is the Goddess's address to her companion <s>Vijayā</s>. In the God's speech: 'I am capable in the matter of conquering passion [<s>Jitvaratā</s>]. But I am not three-eyed — because [I have only] two eyes.' The word <s>Akṣa</s> means 'dice' [or 'eye']. '<s>Kiṃ me</s>' (What to me?): the Goddess says: 'If you have no use for <s>Durodara</s> (dice-play/pot-bellied one), let <s>Gaṇapati</s> depart!' The Goddess says: 'Who hates <s>Vināyaka</s> (Gaṇeśa/obstacle-remover)?' The God says: '<s>Ahiloka</s>' (the serpent-world)! Here <s>Vināyaka</s> [means] <s>Garuḍa</s> [the serpent's enemy]. '<s>Candra</s>' (Moon): by the seizure of the moon (<s>Candragrahaṇa</s>), 'without the moon-wager (<s>Indupaṇa</s>), I do not enjoy' — says the Goddess. The God [replies]: 'If you desire a moon-eclipse (<s>Candragrahaṇa</s>), let <s>Rāhu</s> be summoned.' '<s>Hā Rāhau</s>' (Alas, <s>Rāhu</s>!): 'When <s>Rāhu</s> is present, alas, who cares about enjoyment (<s>Rati</s>)?' — says the Goddess. The God [replies]: 'Let the necklace of serpents (<s>Hārāraga</s>) be removed.' '<s>Vasturahitena</s>' (devoid of substance): '<s>Vasu</s>' means both 'wealth' and 'the eight <s>Vasus</s>.' '<s>Āropayasi</s>' (you place upon): '<s>Aṅka</s>' means both 'stigma/marking' and 'lap.' '<s>Iti kṛta-Paśupati</s>' (thus done by <s>Paśupati</s>).

body.translated_text: The definition for <s>Svabhāvokti</s> (Natural Description):

body.text: sūkṣmavastusvabhāvasya yathāvadvarṇanaṃ svabhāvoktiḥ || 78 ||
body.translated_text: <s>Svabhāvokti</s> (Natural Description) is the accurate description of the subtle nature of a thing as it really is. // <s>RuAss</s>_78 //

children.translated_text: Of what [further] kind? Her gaze like that of a one-tusked elephant (<s>Ākekara</s>), delighted by the pleasure of [her] breast-plate pressing against her back.
<s>Svabhāvokti</s> (Natural Description) is the description of the natural essence of a thing, to be perceived by the discerning.
Now, through the variety of cognition, by determining degrees of vividness,
<s>Bhāvika</s> (Evocative), <s>Dūradurlakṣa</s> (Difficult-to-perceive-at-a-distance), and <s>Vyakta</s> (Manifest) are explained in sequence.

body.translated_text: The perfect description of the nature [of a thing] that falls within the scope of the poet's creative vision is <s>Svabhāvokti</s>. He explains: 'Here, of the thing,' and so on. 'Therefore' — because it is perceivable only by poets. It is as if created by the poet. The word '<s>Ukti</s>' (speech) [in the compound] denotes [the act of] utterance. By this [figure], he will describe the distinguishing feature of its connection — he says: '<s>Bhāvika</s>' (Evocative). '<s>Huṅkāra</s>' (the sound 'Hum!'): when the slender lady removes the itch [caused by her] hair falling [on her back], the 'Hum!' would adorn [even] the ears of the fortunate. Of what kind? With the tip of her nail shaped like a bird's beak, the scratching — marked by that — adorned with a hissing sound (<s>Sītkāra</s>).

body.translated_text: <s>Bhāvika</s> (Evocative) is making the past or future appear as if present before the eyes. // <s>RuAss</s>_79 //
