children.translated_text: Whether the sentence-meaning is clear or unclear—
the instant conveyance that pervades both is the nature of <s>prasāda</s> (lucidity).
As it has been said: 'Like fire upon dry fuel, like clear water, that which suddenly',
'pervades everything else—that is <s>prasāda</s>, established everywhere.'

body.translated_text: The quality of appearing as if directly perceived (<s>pratyakṣāyamāṇatva</s>), arising from the extraordinary nature of past and future events and from their being conveyed through uncomplicated syntactic connections, is <s>bhāvika</s> (evocative). He explains: '<s>atīta</s>' etc. '<s>Kavigata</s>'—the reflection of the poet's imaginative experience (<s>kavibhāva</s>) in the listener's mind is <s>bhāvika</s>—such is the meaning. '<s>Bhāvo va</s>'—<s>bhāvi</s> (future) [provides the etymology of] <s>bhāvika</s>, because its vital principle lies solely in <s>bhāvanā</s> (imaginative realization). An alternative etymology: 'it (<s>sa</s>) exists here'—<s>bhāvikam</s> follows as a continuation. Now, in the forthcoming example '<s>munir jayati</s>' (the sage conquers), will the direct perceptibility of the past and future not be considered a delusion?—to address this he says '<s>na ca iyam</s>' etc. The idea is: when the past and future become directly perceived precisely as past and future, what delusion is there? Now, when the past and future are manifested as past and future, is that not merely a factual narration?—to address this he says '<s>nāpi rāmo 'bhūd</s>' etc. In a mere factual narration like '<s>Rāma</s> existed,' there is no quality of appearing as directly perceived. But here there is the apprehension of vivid direct perceptibility. Nor is this <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole) through the determination of direct perceptibility—to address this he says '<s>nāpīyam</s>' etc. The reason for that: '<s>anyasyānyatayā</s>'—for in <s>atiśayokti</s>, one thing is determined as another; but here that is not the case. In the past and the future and in direct perceptibility, there is no determination of otherness. He demonstrates this: '<s>na hi bhūtabhāvī</s>' etc. The past is not determined as non-past, nor the future as non-future. The reverse too does not exist—he says '<s>abhūtabhāviva</s>' etc. And the direct perceptibility here—is that too not determined otherwise?—he says '<s>na cāpi</s>' etc. The reverse too does not exist—he says '<s>apratyakṣaṃ va</s>' etc. Now, the appearing-as-directly-perceived of the past and future which are not directly perceived—is that not a determination otherwise (<s>anyathādhyavasāya</s>)?—to address this he says '<s>na hi pratyakṣatvam</s>' etc. If direct perceptibility were merely a property of the thing, then the past and future would be non-perceptible, while only the present would be perceptible—such would be the arrangement. But direct perceptibility is not merely a property of the thing. What then? It is a property of the thing only in relation to the apprehender—only with reference to the apprehender is something 'directly perceived.' For without reference to the apprehender, there is no such thing as direct perceptibility in the thing. For authoritative concordance, he says '<s>yaccadāhur</s>' etc. That entity which causes its own apprehending cognizer's cognitive illumination to follow its own presence and absence—if it itself exists, the cognitive reflection exists; if it does not exist, it does not exist—that is called <s>pratyakṣa</s> (directly perceived)—such is the meaning. Therefore, direct perceptibility is not merely a property of the thing; the equipment (<s>sāmagrī</s>) of the apprehender is also employed therein—he says '<s>kevalam</s>' etc. In an apprehender lacking the proper equipment, the thing does not become directly perceived—only this much can be said. But it cannot be said that it is independent of the apprehender—such is the idea. He analyzes that equipment: '<s>sā ca</s>' etc. In ordinary life, for directly perceiving worldly objects, when the object is beyond the senses due to obstruction by space, time, etc., for yogis the equipment is <s>bhāvanā</s> (meditative realization) in the form of one-pointed concentration. The equipment for direct realization applies the extraordinary quality pertaining to literary subject matter: [<s>sā ca</s>] etc. For extraordinary things, when held in the heart with the impression of wonder, generate such <s>bhāvanā</s>. Thus, in ordinary life the equipment for directly perceiving present objects is the eye and other senses; for yogis and those who understand the principles of poetry, it is the <s>bhāvanā</s> for directly perceiving past and future objects. Therefore, just as for yogis, the direct realization of past objects by those who understand poetic principles is not a determination otherwise—hence <s>atiśayokti</s> should not be suspected. Now, since the past and future are perceived as if directly present, would this not be suggested <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy)?—to address this he says '<s>nāpi bhūtabhāvīnām</s>' etc. The reason: '<s>tasyā abhimāna</s>' etc. <s>Abhimāna</s> means supposition; the determination in the form of 'as if it were such'—that is the definition of <s>utprekṣā</s>. But here, the non-perceptible is not supposed as perceptible. Rather, it is directly seen as perceptible. Hence it is not <s>utprekṣā</s>. He gives another indicator of its not being <s>utprekṣā</s>: '<s>nāpi vastu</s>' etc. For the meaning of '<s>iva</s>' (as if) residing in the words is the motivator of <s>upamā</s> (simile), not of <s>utprekṣā</s>. The reason: '<s>tasyā abhimāna</s>' etc. For <s>utprekṣā</s>, being of the nature of supposition, is a property of the apprehender. Therefore, only the meaning of '<s>iva</s>' that falls within the domain of supposition is the motivator of <s>utprekṣā</s>—such is the idea. For concordance, he says '<s>yadāhur</s>' etc. The meaning is: like pleasure etc., when there is supposition in the form of a property of cognition, it is called a statement of determination. Now, if determination is a property of the apprehender, then it would not belong to the poet who produces it—to address this he says '<s>kāvyaviṣaye ca</s>' etc. For the poet too, in the domain of poetry, is a sensitive reader (<s>sahṛdaya</s>). Hence this is not <s>utprekṣā</s>. Now, since from the perception of the extraordinary, direct perceptibility arises here, would this not be <s>kāvyaliṅga</s> (poetic reason)?—to address this he says '<s>nāpy atyadbhuta</s>' etc. For the direct realization of extraordinary objects is the reason for the appearing-as-directly-perceived. He gives the reason for its not being <s>kāvyaliṅga</s>: '<s>liṅgaliṅgī</s>' etc. Even though it is a reason, the cognition here does not occur through the relation of mark and thing marked. For if it were so, indirectness would follow—such is the idea. Then how does the cognition occur?—to address this he says '<s>yogivat</s>' etc. Now, the cognition accompanied by aesthetic wonder (<s>sacamatkāra</s>) caused by the extraordinary nature flashes forth as if directly before one. Therefore, would this not simply be the figure <s>rasavat</s> (endowed with <s>rasa</s>) caused by extraordinariness?—to address this he says '<s>nāpy ayam</s>' etc. The reason: '<s>ratyādī</s>' etc. Even in the regular course, the flashing forth of cognition accompanied by aesthetic wonder is common [to both]; yet there is no identity between <s>bhāvika</s> and <s>rasavat</s>. Why? Because when the mental states of love, laughter, etc., colored by them, along with <s>vibhāvas</s>, <s>anubhāvas</s>, and <s>vyabhicāri</s> states, produce a cognition that resonates with the heart through universality—setting aside particularities like 'mine' and 'my enemy's,' as one who knows the supreme non-dual knowledge does—only then does the <s>rasavat</s> nature arise. We shall analyze the <s>vibhāvas</s> etc. in the section on <s>rasavat</s>. But here, the cognition of the past and future is not through universality but through the apprehender's detached observation (<s>tāṭasthya</s>). For vividness (<s>sphuṭatā</s>) produces detachment—that is the distinction. Just as the cognition of those who know the <s>Sāṅkhya</s> and other established doctrines regarding difference does not involve universal identification. Now, the vividness of the past etc. perceived with detachment is the cause. And vivid cognition is present at the face [of the experience]; but in the culmination, it is indeed the universalized cognition. Therefore, how is it <s>bhāvika</s>?—to address this he says '<s>sphuṭapratipattī</s>' etc. The meaning is: caused by <s>bhāvika</s> which is raised by the vivid cognition arising from the vivid apprehension. For in '<s>munir jayati</s>' etc., the narrative of <s>Kumbhasambhava</s> (Agastya) etc. is first cognized with detachment, in the form of past etc.—at that very point <s>bhāvika</s> is established. Then, at a later time, when the apprehender's cognition attains the character of the <s>vibhāvas</s> etc. through universality, <s>rasavat</s> caused by <s>bhāvika</s> would follow. And this much does not permit the denial of <s>bhāvika</s>—such is the purport. Now, if the beautiful nature of the thing described here were not described, then it would not appear as directly perceived. Therefore, would this not be <s>svabhāvokti</s> (description of nature)?—to address this he says '<s>nāpīyam</s>' etc. The reason: '<s>tasyāṃ laukika</s>' etc. In <s>svabhāvokti</s>, the subtle property of worldly things alone, accessible only through the imaginative insight of the discerning, when described, resonates with the heart through universality. But here, the cognition of extraordinary, unworldly things occurs through detachment. Therefore, the non-common elements are distinguished from heart-resonance. Now, the arrangement is: when worldly things are perceived with universality, it is <s>svabhāvokti</s>; when unworldly things are perceived with vividness, it is <s>bhāvika</s>. If the perception of worldly things were vivid, what would it be?—to address this he says '<s>kvacit tu</s>' etc. Through the force of worldly things, it is <s>svabhāvokti</s>. Through the force of vivid perception, it is <s>bhāvika</s>. Therefore, there is overlap (<s>saṅkara</s>). Regarding the identity between <s>svabhāvokti</s> and <s>rasavat</s> suggested incidentally through the commonality of heart-resonance and universality, he discriminates: '<s>na ca hṛdayasaṃvāda</s>' etc. In <s>svabhāvokti</s> and <s>rasavat</s>, although there is heart-resonance through universality among the sensitive, still there is no identity between them. The reason: '<s>vastusvabhāva</s>' etc. Even though universality is common, in <s>svabhāvokti</s> the resonance is of the thing's nature; in <s>rasavat</s> it is of the mental state. When both the thing's nature and the mental state converge, there is overlap—he says '<s>ubhayasaṃvāda</s>' etc. '<s>Samāveśa</s>' means overlap. He gives the indicator for the occurrence of overlap: '<s>yatra vastugata</s>' etc. Where in a subject possessing resonance of mental states, there is description of subtle properties of things—such is the meaning. '<s>Anyatra tu</s>'—in a subject that lacks description of subtle properties of things and possesses only resonance of mental states, it is <s>rasavat</s> alone. Now, the characteristic here is that the composition conveys meaning instantly through the absence of complicated syntactic connections—and in that case, would this not simply be the quality called <s>prasāda</s> (lucidity)?—to address this he says '<s>nāpy ayaṃ śabda</s>' etc. Here, although the instant conveyance of meaning is caused by the uncomplicated nature of words, still this is not <s>prasāda</s>. The reason: '<s>tasya hi sphuṭā sphuṭa</s>' etc.

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text:
atra śuṣkendhanāgnivadityasphuṭaṃ vākyārthaṃ prasyupamoktiḥ svacchrajalavaditi sphuṭaṃ prati /
ataḥsarvatra vihita sthititvena jhaṭiti samarpaṇaṃ rūpaṃ prasādasya /
asya tu prasāde jhaṭiti samarpitasya sphuṭatvena pratītau satyāṃ samanantaraṃ svarūpapratilambhaḥ /
svarūpaṃ hi asyaśrotari kavigatabhāvapratibimbanaṃ paunaḥpunyena cetasi viniveśasvabhāvabhāvanātmakaṃ vā /
tathāvidhasya tu pratibambanaṃ sphuṭapratītyuttarakālameva /
ataḥ prasādo 'syāṅgatvena prāksiddhikaḥ /
ayaṃ tu tadupakṛta(sa)manantara(sva)siddhikaḥ /
tato 'nya eva /
ado na kutracidantarbhīva iti nigamayati-tasmādayamiti /
sarvottīrṇaḥ bhrāntyādiṣu prasādaguṇāntaraśaṅkiteṣvekatrāpi nāntarbhāvayituṃ śakya ityarthaḥ /
itthaṃ lakṣaṇato 'syanānupapattiḥ kācit /
lakṣyato 'pi prācuryamityāha-lakṣye cāyamiti /
munirjayatīti /
mananāt muniḥ /
yogīndratvānmahātmā /
svayaṃ tu kumbhasaṃbhavaḥ /
tathāvidhena yena ekasminneva culuke pipāsoddhṛtaniravaśeṣārṇavārbhbhasi prasṛtigarte divyau amānuṣānubhāvātiśayau viṣṇordaśāvatāreṣu prasiddhāpadānau matsyakacchrapau yadṛcchrayā culukāntarbhāvāt paryākulaṃ luṭhantau dṛṣṭau /
atrātītavṛtto 'pi muniḥ alaukikatvenātyadbhutaḥsannādara pratyayena hṛdi sandhāryamāṇatvāt anākulasandarbhasamarpitatvāccapratyakṣāyamāṇaḥ tathāvidhaṃ kavibhāvaṃ pratipattṝṣu pratibimbayati paunaḥpunyena cetasi bhāvanāṃ viniveśayatīti bhāvakatvam /
prācuryārthamudāharaṇāntarāṇi-yathā vā harṣacaritetyādinā /
harṣacaritaprāraṃbhe hi devīṃ sarasvatīṃ abhiśatpavate krodhamunaye kruddhānāṃ vedānāṃ svarūpam upavarṇitam /
yathā - "roṣavimuktavetrāsanairoṅkāramukharamukhairutkṣepaḍolāyamānajaṭābhārabhari tadigbhiḥ parikarabandhabhramitakṛṣṇājinapaṭacchrāyāśyāmāyamānadivasairamarṣani ḥ śvāsaḍolāpreṅkholitabrahmayokaiḥ somarasamivasvedavisaravyājena stravadbhiḥ agrihotrapavitrabhāsmasmeralalāṭapaṭṭakuśatantucīvarībhirāṣāḍhibhiḥ praharaṇīkṛtadaṇḍakamaṇḍalumaṇḍalaiḥ mūrtaiḥ caturvedairiti" /
yojanāyāha-atra hi pratyakṣamiveti /
nanu varṇānāvaśāt pratyakṣāyamāṇatvaṃ kiṃ bhāvikaviṣayaḥ āhosvidanubhāvaviśeṣātpratyakṣāyamāṇasya sato varṇanamityata āha-ayaṃ tvatretyādi /
leśa ityalpāvaśiṣṭatā āha-varṇānāvaśāditi /
bhaṇitimāhātmyamāviṣkaroti - prattayakṣāyamāṇasyaiveti /
bhaṇitimāhātmyanairapekṣyeṇa nijānubhāvaviśeṣādeva pratyakṣāyamāṇatvamanusandhatte /
anātapatro 'pīti /
atra anātapatro 'pi sitātapatrairiva vṛtatvamacāmarasyāpi bālavyajanenaivopalakṣitatvam /
anubhāvaviśeṣādeva pratyakṣāyamāṇatvaṃ varṇyate na tu varṇanāvaśātpratyakṣāyamāṇatā /
itthaṃ viṣayadvaye avasthite bhāvikam ekatraivetyāha-atra prathamaprakāreti /
na prakārāntaragocara iti yaduktaṃ tatra hetuḥ - kavisamarpitānāmiti /
ye hi kavinā pratibhayā samarpyante mukhādau candratvakamalatvādayo dharmāsteṣāmevāṅkalāratvam /
na tu paramārthataḥsanniviśiṣṭānāṃ himāṃśulāvaṇyādīnām /
ato dvitīyaprakāre pratyakṣāyamāṇatvaṃ vastusanniveśīti na bhāvikālaṅkāraḥ /
yuktyantareṇāpi draḍhayitumāha-api ca śabdānākulatetyādi /
cakārādabhūtabhāvitvādayaḥ śabdānākulatā ceti hetavo bhāmahānuśāsane udbhaṭalakṣaṇe ca anākulatvarūpaṃ yadetadvyastasambandharahitaśabdasamarpitatvaṃ pratyakṣāyamāṇātvapratipādakamuktaṃ tat kathaṃ prayojakībhavet /
vastumanniveśidharmagatatvenāpi bhāvikasaṃbhave niṣpra yojanameva syāt /
ato na dvitīyaprakāre bhāvikamiti nigamayati-tasmādvāstavamevetyādi /
atra uttare prakāre nanu vāstave 'pi saundarye laukikatayā mā bhūdvicchittiḥ /
kaveḥ kakavinibandhasya vā vaktuḥ nibandhavaśādastyeva sakalavyavahartṛgocarībhātatā durapahnavāvicchittiḥ /
tatra kuto na bhāvikamityata āha-yadi tu vāstavamapītyādinā /
yadi vastusanniveśyapi saundaryanibandhavaśāt savicchittikaṃ prāñca ācāryāḥ svabhāvoktivadalaṅkāratayā varṇayeyuḥ tadā ayamapi vāstavasaundaryaviṣayatayā samāśaṅkito bhāvikaprakāro nātīva duḥśliṣṭa eva satyāṃ sāmagyām /
ayamihāśayaḥ-yathā hi svabhāvoktiḥ vāstavasaundaryāvalambinī vastusvabhāvasaukṣmyāt sādhāraṇyena sacotanasaṃvādācca vicchittimatī varṇitā tathaiva vāstavasaundaryāvalambitayā nibandhā dvicchitti viśeṣo 'yamalaṅkāratayā varṇanīya eva /
tathā ca satibhūtabhāvitvādi sāmagrīsadbhāve 'nyakalpanāgauravādayamapi bhāvikaprakāra iti unmīlanaṃ yogyatayā suśakameva /
unmīlitā ścollekhabhāvodayasandhiśabalatādaya atiprathana svātantrye 'pi cirantanasamayavyatikramaḥ syāditi /
amumevāśayamāviścikīrṣuḥ abhiyuktasaṃvādāyāha-ataivetyādi /
bhūtabhāvinaḥ pratyakṣā iva yatra kriyante ityetāvadeva bhāvikalakṣaṇamakāri yaiḥ khalu tairaśabdānākulatvādiva lakṣaṇatvenoktam /
nāpi vā vastusanniveśinaḥ /
saundraryasyanibandhādvicchittiḥ svabhāvoktitulyanayaśālinī alaṅkāratvena prasiñjitā /
ato bhūtabhāvipratyakṣavadbhāvikalakṣaṇasya bhāvikasya śabdānākulatvavāstava saundaryāvalambenāpi bhāvikaprabhedo 'bhyanujñāyate /
yata itthaṃ svabhāvoktipratiyogitayā mīmāṃsā pravartayitavyā, ataḥ samprati saṅgatimāha--svabhāvoktyā kiñciditi /
vāstavasaundaryatvaṃ sādṛśyam /

children.translated_text: And that [similarity], considering the abundance of differences such as worldliness, subtlety, clarity, commonality, and neutrality of cognition — has been called 'somewhat' with this in mind.

children.text: satyapi sādṛśyaṃ kiñcinmātraṃ athāpi nyāyasañcārāyehāsmābhiḥ lakṣaṇamasya kṛtam /
children.translated_text: Even though the similarity is only slight, nevertheless, for the proper course of reasoning, a definition of this [<s>bhāvika</s>] has been formulated by us here.
This state of being as-if-present that belongs to past and future objects —
through the reflection of that state in the mind and through [its] establishment [there] — that is <s>bhāvika</s> (the evocative).

body.translated_text: Here, 'like a fire of dry fuel' is <s>pratyupamokti</s> (counter-simile) with respect to the unclear sentence-meaning; 'like clear water' is with respect to the clear [meaning]. Therefore, in all cases, the form of <s>prasāda</s> (clarity) is the immediate presentation through established pervasiveness. But in this [figure of] <s>bhāvika</s>, when the clearly presented has been immediately conveyed, and the cognition is clear, [there follows] the recovery of its own nature. For its own nature is the reflection of the poet's inner state (<s>bhāva</s>) in the listener, or the nature of repeated contemplation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) establishing [the impression] in the mind. Such reflection, however, occurs only after the clear cognition. Therefore <s>prasāda</s> is an auxiliary [quality] whose prior establishment [is necessary]. But this [<s>bhāvika</s>] achieves its own establishment immediately after being aided by that [<s>prasāda</s>]. Hence it is different [from <s>prasāda</s>]. Therefore it cannot be subsumed anywhere — he concludes: 'Therefore this...' 'Transcending all' — the meaning is: it cannot be subsumed even in any one of [the categories] such as <s>bhrānti</s> (illusion) etc. that are suspected of being another quality of <s>prasāda</s>. Thus, from the definition, there is no impropriety whatsoever [in this figure]. That it is also abundant in examples — he says: 'And in examples, this...' '<s>Munir jayati</s>' (The sage triumphs) — <s>muni</s> (sage) [is so called] from <s>manana</s> (contemplation). Being a lord of <s>yogins</s>, he is a great soul (<s>mahātmā</s>). He himself is 'born from a pot' (<s>Kumbhasambhava</s>, i.e., <s>Agastya</s>). By such a one, in a single sip (<s>culuka</s>), with the water of the entire ocean drawn up to quench his thirst, the two divine ones — whose marvelous deeds surpassing human power are celebrated among <s>Viṣṇu</s>'s ten incarnations — the Fish (<s>Matsya</s>) and the Tortoise (<s>Kacchrapa</s>), having accidentally entered the sip, were seen tumbling about in confusion. Here, although the sage's deed is in the past, because it is held in the heart through the conviction of wonder, being extraordinary, and because it is presented through an unconfused composition, it appears as if present — thus reflecting the poet's inner state in the recipients and establishing repeated contemplation in the mind — this is the <s>bhāvika</s> nature. Further examples for [demonstrating] abundance — he says beginning with 'As in the <s>Harṣacarita</s>...' For at the beginning of the <s>Harṣacarita</s>, when [<s>Bāṇa</s>] praises the goddess <s>Sarasvatī</s>, the form of the <s>Vedas</s> when angered by the sage of wrath [<s>Durvāsas</s>] is described. Namely: 'With rod-seats released in anger, with faces murmuring <s>Oṃkāra</s>, with the burden of matted locks tossed and swaying, with days darkened by the shadow of black antelope skins whirled in girding up, with sacred threads of <s>Brahma</s> swung on the swing of angry exhalations, dripping as if pouring <s>Soma</s> juice under the pretext of sweat, with foreheads smeared with the auspicious ash of the <s>Agnihotra</s> — their <s>kuśa</s>-grass garments [bristling], their staffs and water-vessels brandished as weapons — the four <s>Vedas</s> incarnate.' For the construction, he says: 'Here, indeed, as if directly visible...' Now, does the appearing-as-present arise from the force of description, or does the description portray what already appears present through its own special power (<s>anubhāva</s>)? To this he says beginning with 'But this, here...' The word '<s>leśa</s>' means '[only] a little remains' — he says: 'From the force of description...' He reveals the greatness of the utterance: 'Of that which appears present itself...' Without depending on the greatness of the utterance, he connects the appearing-as-present to the special power of the thing's own influence alone. '<s>Anātapatraḥ api</s>' (even without a parasol) — here, even without a parasol, the appearance of being surrounded as if by white parasols; even without a <s>cāmara</s> (fly-whisk), the appearance of being marked as if by a gentle fan. The appearing-as-present is described [as arising] from the special power of influence alone, not the appearing-as-present from the power of description. Having thus established two domains, he says <s>bhāvika</s> [applies] in the first alone: 'Here, in the first type...' The reason for what was said — that it does not belong to the other type: 'Of those presented by the poet...' For the qualities such as moon-nature, lotus-nature etc. that the poet presents [as belonging to] the face etc. through poetic intuition — it is these alone that constitute the ornament. Not the qualities such as the beauty of the cool-rayed one [moon] etc. that truly inhere [in the real moon]. Therefore, in the second type, the appearing-as-present inheres in the actual thing — and so it is not the <s>bhāvika</s> ornament. He strengthens this with another argument, beginning with 'Moreover, the non-confusion of words...' By the word 'and' [are implied] the past-and-future nature etc. The non-confusion of words — this quality of non-confusion, stated by <s>Bhāmaha</s> in his teaching and in <s>Udbhaṭa</s>'s definition as the characteristic of appearing-as-present, meaning [the thing] being presented through words free of confused connections — how could that be the efficient cause? Even with the possibility of <s>bhāvika</s> through a quality inherent in the actual thing, it would be without purpose. Therefore, he concludes that <s>bhāvika</s> does not [apply] in the second type: 'Therefore, the real alone...' Here, in the latter type, [one might say:] even in real beauty, being worldly, let there be no aesthetic charm (<s>vicchitti</s>). But because of the poet, or the poetic composition, or the speaker's composition, there indeed exists an undeniable aesthetic charm that becomes accessible to all who engage [with it]. Why then is it not <s>bhāvika</s>? To this he says, beginning with 'But if even the real...' If even the beauty inhering in actual things, through the force of composition, were described by the ancient masters as endowed with aesthetic charm, as an ornament like <s>svabhāvokti</s> (natural description) — then this type suspected of being <s>bhāvika</s> as pertaining to real beauty would not be entirely ill-fitting, given the right conditions. The import here is: just as <s>svabhāvokti</s>, depending on real beauty, has been described as possessing aesthetic charm because of the subtlety of the thing's own nature, its commonality, and its consonance with sentient experience — in the very same way, this special aesthetic charm depending on real beauty through composition deserves to be described as an ornament. And thus, given the conditions of past-and-future nature etc., without the burden of additional invention, the emergence of this <s>bhāvika</s> type is quite easily possible through aptness. And though [figures like] the juncture of <s>ullekha</s> (delineation) and <s>bhāvodaya</s> (rise of emotion) and related complexities are widely known even as independent [figures], there would be a departure from the established ancient convention. Wishing to reveal this very import, for consonance with the learned, he says: 'Hence...' Those who made only this much as the definition of <s>bhāvika</s> — 'where past and future things are made as if present' — did not state non-confusion of words etc. as part of the definition. Nor did they acknowledge the aesthetic charm through composition, equal in method to <s>svabhāvokti</s>, [arising] even from beauty inhering in real things, as an ornament. Therefore, even the <s>bhāvika</s> with the definition of making past-and-future [things] present is sanctioned as a sub-type of <s>bhāvika</s> through dependence on non-confusion of words and on real beauty. Since the investigation should be conducted in correlation with <s>svabhāvokti</s>, he now states the connection: 'With <s>svabhāvokti</s>, somewhat...' The real-beauty nature is the similarity.

children.translated_text: It is not <s>bhrānti</s> (illusion), because there is no reversal [of cognition]; nor <s>ativṛttaka</s> (the transcendent), because of directness;
nor <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole), because of no determination of otherness.
Not only for present objects is the quality of perceptibility accepted —
because, when there is no dependence on the recipient, perceptibility would be destroyed.
And the conditions for perceptibility are: contemplation, wonderfulness, and the thing itself.
Perceptibility is not merely imagined here; therefore it is not <s>utprekṣā</s> (fancy).
Because of the absence of the relationship of mark and marked, <s>kāvyaliṅga</s> (poetic reason) is not intended.
Because of the neutrality of clear cognition, there is no confusion with <s>rasavat</s> (having <s>rasa</s>) at that stage.
Afterward, in the state of universalization (<s>sādhāraṇībhāva</s>), <s>rasavat</s> is caused by that [<s>bhāvika</s>].
Because of clarity, it is not <s>svabhāvokti</s> (natural description) — since the object transcends the ordinary world.
The difference of <s>svabhāvokti</s> from <s>rasavat</s> is [due to] the difference in consonance.
And this is not the quality of <s>prasāda</s> (clarity) — for this [<s>bhāvika</s>] arises only subsequently [to <s>prasāda</s>].
Even in real beauty, this [<s>bhāvika</s>] is possible through aptness.
But out of respect for the ancients, it has not been explicitly proclaimed as such.
If anyone has an intellectual consonance with me regarding <s>bhāvika</s>,
that wise person will be the touchstone of my skill in commentary.

body.text: udāttāya sūtram-
body.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> for <s>udātta</s> (the sublime):

body.text: samṛddhi maddhastuvarṇanamudāttam || 80 ||
body.translated_text: The description of a prosperous [object] with pride is <s>udātta</s> (the sublime). // RuAss 80 //

body.text:
samṛddhimato vastunaḥ kavipratibhotthāpitaiścarya varṇanamudāttālaṅkāraḥ /
sasaṅgatikaṃ vyācaṣṭe-svabhāvoktāvityādinā /
yathāvasthitatvaṃ laukikatvam /
āropitatvaṃ kakavikalpitatvam /
ava(saraḥ) prātpiḥ /
aiśvaryalakṣitamiti lakṣyapadaniruktiḥ /
muktāḥ kelīti-visūtratā chrinnasūtratā /
saṃmārjanībhiḥ prāṅkāṇāsīmni kṛtāḥ yatkarṣantīti vākyārthaparāmarśaḥ /
yadetatkarṣaṇaṃ tattyāgalīlāyitamityarthaḥ /
udāttaṃ tu samṛddhasya vastunaḥ kavivarṇanam /
udāttāntarāya sūtram-
body.translated_text: The description, born from the poet's intuition, of the magnificence of a prosperous object — that is the <s>udātta</s> ornament. He explains with the connection, beginning with 'In <s>svabhāvokti</s>...' 'As-it-is-ness' means worldliness. 'Being superimposed' means being invented by the poet. '<s>Avasara</s>' means 'obtainment.' 'Characterized by sovereignty' — this is the etymological analysis of the term to be defined. '<s>Muktāḥ kelī</s>' (pearls released in play) — 'unstrung' means having the thread broken. 'The sweeping-women, at the threshold of the harem, drag [the pearls] that were placed [there]' — this is the paraphrase of the sentence. 'That which is the dragging — that has the playfulness of discarding' — this is the meaning. '<s>Udātta</s> is the poet's description of a prosperous object.' The <s>sūtra</s> for another [type of] <s>udātta</s>:

body.text: aṅgabhūtamahāpuruṣacaritañca || 81 ||
body.translated_text: And the narrative of a great person that serves as an auxiliary [to the main subject]. // RuAss 81 //

body.text:
pūrvamaiśvaryayoga udāttatvam /
iha punaścaritasya udāttatvam /
ataḥśabdasāmyātsaṅgatiḥ /
tadetadāha-udāttaśabdetyādi /
tadidamiti-atrāraṇyaṃ tadvṛttāntaḥ pātādaṅgī, yadvṛttāntaḥpātāt rāmacaritamaṅgam /
tadetadāha-atrāraṇya iti /
asya ceha kīrtanaṃ darśanāntarānusāreṇa /

children.translated_text: But in the <s>Dhvani</s> school, in the domain of the second <s>udātta</s>, <s>rasavat</s> (having <s>rasa</s>) etc. alone [apply].
And this will be discriminated [later].
A narrative of great deeds that has become an auxiliary in the context of another principal subject —
the domain of the second <s>udātta</s> is covered by <s>rasavat</s> etc.

body.translated_text: Previously, the <s>udātta</s> nature [was defined] through the presence of sovereignty. Here, however, the <s>udātta</s> nature belongs to the narrative [itself]. Therefore the connection is through the similarity of the term. He states this: 'The word <s>udātta</s>...' 'That is this' — here the forest [scene] and its narrative are the principal (<s>aṅgin</s>), and the narrative of <s>Rāma</s>'s deeds is the auxiliary (<s>aṅga</s>). He states this: 'Here, the forest...' And its mention here follows another school of thought.

body.text: rasavadādyarthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> for <s>rasavat</s> etc.:

body.text: rasabhāvatadābhāsatatpraśamānāṃ nibandhe rasavatpreyaūrjasvasamāhitāni || 82 ||
body.translated_text: In the composition of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment), <s>bhāva</s> (transitory emotion), their semblances, and their subsidence — [the ornaments are respectively] <s>rasavat</s>, <s>preyas</s>, <s>ūrjasvin</s>, and <s>samāhita</s>. // RuAss 82 //

body.text:
vibhāvādibhiḥ abhivyañjitoratyādibhāvo rasaḥ /
tathā vibhāvānubhāvaiḥ sūcitā vyabhicāriṇaḥ devatāviṣayā ratiśca bhāvaḥ /
tāvevāviṣayapravṛttāvābhāsau /
prayāsyadavasthā tu praśamaḥ /
eṣāṃ caturṇāmupanibandhe paripāṭyā rasavān preyaḥ ūrjasvi samāhitamiti alaṅkārā iti sūtrārthaḥ /
sasaṅgatikaṃ vyācaṣṭe-udātte mahāpuruṣetyādinā /
tadalaṅkārāṇāṃ cittavṛttivicchittyātmanāmalaṅkārāṇāmityarthaḥ /
ata eveti /
yataśvatvāro 'pi cittavṛttyātmānaḥ ataḥsamānayogakṣematayā yugapadekasūtrakroḍīkāreṇa lakṣitāḥ /
rasasvarūpaṃ vivecayati-tatra vibhāveti /
ratihāsaśokādīnāṃ vāsanātmanāṃ sthāyibhāvānāṃ yāni loke kāryakāraṇasahakārīṇi tāni kāvye sandṛbdhāni nāṭye cābhinītāni guṇālaṅkāramahimnā caturvidhābhinayamahimnā ca vibhāvanā danubhāvanādviśiṣyābhimukhyacaraṇācca vibhāvānubhāvavyabhicāriṇā uccante /
taiḥ prakāśito vyañcito ratyādiḥ sāmājikacittavṛttiviśeṣaḥ śṛṅgārādiko rasa iti dik /
viśeṣaḥ sampradāyaprakāśinyādau jñeyam /
ihānupayogānna prapañcyate /
bhāvasvarūpamāha-bhāvo vibhāvetyādi /
vibhāvānubhāvābhyāmiti /
vyabhicārivyañjane vyabhicāryantarābhāvovyañjitaḥ /
vibhāvānubhāvābhyāṃ vyañjito vyabhicāri vākyārthībhāvadaśāyāṃ bhāva ucyate /
so 'pi trayastriṃśadbhedaḥ /
nirvedaglānyādirūpatayā /

children.text: tathā kāntāvyatirikte devatādiviṣaye vyañjito ratyādirapi bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Similarly, love (<s>rati</s>) etc. manifested with respect to deities and [other objects] other than the beloved is also <s>bhāva</s>.
Therefore, <s>bhāva</s>, having the nature of both <s>vyabhicārin</s> (transitory emotion) and <s>sthāyin</s> (permanent emotion), should be understood as having two kinds.
As it is said: 'Love directed toward deities and transitory emotion thus manifested —'
'— is called <s>bhāva</s>...'

body.translated_text: The state of love (<s>rati</s>) etc. evoked by <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants) etc. is <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment). Similarly, the transitory emotions (<s>vyabhicārins</s>) indicated by <s>vibhāvas</s> and <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents), and love directed toward deities — that is <s>bhāva</s> (transitory emotion). Those very [states], when occurring in an improper domain, are semblances (<s>ābhāsas</s>). And the state of subsidence is <s>praśama</s>. In the composition of these four, in order, [the ornaments are] <s>rasavat</s>, <s>preyas</s>, <s>ūrjasvin</s>, and <s>samāhita</s> — thus [they are] ornaments. This is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>. He explains with the connection, beginning with 'In <s>udātta</s>, of a great person...' 'Of those ornaments' means 'of ornaments that have the nature of mental modifications producing aesthetic charm' — this is the meaning. 'Hence' — since all four have the nature of mental modifications, therefore they have been defined simultaneously in a single <s>sūtra</s> through having the same interest. He discriminates the nature of <s>rasa</s>: 'There, <s>vibhāva</s>...' The causes, effects, and co-factors in the real world of the permanent emotions (<s>sthāyibhāvas</s>) such as love, laughter, grief etc. — which have the nature of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) — when composed in poetry and enacted in drama, through the power of qualities and ornaments, and through the power of the four types of acting, [they function as] <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants), <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents), and <s>vyabhicārins</s> (transitory emotions) — so called from [the process of] making [something] experienced (<s>vibhāvanā</s>), making [it] followed (<s>anubhāvanā</s>), and especially approaching [it] (<s>abhimukhyacaraṇa</s>). The state of love etc. — the specific mental modification of the audience — manifested and suggested by these — that is <s>rasa</s> such as <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic) etc. This is the general direction. The details should be learned from the <s>Sampradāyaprakāśinī</s> etc. They are not elaborated here due to irrelevance. He states the nature of <s>bhāva</s>: '<s>Bhāva</s>, by <s>vibhāva</s>...' 'By <s>vibhāva</s> and <s>anubhāva</s>' — the transitory emotion indicated [by them], in the absence of other transitory emotions to reveal [it]. The transitory emotion manifested by <s>vibhāvas</s> and <s>anubhāvas</s>, in the state of becoming the sentence-meaning, is called <s>bhāva</s>. It too has thirty-three varieties — in the forms of <s>nirveda</s> (world-weariness), <s>glāni</s> (languor), etc.

body.text:
ābhāsayoḥsvarūpamāha-tadābhāso rasetyādi /
tacchabdena rasabhāvapratyavamarśaḥ /
ābhāsībhāvastu aviṣayapravṛttyānaucityāt /
bhāvapraśamasvarūpamāha-tatpraśama uktetyādi /
uktabhāvaprakārāṇāṃ nivṛttau prayāsyadavasthā bhāvapraśama ucyate /
nanu rase 'pi praśamaḥ kiṃ nocyate ityata āha-tatrāpītyādi /
rasasya hi akhaṇḍanirantarāyapratīti carvaṇīyasya paramaviśrāntirūpatvāt madhye prayāsya davasthā durlakṣyeti rasavyatiriktapariśiṣṭabhedaviṣayo 'yaṃ praśamo draṣṭavyaḥ /
eṣāṃ ca rasabhāvādīnāmupanibandhe paripāṭyā rasavadādayo 'laṅkārāḥ /
catvāryapi lakṣyapadāni nirvakti-raso vidyata ityādinā /
yatra hi vyañjanopaskṛte 'rbhidhādivyāpārātmani nibandhe raso 'sti tadrasavat /
priyataranibandhanameva preyojñeyam /
ūrjo balaṃ tadyoginibandhanameva ūrjasvi /
nanu nibandhane balaṃ nāma kimityata āha-anaucityeti /
rasasyānaucityena pravṛttatvāt daurbalyam /
nibandhane tu tadupakṛte balayogaḥ /
samāhitaḥ parihāraḥ /
kasya? prakṛtatvāduktasya bhāvabhedasya yasya praśama ityapi paryāyaḥ /
nanu rasavadādinā dvitāyodāttasya ca kā kakṣyetyata āha-tatra yasminnityādi /
yatra hi bhāmahādidarśane vākyārthībhāvāt pradhānabhūtā eva rasādayo rasavadādyalaṅkārāḥ tatra aṅgabhūtarasādiviṣaya upapadyate /
kalpo(?)dvitīya udāttālaṅkāraḥ /
yasmiṃmastu rasavadādiralaṅkāro aṅgabhūtarasādiviṣaya eva aṅginastu rasāderalaṅkāryabhāvāpannasya rasabhāvādidhvanirūpatayā vyātpatvāt tatra dhava nidarśane dvitīyasyāṅgabhūtamahāpuruṣacaritalakṣaṇasyodāttālaṅkārasya viṣayo nāvaśiṣyate /
kuta ityata āha-tadviṣayasyeti /
iyamiha prakriyā /
yatra rasādayo vākyār(thī)bhūtāḥ tatra rasavadādayo 'laṅkārā ityalaṅkāramātrarasikānāṃ bhāmahādīnāṃ darśane /
yadā tu avākyārthībhāvādaṅgabhūto rasādiḥ, tadāṅgabhūtamahāpuruṣacaritalakṣaṇo dvitīya udātta upapadyate nāma /
dhvanidarśane tu kāvyātmano rasādeḥ prādhānyadaśāyāṃ alaṅkāryatvādalaṅkārabhāvānupapattau aṅgabhūtā rasādayo rasavadādyalaṅkārāḥ /
tathā ca sati rasabhāvādināyakamahāpuruṣacaritāvirbhāvo 'pi rasabhāvādyaṅgabhāvānatirekī vyaṅgyavyañjakamanbandhāt /
vyañjakaṃ hi mahāpuruṣacaritam /
vyaṅgyaṃ rasabhāvādi /
vyaṅgyabhāvāvinābhūtāṅgabhāvaṃ rasavadalaṅkārasyaiva viṣayaḥ /
vyañjakamātra viśrāntānāṃ anavagāḍhadhiyāṃ dvitīyodāttabhrama iti /
kiṃ hāsyeneti-svapnadṛṣṭa nāyakaṃ svarūpasandarśananihnavaparihāsapravṛttaṃ manyamānasya ripustrījanasyoktivarṇanam /
kiṃ hāsyena cirātprātpraḥsan punarme darśanaṃ na prayāsyasi? niṣkaruṇatā taveyaṃ prātpisamakālameva pravāsarucitā ityudīrayannevatamadṛṣṭvā "kenāsi dūrīkṛtaḥ"iti vadan vyāsaktakaṇṭhagraho buddhvā riktabāhulayacastāraṃ roditīti /
atrāṅgāṅginau dvāvapi rasāvaṅgī rasaḥ /
rasavān matāntare /
svamate tvaṅgabhūto rasavān /
ata udāharaṇametanmatadvayārham /
tadetadabhisandhāyāha-etanmatadvaye 'pīti /
tadetadvibhajya darśayitumāha-atra vākyārthībhūta iti /
vākyārthībhāvāt karuṇe rasavān /
matāntara iti śeṣaḥ /
aṅgabhāvādvipralaṃbhaśṛṅgāro rasavān /
asmanmata iti śeṣaḥ /
evaṃvidhe hi viṣaye vākyārthībhāvāt aṅginaṃ rasaṃ rasavantamanye pratipedire /
aṅgibhūtaṃ tu dvitatīyodāttam /
dhvanidarśanavidastu aṅgino alaṅkāryatāṃ aṅgibhūtasya rasavadādirūpatāṃ dvitīyodāttāsaṃbhavaṃ ca siddhāntitavantaḥ /
iyaṃ ca prakriyā rasāntareṣvapi jñeyetyāha-evaṃ rasāntareṣviti /
udāhāryaṃ udāhartumarhaṃ śakyam /
prātpakālatā vodāharaṇasya /
arhe śakye prātpakālatāyāṃ ca kṛtyaḥ /
itthaṃ rasavadalaṅkāre matadvayaṃ kakṣyānibhāgenodāhṛtam /
preyo 'laṅkārādau tu viśeṣāṃśastu jñāta iti sādhāraṇyenodāhīrṣurāha-preyo 'laṅkārādāviti /
gāḍhāliṅganeti /
mānada mānakhaṇḍana māmetyardhoktyā bhāvāvasānaharṣaḥ pratyāyyate /
lakṣyayodajanāyāha-atra niyikāyā iti /
harṣākhyo vyabhicāribhāvaḥ sambhogaśṛṅgāraṃprati guṇātvāt preyo 'laṅkāra iti śeṣaḥ /
vyabhicāribhāvaḥ sambhogaśṛṅgāraṃprati guṇātvāt preyo 'laṅkāra iti śeṣaḥ /
vyabhicāryantarāyodāharati-tadvaktreti /
atra cintālakṣaṇovyabhicārī vipralaṃbhaśṛṅgārāṅgatayā preyān /
tadetadāha-atra cintākhyā iti /
alaṅkārāntarabhramau mā bhūdeti paryāyamasyāha-eṣa eva ceti /
preyān bhāvālaṅkāraśceti paryāyau /
bhāvaśāntyudayādibhyo 'sya bhedamāha-bhāvasya cātreti /
sthitirūpatāyāṃ bhāvālaṅkāraḥ /
śāntyudayādyavasthā tu pṛthagalaṅkārā iti bhāvaḥ /
kau tau śāntyudayāviti ata āha-śāntyudayeti /
śāntyavasthā ūrjasvī samanantaraṃ samāhitatvena vakṣyate /
udayāvasthā tu sandhiśabalatābhyāṃ saha pṛthagalaṅkāratvenetyarthaḥ /
dūrākarṣaṇeti /
kālakalāmapi nāvasthitiṃ prakurute /
atra vipralambhaśṛṅgāro 'naucityena pravṛttaḥ devyāḥsītāyā aviṣayatvād /
ato rasaṃ guṇīkṛtya nibandhanameva balāditi ūrjasvī /
autsukyavyabhicāriṇo 'pyanaucityāt preyo 'laṅkārasaṅkaraḥ /
tadetadabhipretyāha-atra rāvaṇasyetyādi /
śāntyavasthā lakṣyata iti pratijñātamudājihīrṣurāha-samāhitaṃ yatheti /
akṣṇoriti /
utkṣubhitenāśruṇā paryāvilo 'ruṇimā cakṣuṣorapagata ityādinā roṣāpagamaḥ /
kaṭākṣavilāsatārakātāralyādyanāvirbhāvāt prasarāpradānam /

children.translated_text: Therefore he says that the state of subsiding belongs to anger—"atra kopasya" etc.
Thus he states that quiescence should be understood in other <s>vyabhicāri</s> (transitory emotions) as well—"evam anyatrāpi" etc.
From the subordination of <s>rasa</s> and <s>bhāva</s>, and from engagement due to impropriety,
the fourfold group of <s>rasavat</s> (possessing rasa), <s>preyas</s> (the charming), <s>ūrjasvin</s> (the vigorous), and <s>samāhita</s> (the tranquil) arises.

body.translated_text: He states the nature of the two semblances—"tadābhāso rase" etc. The word "tat" refers to <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment) and <s>bhāva</s> (emotion). The semblance-status arises from impropriety due to engagement in an inappropriate domain. He states the nature of <s>bhāva-praśama</s> (quiescence of emotion)—

children.translated_text: By virtue of possessing rasa and charm, by connection with vigor and quiescence,
the basis acquires the designation <s>rasavat</s> and so forth.

body.text: bhāvodayādyarthaṃ sūtram-
body.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> for <s>bhāvodaya</s> (rise of emotion) and the rest:

body.text: bhāvodayasandhiśabalatāśca pṛthagalaṅkārāḥ || 83 ||
body.translated_text: <s>Bhāvodaya</s> (rise of emotion), <s>sandhi</s> (conjunction of emotions), and <s>śabalatā</s> (variegation) are each separate <s>alaṃkāras</s> (figures). // RuAss 83 //

body.text:
uktasarvālaṅkārānyatvāt sarvālaṅkāraśeṣatayautat trayoktiḥ /
pṛthagrasavadādiviviktaviṣayatayetyarthaḥ /
vyācaṣṭe-bhāvasyāṅkurarūpetyādi /
aṅkurarūpasyodgamadaśodayaḥ /
viruddhayoḥ tulyakakṣyatayā viniveśanaṃ sandhiḥ /
pūrvapūrvopamardena bahūnāmuttarottaranibandhaḥśabalatā /
pṛthakpratipādane hetumāha-etatpratipādanaṃ ceti /
kevalālaṅkāratvātsaṃsṛṣṭisaṃkaravailakṣaṇyam /
tayoḥ sampṛktatvaṃ svarūpamityāha-saṃsṛṣṭisaṃkarayorhīti /
ekasminniti-vipakṣanāmagrahaṇaṃ glapitatve, glapitatvamāvege, āvego 'vadhīraṇe,, avadhīraṇaṃ priyatamatūṣṇīṃbhāve, tūṣṇīṃbhāvastu punarvīkṣaṇe hetuḥ /
atrautsukyaṃ bhāvasyodayaḥ tasya ca guṇabhāva iha vivakṣaṇīyaḥ /
vāmena nārīti /
vāmena kareṇa priyatamāyā nayanāśrudhārāṃ dakṣiṇīna kṛpāṇādhārāṃ pramārjayan kartavyamūḍho 'bhūdityatthaḥ /
atra ratibhāvaraṇautsukyayoḥ sandhiḥ /
tadetadāha-atra snehākhya iti /
snehagrahaṇādṛte śṛṅgārasthāyitāmāha bhāvisthāyitve (bhāvaḥ, asyayitve?) tu ratiḥ prītimātram /
kkākāryamiti /
atra kkākāryaṃ kva ca śaśalakṣmaṇaḥ kulamiti vitarkaḥ /
bhūyo 'pi dṛśyeta sā iti autsukyam /
śrutaṃ doṣapraśamāyeti matiḥ /
aho kope 'pi mukhaṃ kāntamiti smṛtiḥ /
kiṃ vakṣyantyapakalmaṣā iti śaṅkā /
svapne 'pi durlabheti dainyam /
cetaḥ svāsthyaṃ upehīti dhṛtiḥ /
ko dhanyo 'dharaṃ pāsyatīti cintā /
atrottarottareṣāṃ pūrvapūrvopamardena avasthānāt śabalatā /

children.translated_text: He states that very thing—"atra vitarka" etc.
He concludes these—"tat etat" etc.
Like <s>sthiti</s> (continuance) and <s>praśama</s> (quiescence), the rise of <s>bhāva</s>, its conjunction,
and its variegation, when subordinated, each constitutes a separate embellishment.

body.translated_text: Since they are different from all previously stated figures, the mention of those three is as supplements to all figures. "Separately" means because they have distinct domains like <s>rasavat</s> and so forth. He explains—"bhāvasyāṅkurarūpa" etc. The sprout-form—

body.text:
saṅkarasaṃsṛṣṭī prastuṣṭūṣurāha-adhunā eṣāmiti /
saṃśleṣaḥsambandhaḥ /
tasyadvaividhyamāha-tatra saṃśleṣa ityādi /
bhedakoṭerudbhaṭatāyāṃ saṃyoganyāyaḥ anutkaṭatve tu samavāyanyāyaḥ /
dṛṣṭāntena nyāyabhedamavasthāpayati-tilataṇḍulanyāyaḥ kṣīranīrasādṛśyamiti ca /
ubhayamapi paripāṭyā sūtrayitumāha-krameṇeti /
body.translated_text: Wishing to discuss <s>saṅkara</s> (mixture) and <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination), he says—"adhunā eṣām" etc. <s>Saṃśleṣa</s> means connection. He states its twofold nature—"tatra saṃśleṣa" etc. When the aspect of distinction is prominent, the principle of conjunction—

body.text: eṣāṃ tilataṇḍulanyāyena miśratdhe saṃsṛṣṭiḥ || 84 ||
body.translated_text: When these are mixed according to the principle of sesame and rice grains, it is <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination). // RuAss 84 //

children.translated_text: Therefore this combination with jingling is, by the process of elimination, what adorns the <s>upamā</s> (simile).
He concludes—"tat evam" etc.
<s>Saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination) is considered to be conjunction according to the principle of sesame and rice grains.
It is considered threefold through figures pertaining to sound, meaning, and both.

body.translated_text: He explains—"uktālaṅkārāṇām" etc. Those figures from <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration) up to <s>bhāva-śabalatā</s> (variegation of emotion) that have been stated separately—if in some domain they occur together according to possibility, then are they—

body.text: saṃkaram upakṣipati-adhunetyādi /
body.translated_text: He introduces <s>saṅkara</s> (mixture)—"adhunā" etc.

body.text: kṣīranīranyāyena saṅkaraḥ || 85 ||
body.translated_text: <s>Saṅkara</s> (mixture) operates according to the principle of milk and water. // RuAss 85 //

children.translated_text: Being a figure of sound constitutes homogeneity of kind.

children.text: udbhāṭaprakāśitastu prakārāntaragocaraśabdārthālaṅkārasaṃkaraḥ saṃsṛṣṭau antarbhāvita iti tasya saṃkaratvamaṅgāṅgibhāva evoktamityāha-śabdārthālaṅkāretyādi /
children.translated_text: However, the <s>saṅkara</s> (mixture) of figures of sound and sense as presented by <s>Udbhaṭa</s>, which pertains to another category, has been subsumed under <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination); therefore its status as mixture is simply the relation of principal and subordinate—thus he says: "śabdārthālaṅkāra" etc.
Through the relation of principal and subordinate, through doubt, and through inclusion in a single expression,
<s>saṅkara</s> (mixture) is threefold; the mixture of figures of sound in a single expression—

body.translated_text: He recalls the governing topic—"miśratvam eva" etc. He restates the nature of <s>saṅkara</s> (mixture) that has been discussed—"anutkaṭa" etc. For the threefold classification thereof he says—"tat ca" etc. Through the relation of principal and subordinate, through doubt, and through inclusion in a single expression—

body.text:

nanu śabdādyalaṅkāratve ko doṣa ityata āha-tadalaṅkāratvaprayojakatva iti /
śrautopamādau śabdānvayavyatirekānuvidhānāt śabdālaṅkāratvaṃ prasajet /

children.translated_text: He concludes: 'therefore, the basis and what is based...' etc.
The disclosure of agreement regarding what has been stated at length.
The placement of terms, the object of examination, the arrangement of difficult meanings, the profound discussion that reveals the insights of the learned —

children.text: itthaṃ bhūmrā rucakavacasāṃ vistaraḥ karkaśo 'yaṃ ṭīkāsmābhiḥ samuparacitānena sañjīvanīyam //
children.translated_text: Thus, by the abundance of polished expressions, this extensive commentary, though rough, has been composed by us as a <s>Sañjīvanī</s> (life-restoring elixir) — through this commentary.

body.translated_text:
He explains: 'thus...' etc.
Therein, regarding the semblance of repetition (<s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s>) — it concerns the repetition of meaning.
<s>Chekavṛtti</s> (clever expression) and <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration) concern consonants alone.
<s>Yamaka</s> (rhyme) concerns the combination of vowels and consonants.
<s>Lāṭānuprāsa</s> (Lāṭa-type alliteration) concerns both word and meaning — thus a fivefold group pertains to repetition.
<s>Citra</s> (variegated composition) concerns the non-repetition of position-specific, closely-joined syllables.
Now, regarding the aesthetic charm of similarity, in the identity-difference-equality of resemblance: <s>upamā</s> (simile), <s>anvaya</s> (connection), <s>upameya-upamā</s> (comparison of the object), and <s>smaraṇa</s> (remembrance).
When non-difference predominates, based on superimposition: <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor), <s>pariṇāma</s> (transformation), <s>sandeha</s> (doubt), <s>bhrāntimat</s> (delusion), <s>ullekha</s> (multiple perception), and <s>apahnuti</s> (denial).
Based on determination: <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) and <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole).
Based on implied similarity: <s>tulyayogitā</s> (equal connection), <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination), <s>prativastūpamā</s> (counterpart simile), <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (illustration), <s>nidarśanā</s> (exemplification), <s>avyatireka</s> (non-distinction), <s>sahokti</s> (co-expression), and <s>vinokti</s> (expression of separation).
Through the aesthetic charm of the qualifier: <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression) and <s>parikara</s> (retinue).
Through the aesthetic charm of both qualifier and qualified: <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia).
When the contextual is understood from the non-contextual: <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant).
Through the relation of universal-particular etc., the establishment of the stated subject: <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s> (corroboration).
When the intended meaning is expressed through an indirect mode: <s>paryāyokta</s> (periphrasis).
When praise conveys blame, or blame conveys praise: <s>vyājastuti</s> (ironic praise).
In contextual matters, when there is a semblance of negation of a desired meaning, or a semblance of enjoining an undesired one: <s>ākṣepa</s> (objection).
Containing contradiction: <s>virodha</s> (contradiction), <s>vibhāvanā</s> (poetic causation), <s>viśeṣokti</s> (emphatic statement), and <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole) — among these, the figures involving mutual distinction, conflict, and duality: <s>saṅgati</s> (congruence), <s>viṣama</s> (incongruity), <s>sama</s> (parity), <s>vicitra</s> (variegation), <s>adhika</s> (excess), <s>anyonya</s> (reciprocal), <s>viśeṣa</s> (distinction), and <s>vyāghāta</s> (conflict) — both types.
Through the aesthetic charm of chain-linkage: <s>kāraṇamālā</s> (chain of causes), <s>ekāvalī</s> (single string), <s>mālādīpaka</s> (garland illumination), and <s>sāra</s> (essence).
By the logic of reasoning: <s>kāvyaliṅga</s> (poetic reason) and <s>anumāna</s> (inference).
By sentence-logic: <s>yathāsaṅkhya</s> (sequential correlation), <s>paryāya</s> (alternation), <s>parivṛtti</s> (reversal), <s>parisaṅkhyā</s> (restriction), <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), <s>vikalpa</s> (option), <s>samuccaya</s> (accumulation), and <s>samādhi</s> (adjustment).
By worldly convention: <s>pratyanīka</s> (confrontation), <s>pratīpa</s> (reversed simile), <s>nimīlita</s> (concealment), <s>sāmānya</s> (generality), <s>tadguṇa</s> (acquiring another's quality), <s>atadguṇa</s> (not acquiring quality), and <s>uttara</s> (rejoinder).
When the meaning is concealed: <s>sūkṣma</s> (subtle), <s>vyājokti</s> (pretextual speech), <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique speech), and <s>svabhāvokti</s> (natural description).
When the meaning is manifest: <s>bhāvika</s> (evocative).
With sublimity: the two types of <s>udātta</s> (the elevated).
Based on mental states: <s>rasavat</s> (endowed with rasa), <s>preyas</s> (the charming), <s>ūrjasvin</s> (the vigorous), <s>samāhita</s> (the tranquil), <s>bhāvodaya</s> (rise of emotion), <s>sandhi</s> (conjunction), and <s>śabalatva</s> (variegation) — these are the pure figures.
As mixed figures: <s>saṅkara</s> (mixture) and <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination).
With this intention he says: 'thus...' etc.
The review of the previously stated method: 'these...' etc.
'The exposition of the nature of what has been undertaken' — this is the reference.
He distinguishes the figures of sound, meaning, and both, group by group: 'there, the figures of sound...' etc.
'<s>Lāṭānuprāsa</s> and the rest...' etc.
He unpacks the remaining ones: '<s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> and <s>saṅkara</s>...' etc.
Now, since through positive and negative concomitance the established classification would be broken — to address this he says: 'as in ordinary usage, the basis and what is based...' etc.
'That which is to be adorned' — by the word 'that,' there is reference to sound, meaning, and both.
And this has been discussed in the section on <s>śleṣa</s>.
Then where do positive and negative concomitance find their ground? — to address this he says: 'the positive and negative concomitance...' etc.
When the figures have the nature of effects of sound etc., the positive and negative concomitance of sound, non-sound, etc. is the ground for that classification.
Now, what fault is there in classifying them as figures of sound etc.? — to address this he says: 'the productive cause of that figure-status...' etc.
In cases like <s>śrautopamā</s> (heard simile) etc., because positive and negative concomitance follows sound, the status of being a figure of sound would undesirably follow.

children.translated_text: May the accomplished ones, the experts in the secrets of poetry, partake of this subtle, clear examination,
supported by the reasoning of the <s>śāstra</s> (science).
In this world, the learned have the greatest reverence for the <s>Kāvyaprakāśa</s> and the <s>Alaṅkārasarvasva</s>;
therefore both have been commented upon.

body.text: ityālaṅkārikacakravartidhvaniprasthānaparamācāryakāvyamīmāṃsāprabhākarasahajasarvajñamahākaviśrīvidyācakravartiviracitāyāṃ sañjīvanyāmalaṅkārasarvasvaṭīkāyāmarthālaṅkāraprakaraṇaṃ samātpam //
body.translated_text: Thus concludes the section on figures of meaning (<s>arthālaṅkāraprakaraṇa</s>) in the <s>Sañjīvanī</s>, a commentary on the <s>Alaṅkārasarvasva</s>, composed by the illustrious <s>Vidyācakravartin</s>, the great poet who was naturally omniscient, the luminary of poetic inquiry (<s>kāvyamīmāṃsā</s>), the supreme teacher of the <s>Dhvani</s> school, the emperor among literary theorists.
